translations.text: A discourse by Titus against the Manichaeans
For all those whose concern was to dissociate God from the causes of human sins,
there was a true aim of justice in such statements—if only they had not departed from this:
that God also exercises care over us [?], and they maintained that human sins truly originate with human beings themselves.
But while wishing to cure a small matter, they were seized by a great and severe disease of impiety: they fell into denying God's providence over everything that is visible.
Now Mani, who comes from among the barbarians and whose name means “peace” when translated,
made still greater use of the harmful drug of impiety, daring to undertake to show that God is not the cause of evil.
He set evil up against him, claiming that it exists equally with him: a self-existent being, as he says, opposed to the self-existent Being, and a living being opposed to the Living One.
He says that it always stands against him and fights with him; that from eternity it has never ceased attacking him; and that it cannot be completely destroyed by him,
because it is a self-existent being from eternity and, he says, his equal in being, since, as he claims, it was not brought into existence.

It is like the saying, “While fleeing from the smoke, he fell into the fire.” For, so that God should not, he says, be considered the cause of evil, he himself, in his own person, from the whole of evil that stands as his counterpart,
must receive [?], even though, as he says, through patience and wisdom he devises a way to deal with it. Yet even so, he cannot accomplish this by his power without warfare,
as his account teaches. What could be more alien than these things to thoughts and beliefs about God? For this is the concern of the first discourse
of the catholic Church: that it is just and right to confess with all our strength that God is not the cause of human sins. But in this inquiry,
into how we sin when God does not will it, we do not, like that man, accuse God of greater things
when we wish to vent our anger on him over small matters. Rather, on the very path of truth, drawing on the holy Scriptures and on commonly held ideas,
and on commonly held ideas, we proceed toward this inquiry, carefully restraining ourselves, since, as lovers of truth, we hold ourselves to account.
We offer a demonstration of God's justice instead of venting our anger on him. For it is not right that, to escape through our argument from the blame
for the wrongs we commit against one another, we should speak impiously against God and invent things about him that are utterly disgraceful and do not exist.
Along with these considerations, we also believe that human sins can be healed,
and do not flow from another, opposing ruling power, but are committed by us in another manner. Our discourse will explain this clearly at the appropriate time.
And not only do we avoid speaking impiously against God by not daring to invent a weakness in him
that amounts to blasphemy, and to say that he has an adversary—evil, which has no such existence—but we also devise ways to deal with the things we do that take the form of evil,

so that we may bring them to a halt and put an end to them. Through this it becomes clear to those who look attentively that sinful actions truly have their beginning in us, and also receive their end from us,
so that they cease to exist, even if this is not the case with everyone. For what belongs to everyone is not seen in each individual [?].
But it is clear to anyone who pays attention. This, then, is everyone's experience, which can be observed in each individual.
That impious barbarian, then, devised a scheme and invented a beginningless evil opposed to God, who alone is truly without beginning; and in his madness he called this the rule of two principles.
And he not only placed evil on an equal footing with God, thus honoring it—
he who claimed to hate it—but also said that the evils flowing from this beginningless evil are necessarily incurable. And, to deceive people, he induced those persuaded by him

to believe that their wrongdoing and sins admit of neither correction nor healing, and henceforth, in anticipation of relief from sins, [?] to bring upon themselves an expectation of uncertainty instead of repentance, on the grounds that the course of evil, which is beginningless, can no longer
be restrained—unless someone, out of a desire for praise, supposes that through his diligence he has gained a greater victory,
so that he can overcome sins. And from this it is clearly apparent that he was not sinning because of some other source, but from himself and within himself.

Yet those who suppose that he is virtuous by nature because of his constitution deprive him even of genuine praise—the very man who expected to be praised, although he acted not by nature but through labor and sweat.
And they abandoned the genuine praise that belongs to the labor of virtue when it is undertaken in righteousness for God's sake.
They falsely seized it for themselves by positing in their minds the compulsion of nature. And through love of the labor he performed, they contrived impiety against God.
Consequently, even someone who is always contemptuous and negligent would no longer reproach himself in his mind for his evil deeds,
if he supposed that his deeds were attributed to another principle, that of evil. Nor would someone who exercised great diligence deserve admiration when he acted deliberately.
And besides all these things, the gravest of all is that his disciples are trained and brought up in impiety against God.
Because they did not understand the convincing account concerning God's creatures, they not only questioned and went astray concerning people's evil deeds in the manner already described,
but also blamed and accused most created things—that is, all these things that admit of no blame at all—and called them evil.
Some of them, they say, consist of a mixture of opposites, of good and evil, while others, they say, consist of evil in a single form.
They spoke falsely, and on their own authority entangled and confused everything, calling evil those things that are never evil at all.
For if their argument had condemned only wrongdoing and human sins, which alone are evil,

they ought even then to have been careful both about the name of evil and about their conception of it: how it exists and how it does not exist, since through action it exists and through action it does not exist.
And they ought not to have introduced another principle opposed to God. Yet their folly in this would have been comparatively slight.
But now, by insulting the whole creation, they have committed great and grave blasphemy against God.
And they strive through their argument to persuade people that all animals and all creeping things are unquestionably evil, and that they ought not to have come from the good God—
creatures which, as they supposed, were not merely useless but, they say, even harmful to human beings.
Yet it is possible to show that they are exceedingly helpful and more useful than those things that are truly considered beneficial to human beings.

And they string together many other arguments to blame and insult both created things and the providence and governance over everything. But our discourse leaves none of these things, whether already stated or still to be stated, without explanation and demonstration.
For they suppose that a mixture of two opposing natures exists in creation.
And they divide created things between these natures however they please. For they say, “Where do evil things come from?”—to these natures [?].
For they say, “Where do evil things come from, unless they too come from another first principle?” And if someone asks them what these things are…
They string together both human sins and God’s creatures, and they also revile this whole providential order, full of every kind of wisdom.
Thus, if someone demonstrates that everything came into being and continues to exist well, [?], and necessarily,
their tale about an opposing first principle is inevitably nullified and destroyed. For because they did not understand how the things below exist,
they invented stories about the things above. And because they did not grasp how visible things are arranged, they maligned what is invisible.
And when they tried to learn [?] what they did not know, they were caught in great ignorance. For they investigated visible things as though in the darkness of ignorance.
And not only did they fail to find what they thought they were seeking, but they also stirred up the darkness of their ignorance, making it greater.
But let us first take up and discuss those two opposing first principles and kingdoms that they posit.
Then let us turn to the demonstration concerning all created things and show that they all exist well and excellently, as I said before,
especially those against which they spoke and which they reviled, claiming that they are undoubtedly evil. Then we will also discuss providence,
which governs everything. Although they also speak against it bitterly and maliciously, accusing and condemning it, we will show that it is excellent and glorious providence. And not only this, but
also concerning human sins and wrongdoing: it is not right, even on their account, rashly to invent another first principle of evil opposed to God. For this too
can be demonstrated: even these very things reveal the goodness of our Maker. They are not committed by human beings according to his will, nor do they flow from another opposing first principle
to harm us. And now we should turn to the beginning of their impious tale, asking whether the common thoughts and understandings inherent in our nature admit
two opposing first principles and kingdoms. For if not even two that are in harmony are admissible, how much less shall we admit those that are in conflict and opposition?
Now that wicked madman Mani writes, and everywhere he begins like this: “There existed God and also matter, light and also darkness, good and also evil.
They are completely opposed in everything, and neither has anything at all in common with the other. They exist without having come into being, and both are alive.”
Now let him himself tell us whether the two are separate from one another, or whether they exist together. If they exist together, they are found to be friends
and are never seen to be opposed. But clearly he too says that they are separate from one another. Consequently, each of them is limited
in its being by the other, and neither of them is infinite and without boundary. But to limit and circumscribe God in his being,
rather than acknowledge him and confess that he is infinite—how is this not utterly impious?

He not only thought and said that God is limited and circumscribed in his being, but even dared to say that this happens to him through evil and that he is limited by it. This is, first of all, outside the common understanding and thoughts inherent in our nature,
which enable us to know that he exists everywhere and that his nature cannot be contained, circumscribed, or limited by anything.
And again, if these two self-existent beings are necessarily distant from one another,
not only is God himself bounded and limited, according to that man's account, but he also exists in his own place, and [?] resembles his opposite.
For those who are kept apart from one another are completely enclosed and confined within their own places. And now you must ask whether these beings are older than their places—
both of these opposites, as self-existent beings that never came into being. And if this is so, there was once a time when they already existed on equal terms, far removed from opposition.
But if, from eternity, the separation of each also existed along with its being, then the place of each either precedes its being or exists together with it.
But if their places precede them, so that they are considered to be in their [?] and to be the offspring of those places themselves, then these are not self-existent beings.

Nor are they eternal [?]. And it seems that existence belongs to their places, since these beings derive their existence from them. But if the places coexist with them, then they have many self-existent beings,
and not merely two. For they are necessarily distinct: they themselves are different from the places in which they exist, without which they cannot even exist.

Along with those places, his argument also requires boundaries for both beings, restraining and confining each one from contact with its counterpart, lest at their extremities they mingle with one another and destroy the claim that they are opposites.

What, then, is there that restrains and confines them both? Thus the fabrication of their stories requires yet another, a third, self-existent being. And will they perhaps tell us of a wall of adamant,
or something else, as though, in a moment of madness and through the care of that one—whichever it is that they mean—it was placed between them?
For whichever of those opposites they wish to attribute this to—that subsequently, at a later time, through its care, this
boundary came in and was placed between them—their account proves open to doubt. For when the argument is taken back to the beginning, to antiquity and primordial existence,
it becomes apparent again that those beings which were opposites were not separate,

and were not opposites. But if they say that what they call the boundary did not come into being and was not placed there through the care of one of them, then another self-existent being is again necessarily

admitted and introduced, which [?] shares anything in its being with one of those opposites, so that, being foreign to them in every respect, it may separate them from one another. Thus they turn out, in their madness, to posit a whole multitude of self-existent beings, although only two
self-existent beings were said by them to exist. This boundary, then, which restrains them, whether it is a wall or a desolate land
that is uninhabited, or anything else they wish—where exactly does it have its base and foundation, and where exactly does its top reach?
But plainly its base is below. Yet where exactly, and how far? And its top is above,
but where exactly, and how far? For ‘above’ and ‘below’ are terms belonging to created things; they did not exist before created things.
Consequently, this boundary would have to extend lower and rise higher than the being of those whom it separates, lest either below or above
it fall short and give those opposites room to pass into one another.
But if they compare what they call the boundary to shadow and sunlight,
supposing in their error that shadow has nothing in common with sunlight, they are convicted of having gone grievously astray after that madman.
For shadow is connected with sunlight, and it comes into being [?] through the arrival of sunlight, when a solid body stands between and prevents it from spreading to the other side.
So a shadow is nothing else [?] but a sign of light being blocked by a thick body situated in between. For at night, when there is no light,
no shadow occurs either [?]. Consequently, wherever there is a shadow, there is also light.
For the things beyond the shadow shine in the light itself. But if what casts the shadow and produces it is not very high,

the illuminating light passes over it. Even if it is that wall of theirs, which they ludicrously said stands in between, evil is clearly found dwelling in the light. For how can there be a shadow when all the light is above matter?

There must instead be something in between that blocks and confines all of it. And when what stands in between is not very high, and the light passes over it, evil has continual fellowship [?] with the light.

Again, they assign the southern region to evil, and, as though dreaming, they mark out and divide the places of creation before they are created. For where was the south before the south came into being?
Nor was there any other place in creation inferior to its neighbor. For the things on the left of someone facing west are on his right when he turns and looks east.
But there is great error and folly in this barbarous teaching. For how can there be two first principles, or how can they be called that?
For a first principle is what is older than everything and precedes everything, holding and ruling everything.
Yet, according to their claim, this description does not apply to either of them. For they say that both are of equal age and that they are self-existent beings.
According to their claim, neither has any precedence by which it is prior to the other. Moreover, as regards primacy and authority over one another,
as opposites they are not only entirely deprived of these, but they also fight by their very natures. How, then, do they have any basis for being considered first principles?

But if the definition of a first principle does not truly apply to either of them, how are they called by the name of first principle? And how, moreover, can natural thoughts and conceptions accept that there are two things

opposed in their very being? For when, in the first place, even the name of being belongs equally to them [?], then, first of all, since both are said to be self-existent beings, it is clear that they agree with one another in this
and are not opposed. Then there is also this: both, they say, are alive. Again, they say that they are equal in this respect, that their existence did not come into being.
Since their names are identical, and the distinguishing mark by which they are known is identical, how can their being be opposed and in conflict?
For names are the indicators of the things themselves: they show what each individual thing is,
insofar as it can be known. Consequently, we know from this that the meaning of names consists in the things themselves.
Consequently, if both those opposites imagined by the mad Mani are called being, life, and self-existent beings that never came into existence,
is it not clear that this error originated among barbarians? For in his teaching he corrupts the order of conceptions and common reasoning.

For, according to their claim, the designation and name of both are entirely equal and identical. This statement not only excludes every conception of opposition, but does not even allow any distinction to be found between the things so named.
For they say that one is good and the other evil.
To put it one way, those who rushed into error with that madman undertake to speak of likeness and shadow before being itself.
Yet being is equally predicated of both. Those who rushed into error with that madman undertake to speak of being.

Yet being is equally predicated of both. For they call both being, life, and self-existent beings that never came into existence. Consequently, the claim that they have opposing likenesses is superfluous. For although it is not proper to apply the term likeness to God,
But it is in thought that we consider it in this way: that his being is prior to his being such as he is.

For “he is” indicates existence and life, and corresponds to “he came into being.” But they will not wish to say that something [?] occurred afterward and was received, so that the two would be opposites. This is [?].

Without limit. For nothing occurred afterward in that being which did not come into existence. His being did not happen to him [?], nor did his being such as he is; and something that he was not did not happen to him.
Opposing qualities, then, can be found in all the things that exist in the world, but an opposing substance is found nowhere.
For white is the opposite of black, and both exist in bodies, in their very substance. In one respect they are indeed opposites of one another.
And in another respect they are not opposites. First, they belong to a single kind, for both are colors. Then, although they seem to be opposites,
they nevertheless offer sight a mixture of pleasures of various kinds. For neither of them, in its proper measure, distresses the sight.
But they are also designated as belonging to a single kind, for both are [?]. They also happen to arise afterward in the soul, and for this reason they can also cease to exist.

These very things cease when the soul in which they exist becomes different at another time. From this it is clear that the account of substance is distinct, and the account of the things that occur in it is another.
Afterward, although white and black exist and are not separated from the things in which they exist, nevertheless, even so, no one ever names them after the things in which they exist. For

when someone wishes to speak of milk, does he not prefer to use the name given to the substance’s distinctive character rather than “whiteness,” so that he will not seem to be naming many things in which whiteness exists instead of one?
Moreover, we do not call a raven “blackness,” but use the name proper to the animal and its kind. These qualities, then,
and others like them are not separated from that in which they exist. But virtue and wickedness in the soul are qualities that arise in it afterward.
Since this is so, it is all the more fitting that a human being’s substance should never be thought to be identified and described from these qualities. Nor should this alone be stated.

For no one ever, if asked what a human being is, from the wickedness in a person—no one ever, if asked what a human being is, names and describes it from the wickedness in a person. Rather, first he states the distinctive character of the person’s substance; then he names who he is.
And finally he speaks about his condition. Thus, as I said before, one can find opposing qualities among these lower things, some separable and some inseparable.
But as for God, every quality is far removed from him, because none of the things by which he is named is something other than him, outside him.
For he is simple, not composite. Nevertheless, in terms of human thought,
as we said earlier, his being is prior to his being such as he is. For this reason we speak in accordance with those earlier statements:
if both those of whom they say that they are opposites are substances and beings that did not come into existence—
for they do not deny this—then surely both are good, so that we should more properly give them this honorable name, as justice requires.
For he who exists is good in his very being alone. And the opposition of which we spoke is found never to exist.
For we do not turn the argument back against them by saying that both are evil. For the being that did not come into existence
is perfectly good. And if God is a being that came into existence,

he is perfectly good. And if God is a being that did not come into existence, is this very fact that he did not come into existence something evil for him? Or is it not so, but clearly something good?
And what, indeed, is this division, when the thing is one and the same, and the name is one and the same, yet in the case of God it is good

and beautiful, while in the case of evil, as they say, it is an evil opposite? For distinction is found among things that have come into being, but distinction is not opposition. But in being that has not come into being, what distinction can anyone find?
Much less can an opposite be found in it. For this reason it is altogether impossible for one self-existent being to be the opposite of another self-existent being.
For if it is to be an opposite, nothing should exist in it, or be named in it, as in its opposite, so that it may have nothing at all in common with its opposite.
For if it is not completely opposite in every respect, then in whatever respect it shares something with its opposite, it is found not to be an opposite.
For an opposite is something that exists in opposition to something that does not exist. Yet perhaps not even this is so, for they are not in conflict.
But what exists cannot be the opposite of what exists. If, then, what exists agrees with what exists, that which exists is one, and it alone is truly self-existent. It is the source of everything

and grants them existence.

14. They themselves also say that matter ought to be called the opposite of God in every respect.
Thus they say, “If we call God light, let us call what is opposite to him darkness. And if we call him good,
let us call it evil.” If, then, we call God the truth, it is clear that what is opposite to him is called falsehood.
How, then, can what exists, as they suppose, be falsehood? For it is what does not exist
that becomes a falsehood if it is said to exist. But that which truly exists,
if it really exists, is true by the very fact that it exists, and is not falsehood. For if it is said to exist, it is true. But if it is not said to exist, so that it will not be true,
neither is it said not to exist, so that it might be false. But even if someone says that it does not exist,
he lies by this very device: it is not falsehood, for in its being it truly exists.
And now, after these things, if they call the Good indestructible, they call evil destruction. But whose destroyer, then, is this destruction?
For it cannot be the destroyer of the Good. But if evil destroys itself, then in this long stretch of time from eternity it would have destroyed itself.
And they vainly imagine that it exists, as though in a mirage. But how can it, being destruction, be destructive of itself?
For it always destroys something else. It would be destructive of itself. For it always destroys something else, not itself.
But if it destroys itself, it would not have endured even from the beginning. For it would have been all the more prompt in destroying
itself before its own existence. For destruction, with regard to what is indestructible—as ordinary reasoning teaches—
cannot be thought to destroy it. Therefore the self-existent being is entirely indestructible and everlasting. Consequently, it is not death either, for being is above indestructible things.

But if matter possesses this greater thing—that it did not come into being but has existed from eternity—how can it not also possess the lesser thing, namely, not being destroyed? But if it is indestructible,
as something everlasting, it is not destructive of itself either, and its being cannot be destructible.
Whenever, then, those who are Mani’s disciples hear statements like these,
When they found themselves in doubt, my lords, they asked, “Where, then, do evils come from?”
“And where,” they ask, “does this disorder that appears in things come from?” But it was also said a little earlier that, because of their ignorance, they did not understand the ordering of things
and divine providence [?], and acquired for themselves a knowledge of error and blasphemy. In their ignorance they imagined that they knew—a knowledge worse than ignorance.
They truly lost what they were seeking before they even sought it. But our discussion will address this in its proper time.
And concerning this apparent disorder of things, when God grants it to us, our discussion will show that it is an excellent and wonderful order. And also concerning this apparent
disorder of things in their eyes, when God grants it to us, our discussion will show that it is an excellent and wonderful order. It will also demonstrate, concerning the things they call evils,
that some of them exist only as actions, while the rest—not one of them exists as a substance.
[?] For now, however, after what has been said, let us relate the things Mani says against God.
For there was, he says, as he puts it, a time in eternity when matter was in turmoil. It was giving birth, growing, and acting [?].
It was producing many powers. Then, he says, as it grew, it rose upward without knowing that the Good One existed. And when, he says, it rose still higher,
it saw, he says, the land and the light of the Good One, and eagerly sought to enter what did not belong to it. The Good One himself, he says, sent his power, which he names as he pleases,
supposedly to guard the boundaries, but actually to act as a deceiver, so that matter would be humbled and brought into order against its will.
And this is what happened. For when matter saw the power that had been sent, he says, it seized it with an intense desire of love.
With great eagerness it took it and swallowed it, and became entangled with it like a serpent being bound. For he also uses this illustration: as though by an incantation, he says, through that power

which had been sent, matter was put to sleep. And thus, he says, the blending and mingling took place in this way: of that power which had been swallowed, which came from the Good One, and of matter, which had swallowed it.
And so, he says, this whole world was created from the two of them, from the Good One [?]. For evil, he says, could not devise the world's coming into being.
And hence, as he says, some things are good and some evil. The blending and mingling of the two, he says, can be seen and recognized from the opposition between things here.
And he says that the soul belongs entirely to the Good One's portion, while the physical body and flesh come from matter. Sometimes, he says, it holds the soul as though in a prison,
and sometimes it is held by the soul, like a serpent held by an incantation. And thus, he says, matter was outwitted
by the Good One himself, who became the maker of the world, although he had no intention [?] of making the world. For, he says, it stood opposed to him.
But because of evil's arrogance, he says, wishing to discipline it, he devised this plan, since he could not remove the bitterness of evil from visible things.
And that this bitterness of evil persisted, he says, is evident from the very disorder of things. From this, as he supposed, it follows that there is no equality among human beings,
since one, he says, is rich and another poor, one honored and another despised, and other things of this kind.
But the Good One's plan and providential care, he says, consist in this: to free the soul from evil and to draw it up, by whatever means,
from matter. This, he says, happens through the moon, when it grows full and when it wanes, as we suppose it visibly does.
For truly, he says, as he puts it, the moon is filled like a pitcher from that power which holds smoke.
And it supplies this to its good kindred being. Although he did not say it in those very words, this is what he meant to say.
These things have been stated by us very modestly and decorously. For in his account there is great confusion, without any convincing explanation.
And how many other tales he writes down, like an old woman, using the Aramaic language!
How, he says, the earth is carried, in the manner of the poets’ tales; and where the rains come from, which, he says, are the sweat of the rulers of matter.
It is therefore unnecessary for us to bring these fabrications and others like them to [?]. For he hid his writings and placed
them in darkness, because he feared the refutation that would arise from them against them. Yet it is right that the things he writes at any moment about every subject should be known, even if [?].

We should not be drawn into undertaking to prolong our discussion against the emptiness of his mad discourse, because even the beginning of his mad and ignorant teaching is enough to expose and discredit his other claims.
For indeed, were it not for the discussion of God’s providence over everything, which has been taken up and included in this account,
in which it is right to see that everything is ordered justly and divinely, and which points to God’s inexpressible wisdom,
it would have been ridiculous for us even to consider those words spoken in madness worthy of an answer.
They were gathered together and spoken outside ordinary reasoning, and to the wise their refutation lies in themselves and comes from themselves.

And this would have been enough, since we have shown at considerable length that two principles [?], especially opposing ones, cannot possibly have existed from eternity, for us to proceed to his account of humanity and the rest of creation.
Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from again [?] showing that these things spoken in madness have no convincing explanation.
For matter, he says, as he puts it, was once in turmoil. What, then, was its turmoil? Was it in turmoil within itself,
or against something else? For any injustice directed entirely toward oneself is not [?]; rather, it requires another to be its opponent.
So this matter, which, he says, had no other [?] association—against whom was it in turmoil? And what, then, was the form of its turmoil?
Or what was the explanation of its confusion? For it was giving birth, he says, [?] entirely toward itself. It is not injustice; rather, it requires another to be its opponent.
So this matter, which, he says, had no association with anything else—against whom was it in turmoil? And what, then, was the form of its turmoil?

Or what was the explanation of its confusion? For at first, he says, as he puts it, it was giving birth, increasing, and growing. It must therefore have been giving birth continuously, at all times, from eternity.
For it must be one of two things: either it was doing this deliberately, of its own will, and had control over its will, or it was giving birth under the compulsion of its nature.
And there was no time when its nature did not compel it to give birth. But they deprive it of both sensation and knowledge, and say that its nature is without knowledge.
If, then, under the compulsion of nature it had been intent on this growth and increase from eternity—as someone might say that a mountain has existed from eternity—from the time when it ceased

until now, it is now evident that for myriads of times the duration of eternity [?], it, which exists eternally, had been giving birth. Hence there is no room for anything new to arise, since it is eternal.
For either renewal takes place in it by nature, and it has never ceased from this renewal—if it is right to call this renewal.
So that it should never have a beginning in time. As for renewal and a change opposed to it, coming from the Good [?]. Or if it was knowingly that this
deed was being done, it has knowledge, and that argument is invalidated—the claim that evil is without knowledge. So whether knowingly or unknowingly, it was advancing and growing

and rising up. What convincing argument is there that throughout those eternal ages, those limitless times, it neglected to grow and rise up? For from the time when it was restrained, as he said, until now is only a moment of time,
if compared with those limitless times stretching back into eternity. For this period during which it has been restrained is bounded by a beginning and an end.
Those times, however, are entirely without limit, since they extend back into eternity. Again, if it was knowingly becoming evil in order to rise up,
how did it not recognize, through that very knowledge, that it could not prevail and had no means of advancing and conquering that unconquerable wisdom?
For this reason they avoid admitting that it has thought and knowledge, so that there may be room for their fabrication about evil’s rising up against
God, and so that it would be driven as if under compulsion, without knowledge, by a nature without thought, and would not wait to arm itself over the limitless ages of eternity
and equip itself with forces, so that it could easily carry out its insolent attack. For even if it multiplied through those offspring it was bearing,
nevertheless, the impulse of its nature did not grow, nor was anything added to it through the movement of its nature.
Nor would it wait first to grow and then to rise up. For this belongs to a will that knowingly does evil.
And how, then, was it being made complete in evil through the very beings it bore? It was not complete in its wickedness,
nor did it possess the fullness of evil. But if it was complete and possessed fullness in evil, it was not complete in its wickedness,
nor did it possess the fullness of evil. But if it was complete and possessed fullness in evil, as they claim, the two claims contradict one another.
And it is never plausible that evil was growing through its offspring. Nor was it acquiring courage, since it is without knowledge. Nor was it leading those offspring of its to its assistance.
For if it was being made complete in evil through the very beings it bore, it was not complete in its wickedness, nor did it possess the fullness of evil.
But if it was complete and possessed fullness in evil, as they claim, the two claims contradict one another.

And it is never plausible that evil was growing through its offspring. Nor was it acquiring courage, since it is without knowledge. Nor was it leading those offspring that came from it to its assistance.
For it seems that before it gave birth, evil was incomplete not only in its wickedness,
but also in its power and activity—something foreign to a self-existent being.
He also recounts the manner of its activities. He says that those who were being born from it used to pursue and devour one another,
and do bitter and cruel things to one another. At first, he says, they were not restrained from rising up against one another,
as he says in his own account, until later they saw the light. For while they were being pursued by one another, he says, they did not know.
Nevertheless, he says, they dared even to ascend to the light. What could be as unconvincing as this,
or as much like something in a ridiculous story: that those who have one mother and are bound by their natural kinship and [?]
They will rage against one another to no purpose and eat one another’s limbs. They will never stop doing this, and they will be destroyed by one another.
And that madman ignorantly calls it confusion and disorder, to no purpose—

something that is actually beneficial. For he especially calls this the confusion and disorder of evil, which, he says, existed before the world. He describes matter this way as though he were distressed and felt sorry for it,
as though, he says, it were unjust for it to be destroyed by its own action. Like a friend of its own, he is distressed and grieved over what it was itself suffering.
He calls what it was doing for its own benefit disorder. This ought to have been called an excellent arrangement: evil being destroyed by its own action.
He said that they were in turmoil and were pursuing one another, but when they saw the light, they left one another alone.
Then that light actually harmed what was beneficial, if it rescued those evil beings from the harm they were doing one another.

Like a physician’s medicine, it helped those who were sick. Yet it was not fitting for the good to pity evil in this way, so that it should remain, be preserved, and not destroy itself. For if he restrained it and put it in order so that it would not ruin and destroy itself,
he is plainly its protector. And this truly constitutes confusion and disorder: what he says restrained its disorder.
He therefore says, and records in his own account and book, that while they were in turmoil against one another,

they approached the boundary and saw the light—a beautiful and wonderful sight, he says. Then, prompted by the agitation within them, in their madness they also took counsel together against the light, considering what

they should do to be able to mingle themselves with its excellence. They were unable, he says, to think this through or understand it. Rather, in the desire with which they desired its excellence, they thought it would become
their prey. And because they were numerous, he says, they gathered against it to fight. The madman has forgotten how he is testifying to these excellent and good qualities in those offspring of evil.

For if they saw what was excellent and beautiful and loved it, and in their desire thought that it would become their prey, it is clear that this expectation and intention of theirs was upright and good.
And again, he says that those who had no knowledge took counsel about how to mingle themselves with the light. Consequently, it is envy not to allow
these beings to enjoy the good light that appeared to them. Indeed, there is no limit at all to this madman’s folly, for he says that they were in turmoil against one another.
Then they ought to have been left alone to be destroyed by one another. Or, if they desired the good light like discerning beings,
he ought to have allowed them to enjoy it, just as the madman represents them in his book, saying that they desired and loved it. For they were wholly incapable of harming it.
For it is so completely good that it cannot be destroyed or otherwise harmed by those who share in it.
“They all gathered together,” he says, “and fought.” But how, when they did not know the one who opposed them? For their own book, from which these tales of Mani’s madness
are related, says that they did not even know that God dwelt in the light. Nor could they venture against God’s dwelling and withdraw unharmed.
If, then, they had absolutely no knowledge of the one opposing them who was restraining them, how could they gather and fight against someone they did not know

was restraining them? For, as he said, “The waters were arming themselves with fire and darkness” [?], if they had known beforehand that they were being restrained by things that were not their own. But since they had no knowledge at all,

this statement is not merely unconvincing; it also plainly contradicts itself. For he writes that they were arming themselves and gathering for battle against someone whom they did not expect at all to be opposing them. This is no small

self-contradiction in his statement: at one time he says that they intensely desired the light, and at another he admits that these same beings made preparations for war against it. For everyone who fights against an opponent puts on weapons of war.
And not against the one whom he desired in love, as though for victory. If, then, he did not exist, how did the one who stood against them not know them? How was it not
a contradiction for them to desire what they were going to fight against? And how, indeed, does this not contradict itself still further: that if those who had never been at peace with one another

in matters belonging to their nature agreed and made peace with one another in matters outside their nature—for, as he said, “Together they took counsel against the light.” And those who were one another’s limbs [?]—for, as he said, “Together they took counsel against the light.”
And those who used to eat one another’s limbs had never even ceased their madness against one another.
How, in matters outside their nature, did they make peace with one another, united in desire and in anger against that superior being?

But if the sight of the light benefited them, should they not have accepted, as from something good, a complete transformation of their nature, by consenting to the delight of the light’s excellence? And how
did the sight of the light that appeared to them benefit those who gathered to fight against the light, those whose madness, which had until then been directed against one another with justification,
was restrained and turned unjustly against the one they desired? But great is the foolishness and madness in these fabrications, and [?] they are also seen in another way to contradict themselves.
For they speak of the land of the Good One. And what, then, is this land that belongs to [?]? For before this mad Mani acknowledged
that God made things, he said that something existed when it had not yet come into being. For if the land came into being, it exists.
But if it exists without having come into being, it is another self-existent being alongside God. And why did God need land, when he made no use of it?
But foolishly and without understanding, he speaks of land before explaining its coming into being. For it is not even possible to testify to its existence before creation.
Then again, there is also this: this perceptible light, which is seen through the senses, is a work of God. God, however, is intelligible light that cannot be seen, and he is not perceptible
or visible. So, he says, evil saw the light of the Good One. But if it saw this visible and perceptible light, the world did not yet exist,
and the world had not yet come into being. How, then, did it see something that had not yet come into being? Whom did that light serve?
For whatever comes into being for someone’s use is of the same kind as the one who uses it. It was not useful to God, who is exalted above all participation in the senses.
But if it saw [?] God himself, who is intelligible light that cannot be seen, then it saw one like itself because it resembled him in nature.
For this reason, then, it must have seen this visible light. But that thing whose use is through the senses—before the senses existed and without the senses,
why did it exist? Yet how can darkness see light? For if it saw the light, it can no longer be darkness.
For desire has a close connection with what is perceptible. By nature, [?] falls upon what it sees, because it is like the thing it sees.
And immediately it readily receives its form through the shared law of nature. For it is a body that sees a body, and whatever resembles something like itself
falls upon it. And it is impossible for something superior and exalted in its nature to be visible to the sight of a nature inferior to it. How much more is it invisible to what is opposed to it!
But if something exalted in its nature, though not an opposing thing, is entirely invisible to something inferior because the former is incorporeal and the latter is a body,
how can something opposed to another see its opposite? If it sees it, surely it is of the same kind and is its friend, and is not its opposite at all.
But this barbarous fabrication of tales is full of many absurdities. For he said that matter not only saw the light, but also wanted to enter it.

Like someone concerned to show her fellowship [?], the former ages, which from eternity without limit did not know him, approached the light. And in what manner, you barbarian, does darkness desire and love light?
Or why does it want to approach this light? Is it perhaps to change its nature and become light itself? Or is it to be nourished by light, with nourishment contrary to its nature?
Unless she wanted to enter it without knowing it. Now, if she had known it, she would have had some reason for this: to be changed. But since, as he said, she is evil by nature,
and, moreover, does not know it, this whole account is completely invalidated by her failure to flee from what is opposed to her.
And this is great madness and folly: a power, he says, was sent from the Good One. It was not this perceptible light, but, as he said, God's own [?].
And when Matter saw it, he says, she loved it with desire and rushed violently upon it. She swallowed it and divided it among her powers.
She who could not even see what had been sent from the nature of the Good One—this very same being, he says, was even able to swallow it! For it is precisely this argument that
I make particular use of: if she so much as saw what flowed and came forth from God's nature, we need no other argument to demolish and invalidate this fiction.

For it appears that she saw what resembled her as something like herself. For what is permanently opposed to something by nature, and is wholly and completely contrary to it, cannot even see it or approach it—

that which is opposed to it cannot. Otherwise, the claim that they are opposites is completely invalidated, if it can so much as see it. And this further addition to the statements already made, which is more foolish than they are,
fights so vigorously against himself that no one else needs to say anything against him. For he said that Matter desired the power that appeared to her, as though she had forgotten
her nature completely. Yet it was not she, who does not exist, but this madman himself who forgot his fictions. For if, before she was stirred up, he said of her that she had no knowledge

of the Good One, so that they would not praise that nature of evil which they invented for its knowledge of the Good One, how is this not foolish: that she whose nature contained no knowledge by which to know that the Good One exists should herself
be able to see him, and after seeing him, desire him? For seeing his being directly is incomparably greater than knowing that he exists. For it is not only we,

but also those powers that are higher than the angels, who know that the Good One exists; and by this knowledge alone we are sustained in worshiping him. And it is clear that the angels, just as they are higher than we are

in nature, are also higher in knowledge. But to see God's being is permitted neither to us nor to them. Indeed, we are not permitted even to see the angels themselves, as long as we are clothed in this body belonging to our nature.
For this is clear, and everyone acknowledges it: whatever sees, sees what is like itself. But if someone, through ignorance, should suppose that this statement is weak,

saying, 'For we see the sun, the moon, and the stars, and also stones, gold, and silver, as well as the earth, the sea, and all animals, although we are not like them,' let the person who says these things learn
that although they are distinct, they are indeed those things [?]. In terms of being, however, there is that which is invisible because it is incorporeal,
and there is that which is visible because it is a body. Thus the first division distinguishes all those things as members of one class, namely, body. It is therefore a body that sees a body,

which is visible, even though their appearances differ for the adornment and [?] of the universe. For it is ridiculous to suppose that, because the gleam of gold is beautiful to look at and the appearance of ashes is not beautiful, both should not
be called colors, which is what they truly are. For both are colors, even though they differ, since [?] is shared equally by both. So too, then, all bodies that are visible,

even though they are distinct and differ in appearance—nothing prevents us from saying that some bodies are superior to other bodies—nevertheless are all bodies. Especially for this reason, neither is it worshiped
that which is seen, by that which sees it, because it comprehends it. If, then, matter saw that which comes from the being of God, because it closely resembles him and is of the same kind as he is,
she came to him. Nothing more needs to be said against this story, which has neither sense nor order. But if she desired that power which appeared to her,

that which is superior to everything, this madman himself testified about her, although he thought he had given her the name of evil, and acknowledged that she is a good being. For what greater proof is there of the beauty of goodness than this: that she should desire the Good One?
He also said about her, “She took him and swallowed him, so that she might even become pregnant from the being of the God opposed to her; and she divided him among her powers.”
What a great rebuke to this madman, who says, “Not only did she see him, but she also desired him; and not only did she desire him, but she also swallowed him; and not only did she [?],
but she also holds him.” All these things clearly undermine and invalidate the opposing natures, and most fully and emphatically acknowledge that both are of the same kind.
For if, even when she is enraged, this vision belongs to knowledge, and if, again, in her desire she swallowed the one who appeared to her, it is clear that this is a nature which has
something in common with its fellow. For if they were completely opposed, they would never agree and join one another.
Nor, again, did this barbarian consider this point concerning that power which was sent from God:
if it is without a body, it would not admit any cutting or division at all, and could never be divided in its being among those powers opposed to it.
Nor could it be swallowed. For how can something without a body be swallowed? But if it was a body, every body that is cut and severed is in some way killed
and comes to an end, and can no longer live its life. Consequently, if that power sent from the Good One was without a body, there was no possibility of its being swallowed or divided among many,
and in this way too their story is completely nullified and silenced. But if it is a body, it was cut apart and utterly destroyed by this evil, which is harsh and wicked.
This is enough to dishonor the Good One—that is, the mighty one. It is enough to nullify and dismantle their story. For what sort of body was it through which he was to subdue evil
and defeat her, when it endured all this injury and dishonor in its own nature, so that it should be considered lost and destroyed? For this is characteristic of a body: to be cut and divided.
And this, again, is more foolish and senseless than those things: they say that when God wished to save his land from evil, he handed over what belonged to his own nature, naked, to cruel dishonor
and destruction, and that which comes from his being sins along with her. This, even if it should suffer and sin for a single hour or an instant of time,
is more foolish and evil than anything else. How much better it would have been for the land to be surrendered rather than for the being of God to be taken captive!
For if he could not endure matter’s arrogant tumult and her coming against the land, how much less would he have endured this slavery and subjection
of something belonging to God’s own nature! And evil would not cease from her sins and her foolish deeds,

and God would sin along with her through his power, which came forth from his being and was sent. From this it appears that God did not wish to send what belonged to his being to sin along with matter.
Nor would the power itself have consented and obeyed, [?] and wickedness, in order to free that land
which had not yet been taken, but was about to be taken—as though God could not have helped this land in any other way.
We should see how much weakness Mani falsely attributes to God—he who openly spoke against God in his madness. Like someone pronouncing judgment concerning the affairs of orphans,
he is compelled to acknowledge his weakness so that his case may be brought to completion and prevail. For he is like someone helping an adversary—evil, which does not exist at all.

That she did not do everything against God, he says: “You exalted yourself against him, and you wanted to enter his domain.” And this conflict, worse than anything else, was against God: “You seized his nature,” he says, “and conquered him all this time.”
“She cuts off for him,” he says, “that thing which she cannot cut off [?] without a covering. She chokes him and constrains him with it, and makes him her partner in all her evil deeds.”
And in her recklessness, he says, God could not even forcibly rescue his own territory in another form. Nor did he preserve even this: that he should remain without sins,

which is fitting and proper to his nature. For the wicked and unjust things done together with matter by the power that came from his being and his nature are plainly attributed to him—to the one who sent it.
Thus he testifies to all the strength of evil against God. And he dares to say of God that he suffered from evil all these things for which there is no cure.

After these things, he says: “The power sent from God put matter to sleep, like a woman charming a snake.” And not only does he unconvincingly mingle things that are completely contradictory in his account,
and tell, in his fabrication, of things that cannot possibly happen in nature,

but here too he goes further, saying the opposite of what he intends. For, as he says, “God created everything from both of these. The human body belongs to evil, and the soul belongs to the Good One.”
Whether it has a single form or is compounded of opposites, we shall shortly show that neither of these two assertions has any proof.
For the body, in and of itself, neither devises nor commits any evil. It does not murder, commit adultery, or steal, nor does it commit any other wrongful act
when there is no soul in it. Yet it was precisely because of these things and others like them that Mani devised the existence of another, opposing principle and a mixture of opposites, so, he says,

that the cause of sins might be discovered. If, then, it is the mixture of the soul belonging to the Good One with the body belonging to evil that causes human sins—for the body, alone and by itself, does not sin—

it would have been better for that power belonging to the Good One not to have mixed, according to their fabrication, with evil, which does not exist. For none of humanity’s sins would ever have been committed or come about at all.

For what murder could there have been when there was no one to be murdered, if the world had not come into existence through the mixture of opposites, according to their ridiculous account? And what adultery could there have been when it did not exist in the body,

and when the body, in and of itself, did not [?], had it not been for the soul sent to it from the Good One? But it must be one of two things. Either he must say that, by the Good One’s arrangement, those things were brought together

that are opposites, so that the world might come into existence from the Good One—and in another way he himself is the cause of humanity’s evils, if he willingly employed evil against those who were created—or
he was forcibly driven by evil, and evil itself, through its wickedness, won the victory over the Good One. For I ask again: what murder could there have been if there had been no human being,
no sword, and no other murderous weapon, if the world had not been formed through the mingling and mixture of those opposites? For matter, in and of itself, even if [?]—for there was a mortal being

for it to kill—and it would not have known adultery, since sexual union did not take place within it. Nor, again, would it have committed oppression, since it had no ability at all to interpret and judge,
because it was without reason. As for the love of money, which is the root of all evils—for the love of money exists among human beings because of need—matter was free from this.

And the love of praise is a passion arising from awareness, which matter did not possess, since it was without awareness. Dissipation, sexual immorality, and corruption had no place in it. And, taken together,
all the evils seen among human beings were entirely absent from matter before the world existed. Consequently, it was certainly not restrained by this mixture.
On the contrary, according to that madman’s account, like a horse that has found an open space, it runs fearlessly, scattering evils.

For those evils that did not exist at all before the world came into being are precisely the ones committed in the world since it came into being. For even if someone assumes, according to his account, that they were in turmoil and were madly
opposed to one another—those who came from matter—and were committing countless evils against one another and gathering to fight against the light, he still cannot say that the entire list
of evils enumerated among human beings existed among them. For it was not even possible for those human evils to be committed before human beings existed. And where does that

statement of his stand, that evil was supposedly put to shame after it was fettered? Before it was fettered, it had not even heard mention of those human evils; but after it was fettered, it is reproached for those very things.
For how was it harming the Good One when it was in turmoil within itself, and he was not there for its disturbances to buffet and batter him? For it was utterly unable to change the Good One.

But if it was able to enter places that did not belong to it, he ought to have restrained it by some means other than this ignorant assault. For whereas formerly it displayed its disturbances harmlessly within itself,

now it seems that something else has been added to it: it has shown its turmoil to be harmful toward its opponent, just as it was within itself. For even human beings, when they are entirely on their own,

if they are wicked and wish to do something evil, remain idle unless they find someone else against whom to commit their wickedness. And through their agreement about evil, they remain united with one another.
But matter itself did not even have a will. Nor did it have thought, since it was irrational. Nor was it capable of acting, since it was alone and existed by itself and for itself.

Consequently, what Mani called matter must be understood as having acquired, through the soul that truly comes from the Good One, an addition to its practice of evil that it had not known. For it used to be blamed for the turmoil

before the world, which was neither apparent nor visible to us; but it learned to commit those evils that are apparent and visible. Thus that incantation actually roused the creeping creature instead of putting it to sleep, as he said.
But if he says, “God did not wish the world to come into being,” let him be asked who it was that did wish it.

Was it perhaps evil, which had no knowledge? And who was it, then, who fashioned this universe out of the two of them? Was it perhaps matter itself? Then its achievement is remarkable! Or was it perhaps God himself who did not

wish it, but acted under compulsion? Then it was he, rather, who was subjected, and he did not subject anything. And it is superfluous, as that man said, to marvel at the wisdom of the Good One, which was directed under compulsion
toward the injury and harm of those who were created. For those evils that had never existed before the opposing powers approached one another had not even been named.
These very things, after the world came into being, greatly [?]. And how is it not foolish to say that, when God wished to quiet the turmoil of matter, which was neither apparent nor known to us,

he became the cause of the turmoil of those human evils that are apparent and visible? For the turmoil of matter, which he condemned in words, is something he alone speaks of; he cannot demonstrate it plainly in actual fact.
But those evils that he said arose from the mixture, as though telling some impossible tale—although he saw them with his own eyes, the madman himself was not ashamed.

Consequently, when he wishes to show that God is not the cause of human wickedness, he admits the opposite: that God is the cause of its cause—even more clearly than if he had deliberately contrived to say this alone.

But let us approach and, with love for the truth, examine those evils committed by human beings and see to whom they properly belong. For perhaps it may even be allowed that the soul's mixture comes from those opposing powers, as he supposed.

If, then, he said that this soul comes uniformly from the Good One, or, alternatively, from the combination and mixture of those opposing powers, it is easily seen whether it is from the Good One's portion,

according to that wicked man's account, that evils exist and arise. For the soul is incorporeal and in its essence admits no composition at all, still less a composition of opposites. For those who supposed

They wrote of it that it is composed of distinct parts, not because its being is itself divided and mixed, but on the basis of its activities, from what can be observed, because a single simple expression

that encompasses it was something they could not formulate about it. For although it changes within itself in different ways through the various forms it receives from time to time, nevertheless, in its being, because
it is God's creation, it is unchanging and is not composed of distinct things. All this is far removed from a mixture of opposites, so much so that it cannot
be considered a body in itself. But let us suppose, in accordance with their lying words—if we dare to say even this—that the human soul too is composed of good and evil.
Why not, then? Look: he assigns its knowledge and capacity for thought to the good, but its ignorance, if it has any, he assigns to evil. It is clear that he has nothing else to say besides this.

So whenever desire is violently stirred, whether by the body alone or by that part of the soul that belongs to evil, does the action really proceed spontaneously from it? Is it not preceded, at its very beginning, first by

thought and understanding, then by discernment and also the choice of the action itself? Only then does desire proceed to carry out the action. But the accusation and punishment for evil arise from the action and the deed,
not from desire. Thus, if the thought of desire remains where it is and does not proceed to deed and action, but instead quickly comes to rest, having flared up and [?] at once,

then it is not considered deserving of any blame or punishment—not merely by ordinary standards, but it is not blameworthy even if judged by the standard of virtue. It therefore appears right and proper
that sins are assigned to the soul's knowledge and capacity for thought, not to the body or to any other part besides this. Consequently, you have acquitted evil, which is without knowledge.
It has no part in causing human evils, since it does not even exist. According to his own statement, however, it appears that they proceed and arise from the part belonging to the good.
But, out of love for truth, let us use another argument. For if the soul, without knowing the character and strength of desire, approached action without understanding, it would be possible
to say confidently that wrongful deeds flow from the part that lacks knowledge. But if, on many occasions, the mind itself and knowledge itself sometimes choose and desire, as
the mind willingly inclines toward desire through shameful conduct, and at other times withdraws from it again, whenever some fear restrains it or love of virtue draws it toward virtue, it is clear
that the mind itself and knowledge itself alone choose and carry out either deeds that are done well or those [?]. From these demonstrations, [?] Mani's evil argument and teaching.
For none of humanity's sins appears to belong to matter, but to the soul alone—or to the soul's own mind and knowledge, which belong to the part of the good, as Mani himself said.
Furthermore, if those trained in chastity were not stirred by desire in their conscience, one could absolve the mind and knowledge of those who live recklessly from

accusation and punishment, so that desire itself would bear all the blame for the things done—desire which, he claims, belongs to the part of evil, as he said. But if it is especially among those who love chastity that

the expenditure of great effort is found, and it is apparent that they struggle and discipline the desires of nature through knowledge, then it is clearly established and apparent that it is the mind and knowledge that both sin and overcome—the mind that knows both virtue and evil.

As for why the desire for sins exists in our nature, we will speak about that in its proper time, showing that this very thing accords all the more with the wondrous glory of our Creator. For now, however, let us remain with this inquiry.
But what has been said is sufficient: our sins cannot be the work and activity of matter or of evil, which does not exist, but belong solely to the mind and to knowledge.
For we can also establish our argument in another way. What, indeed, does he say murder belongs to, if not to evil? And likewise sexual immorality, adultery, theft, and lying.
It is evident that these are especially called evil. What, then, if a judge kills someone who has broken the law and committed an offense? Is he considered a murderer, when here the very
act is the same for someone who kills by violence and someone who kills according to the law? There is also the intention involved in a man's intercourse with his wife and with another woman.
The understanding distinguishes by intention an act that is similar in its execution. Again, if someone steals from a person who is insane whatever weapon is near him,
or foods that are harmful to him, how does this not appear to be the very same act of theft that is contemptible and subject to punishment,

although, in its understanding and discernment, it is not the same, but entirely different and distinct? Again, along with these examples, if a man who has gone mad demands a sword that he entrusted to someone while he was sane, is it not necessary for the person to whom it was entrusted
to lie and say that he did not receive it? How, then, is this excused, unless the two cases are distinguished from the act itself by their intention?
It is therefore evident from these examples that the act itself is not examined and judged primarily in and of itself, but by the understanding and purpose of the person who performed it. For one can
also apply the same reasoning to the opposite cases. For if someone gives money or food to a person in need, not because he has compassion on him,
but because he hunts for and gathers praise for himself from those who see or hear about it, how is it not evident that the act itself is good

and compassionate, but his intention is very base and contemptible? Again, if someone prays at length and fasts continually, while displaying his endurance and hardship to other people, how is it not evident that, although he is praised for his deed, he is condemned for the intention and deliberate choice of his will?
And not only this: if someone else practices chastity and deprives himself of many pleasures, not because of his love of virtue,
but because of the stinginess that comes from love of money, how is it not evident that this person overcomes other desires through his desire for money? And this very endurance of his, as

it appears, he practices with an intention directed toward evil. If, then, in many cases even things that appear evil are seen to be good because of the understanding and intention of the person who performs them,
or at least not evil; or, conversely, even things that appear good are exposed as evil because of the choice and intention of the person who performs them, who, then,
can dispute this: that, in truth, it is not the acts themselves that are judged, but the understanding and intention of those who perform them that are questioned and examined?
35. Which deeds and actions, then, are classified as evil? Are they those that appear evil, but are sometimes performed with a virtuous understanding? And which, in turn, are classified as good?
Are they those that appear good, but are frequently performed with an evil understanding? Clearly, then, not one of them belongs categorically to either class.

Rather, an action is distinguished and judged only by the understanding, discernment, and direction of the knowledge of the person performing it: whether it has been carried out rightly or not by the direction of the knowledge of a human

being. This belongs entirely, according to his own statement, to the superior part of the soul—a point that the disciples of the madman Mani cannot deny, however greatly they rave. Thus it was an entirely
unjust judgment that Mani pronounced against that matter from which I was created, when he asserted that human actions come from it, although they have absolutely no connection with it whatsoever.

On the contrary, they would appear to belong rather to the portion of the good [?]. But if there are indeed two principles, and God, they say, devises a way to gather and draw back to himself that power which was swallowed up, which he calls the soul of everything, so that

what comes from him should not remain forever under punishment, bound in matter, why, then, did he surrender it to this in the beginning, so that throughout all this time, from eternity, it has not even been able to catch its breath?

And he himself would suffer far more than act. For if their story had included the claim that God suffered no harm in his own being, and that not even a small part of him was seized by matter, this would have been far less unfitting.

to him, but is someone else, alien to his nature, and this one was rescued quickly and immediately, so that he might be thought to have employed this scheme out of pride rather than condescension, there might perhaps have been some plausibility to this lying fabrication.
But now [?], throughout all this endless time, it is he himself who, as they say, belongs to the nature of God,

who is in confinement and chains, so that God himself must be regarded as seized and imprisoned through the likeness of the one who is held captive. Because, they say, he belongs to his nature, he therefore wishes,
with care and great ingenuity, to gather him to himself [?]. Matter itself, however, is without suffering or injury, so that it has acted primarily as an agent and has not suffered.
From these things, then, it is clear that everything that deceiver and madman put together, he put together as blasphemy against God, who had done none of these things against him.

He therefore wishes, as he says, and devises ways to gather and bring up to himself that power which comes from him. This, in their view, is the salvation and blessedness they await: that what comes from God should return to him. Meanwhile, he himself continues to the end,
waiting and hoping that a favor will be done him, if what belongs to his nature is to receive its freedom, so that he may rebuild those things which he himself demolished.
There is nothing more for him to do than sit and be nurtured and sustained by hope and expectation, enduring and looking toward the end to see how he will free himself from evil.
If this is delayed and does not happen quickly, it turns out that he himself receives punishment through the delay.
For it is clear that hastening the end is not in his power. Otherwise, he would have made use of it and would long since have been released from this expectation.
Mani the madman also has another ridiculous claim: those who belong to matter, he says, realized that they were perishing miserably, because the light was gradually being taken away from them.

They therefore devised and ingeniously contrived the structure of the body, he says, so that it would be a fetter and a great chain for the soul. Thus it is clear, according to his account, that as long as they fashion and provide

bodies, the souls of the Good One also continue to be captured and bound. It therefore rests with those beings to keep the world from reaching its limit in time and coming to an end; its ending is not in the Good One’s power.

What, then, can anyone say when he considers that Mani the madman’s account never stays in one place, but is exposed by its own statements as shifting this way and that? For after saying that God is the creator of the world, how

does he then say that those who belong to matter fashioned and set up the body against him? It is as though God had divided creation between himself and them, and moreover, in this very arrangement, endures their violence in what he gave them.
Their work is carried through, and not according to his will—as though he had forgotten that madman’s account, which said that the abolition and destruction of matter consisted in this:

the removal of that power which had been mingled with it. Yet he had previously asserted that its disorder was restrained and brought into order through that very power. For if, by its coming, it fettered
and bound evil, then by its removal and departure it releases and abandons it. Its departure brings evil very great relief indeed.
If, then, the hope and expectation of the end consist in this—that what comes from God should return to him—

why was it separated in the first place, to endure the misery and filth of evil throughout all this endless time? And why, instead of good hope and blessedness, should this be appointed for him: to receive and lift up what comes from him? For matter itself is not found in any respect,

or seen, to have been restrained. On the contrary, it has acquired great authority for devising evil deeds. Yet according to what he said, this matter ought to have been bound and fettered. When, then, that power which was held captive within it has gradually been taken and led away,
what will happen? Is it not clear that matter will return once more to its natural disorder? But he says, ‘No! For in the end he overcomes

it, makes a [?] for it, and arranges for it to burn of itself.’ Why, then, did he not do this from the beginning? Was he unwilling, or was he unable? For if he was unwilling, how does he become willing afterward?

Is it because he changed his mind, or because he later discerned something better? For there could have been no other course than for the Good One to abolish evil completely from the beginning, if he was able.
But if he was unable, there is a danger that his weakness will give rise to blasphemy against our Creator. Yet how, then, can he afterward, in the end, accomplish it by his power?

Can power that he did not have be added to him, either as he grows or as he receives an addition? For if both those opposing principles are self-existent, neither of them admits growth or increase, nor diminution or loss.
Tell me, then, what awareness there was that either a large or a small portion of that power which was mixed with matter had been taken and removed from it. If indeed...

Whenever the moon waxes and wanes, God gradually receives and takes what belongs to him. Yet look: all this time has passed since the beginning of the world, and the human race has neither decreased nor diminished in the number of those who are alive.

Nor has there been any decrease among the four-footed animals. Rather, all these creatures continue in their customary way, coming into being and dying; and humanity has received still greater abundance

and increase. How, then, does the man who tells this story in his madness suppose that the power which, in his fabrication, he said was mixed with matter is gradually being separated, while those same things, just as they are,

continue in the world? For the length of the day remains the same, and that of the night also remains the same. Light has not diminished, nor has darkness increased: what existed from the beginning has continued.

Let us also ask him this: whether they are punished for their sins or not. If, then, they receive punishment—as he himself admits when he says that they are confined in the globe together with evil—then, according to his statement, God turns out
to be punishing his own nature. And what could be more foolish and wicked than this? But if they remain without punishment,

sins are not merely free from distress and loss; they even appear to be better than righteousness, if they give pleasure to the person who commits them in this world and do not become a cause of punishment for him in the world to come.

Besides all these things, there is also this astonishing statement of his: he says that throughout the intervening time he fills the abyss with clods—the abyss from which, he says, matter peered out—in keeping with
his own bitter madness [?]. He has not realized that, if what falls into the abyss comes from the land of the Good, how can it find room to exist in the territory of its opponent?
