But if it is a portion of evil, what belongs to evil itself did not restrain the thing that rushed from there to peer out. Yet, according to the statement of that madman, God himself sits there,
bringing clods, and little by little he scoops them up, blocks the opening, and fills the abyss. What madness! It is ridiculous even for someone to come and give him an answer to this.
The first discourse against the Manichaeans is finished.
The second discourse of Titus against the Manichaeans.
Our argument now draws us toward diligence and care in discussing God [?]. For perhaps what has already been said so far has contributed nothing toward refuting and dismantling
the fabrication of his tales. Yet, lest we should deserve ridicule among discerning people for diligently investigating through inquiries a fabrication that has absolutely no stability or foundation,
we examine those things that are found to have been told by Mani as tales. There are many, however, that we will not consider worthy of an answer in our discussion.

Now let us try to show that evil does not exist anywhere at all as a substance and an independent entity, and that there is no beginningless first principle of matter opposed to God. Rather, there is one first principle over everything, and one God, who created everything beautifully and well.
And it is worthy of his wisdom. For even that man's disciples, when they are refuted by argument concerning the two first principles, which have no firm basis or convincing proof, at this difficulty
come to a halt, like someone who has no proofs but offers many objections against the person debating with them, saying, “Where, then, do evil things come from?”
But we say boldly and confidently that there is one good God, who created everything.

Nothing among the things that have come into being is evil in its substance and its own being. Rather, everything is exceedingly good. Each thing individually is good, and things have been fitted together in various combinations for the needs of every kind. Nothing that comes into being does so without providential care.

Rather, each of all the things that have come into being, small and great alike, has in itself and within its own being a reason that explains it: the things in heaven, the things on earth, and also those things

that in the days [?]. And in the likeness of a complete body, fully constituted by the arrangement of its parts and members, the hidden, inexpressible wisdom of God fashioned this whole world. And now, every

thing you wish, take it away in thought from the things that have come into being, as something that seems superfluous and serves no useful purpose: the body of the whole is harmed and diminished. For even

whatever among the things in the world seems utterly contemptible and insignificant contributes to the completeness of the body. There is nothing useless or empty among the things that exist in the world,
nor anything that came into being in vain, nor anything fashioned for excessive display. Only the injustice of human sins is rightly and justly despised and condemned as evil.
And it truly is evil. But it is not evil from the beginning, since it has no existence.
For from this, namely, that it exists, [?], as our discussion also showed sufficiently, though in a veiled manner, a little earlier in what was said. And it also clearly

shows this in what follows. For this reason, let us first undertake to speak about this, and thus proceed and advance along the same path, showing that nothing that has come into being is evil in its very existence.

And further, everything that God distributed, carried out, directed, and administered, he did as was fitting and appropriate to his wisdom, for the benefit of those who were being governed and provided for, on whose behalf he carried out and performed these things.
God, then, created the world, and those against whom our argument is directed do not dispute this, although they criticize it, saying that the world [?] is without order.
They disagree about the manner and the cause of its coming into being. Nevertheless, they acknowledge that it came into being from God.
The human being is a part of the world. God established the human being as a rational inhabitant of a city. And all those things that [?] neither virtue nor evil,
he reserved for him to govern, so that virtue should come from him himself alone,

and evil. He did this after first placing knowledge of both in his nature, so that he might examine this as though by sight, and not merely conduct his life with complete knowledge, but also become one who achieves the victories of virtue.

The human being who does wrong through sins, then, is justly blamed. But if he commits sins as though he cannot refrain from them, he acts unjustly and is rightly blamed as an unjust person. And appropriately, as an expression
of blame and accusation, it is called sin, because it is unjust. The person who has the power to make use of it performs it. Thus, everything done unjustly is sin, even if it takes its occasion from
things that belong to nature. For it is the unjust use of natural things that constitutes sin. Discerning reason also belongs to our nature, and because of this, the sin

that is committed does not remain hidden. If, then, we train the reason within us through perseverance in the pursuit of virtue, we make it healthy and strong, like the body through exercise involving measured movement.
But if we neglect it and do not consider it worthy of training and care, it becomes sick and deteriorates, and finally becomes blind through neglect.

Hence it is in our power and depends on us to use the reason within us discerningly in every situation, like those master builders whose excellent workmanship is revealed through the measuring rod and compass.
We must therefore diligently train and cultivate it, like soil cultivated for the seed that falls into it. But when it is neglected, it deteriorates.

Here, however, a difficulty arises for us concerning the question of why we were handed over to all this danger and turmoil, in that it is in our power and depends on us whether to care for ourselves or neglect ourselves, rather than having been made completely good
and perfect. Instead, we are very often even evil. Yet this danger and turmoil is necessarily beneficial, and not merely incidentally so.
Otherwise, we would be deprived of the full attainment of perfection. For if God had [?] us perfectly, so that we could not sin,
we could not be good. For among human beings, a good person is just and chaste. A person becomes just when he restrains himself from injustice,
and when he flees from licentiousness, he attains chastity. Thus, it is the power to do the opposite things that makes possible the acquisition of their contraries.
Just as, unless someone is subject to the power of licentiousness, he cannot be temperate either. For someone said, “What licentious act was he able
to do, yet did not do?” For someone is not temperate merely because he cannot be licentious, nor is someone just merely because he cannot commit injustice.

Rather, when someone can do and carry out these things but refrains from them through discerning reason, this is the virtue of temperance and justice. And it is not merely that he can carry them out, but that he is also naturally tempted.
Thus he may truly be praised for choosing not to act. This, then, alone is virtue among human beings, and no other is to be found. For we do not call God temperate, or courageous

and steadfast, or anything of that kind, for he is high and exalted above this human virtue. Even if he is called just, it is in a different way, not as we are. But concerning a human being, insofar as he is human, we inquire how he becomes good.

For each of all the things that have come into being has the measure of its nature assigned to it, beyond which it cannot go or pass. But not to fall short of it or diminish it—this is perfect virtue.

What measure, then, has been assigned to a human being for the perfection of his virtue and for his being good, except temperance and justice and those other virtues? For apart from these a human being
cannot be good. And if temperance is restraint in the face of desires and pleasure, it is necessary that he be subject to the power of desires and pleasure, which are opposed to temperance,
since it is in opposition to these that restraint receives both the name of temperance and its function. But not being subject to the power of desires and pleasure produces the opposite
of this, namely the absence of temperance. Justice and those other virtues are also of the same kind. But if someone says, “They ought to exist in this way,
without our admitting their opposites, licentiousness and injustice, just as God does not,” he is saying nothing other than, “We ought not to be human beings.”
It is as if someone were to see and observe an eagle flying high above, but become angry at the nature of a horse and bitterly reproach it for not resembling the eagle’s nature.
He ought instead to compare and examine the horse alongside another horse of the same nature.
God, then, made the human being a human being, a soul together with a body, for he is an inhabitant of the physical world. If, then, this person is good to the extent that human nature allows,
he is found excellent and perfect; for as God [?] this person in this way. Hence, then, if he is good to the extent that human nature allows,
he is found excellent and perfect; for as God [?] this person in this way. Hence, then, a human being becomes good if he is temperate and just.

For if it were possible for a human being to be good in some other, better manner, the Creator would be blamed for not having made the human being good in that manner. But if, according to the measure

of human nature, there is nothing better for a human being to receive than temperance and justice and those other similar virtues, then the question must be asked in turn: how can a human being become temperate and just?
For his Creator wishes him to possess these very qualities. Now temperance cannot exist without comparison with, and testing by, its opposite; and the same is true of justice. Otherwise,
neither temperance nor justice exists. But if he were unable to be temperate and just in this manner, while it was impossible for a person to become temperate and just in any other way,
then the Creator would justly be blamed for having made the human being unable to be good.
I mean temperate and just: only in this manner, and in no other at all, was he to achieve excellence and be shown worthy of the wisdom of the one who made him.
But if he persists in what he says against us and says that a human being ought to be temperate by nature and not through effort, this person again lets go of and abandons
what temperance is and what it consists in, and turns toward a choice without discernment and without knowledge. If, while maintaining this, that it is impossible without temperance
And he does not wish to ask to be equal to the one who made him without righteousness. The manner of acquiring these things [?], for this would mean being bound by nature.
It is not chastity when there is no possibility of acting otherwise. Rather, it is recognized and tested in opposition to desires and pleasures. It therefore encounters
those things that stand against it, so that, by struggling against them and overcoming them, it may truly be chastity and be called chastity. The same applies to the other virtues.

Thus God fashioned the human being in his nature neither good nor evil, but permitted and entrusted the choice of virtue to his will and understanding. But as for what someone is who is neither good nor evil, and therefore belongs to neither of these two categories:
I say that he is neither good nor evil. His very existence is beautiful, but being good through virtue has not yet been added to him. So too
gold is beautiful by nature, but it is not good in the sense of virtue, because it has no soul. The same applies to precious stones and all the things that have come into being: each of them
has the beauty of its own appearance. In this same sense, then, the human being too is beautiful.

Indeed, he is especially beautiful in his existence, in the very fact that he has come into being and exists. But being good, which is added to him only through virtue, is something he acquires through effort. For this purpose also

God made him, so that this might become his through himself and his own agency. If, then, God had given him freedom of action without first placing knowledge of virtue and evil in his nature, it would have seemed that he had set a blind charioteer upon a chariot
that was swift. But if he combined both together, he also gave him freedom of action, and had not first placed in his nature [?] set upon a swift chariot.
But if he combined both together—both freedom of action for acquiring virtue and knowledge for discernment and care in making his choice—he first made this charioteer skilled, namely,

knowledge and the governing mind. This charioteer guides the chariot of his nature safely, provided that he does not grow drowsy and fall asleep during his course, and become overturned and fall through pleasures and desires.

In his existence and his nature, then, the human being is beautiful, like gold and precious stones, and as a work of God. But whether he becomes good or, on the contrary, evil is a matter of his will.
For these things are within his reach, so that he can do them. They are conditions that occur in him, like habits and ways of conduct that develop in him,

and according to his will and choice. Likewise, evil itself comes into existence only through action, and before it is done, it does not exist. The human being therefore has power over the evil that can be done, not so that he should do
it, but so that, by not doing it, he may prove virtuous and victorious. For if he had no power to do it, it would seem that his Creator, out of envy,
had held him back from this victory and deprived him of freedom, so that he would not be good through himself and his own agency. Thus, this very thing that seems to be a deficient endowment
is in truth an excellent and great endowment of nature. Consequently, evil never comes upon him by compulsion at all, because it has no substantial existence.
And if he had no power over it, neither would he have within himself the ability to flee from it. Yet he does not flee as though from something that exists, because it does not exist,
but from that which can arise from himself. For how could he acquire hatred of evil, which is virtuous, unless he were able to do those very things and voluntarily refrained from them?

For virtue among human beings, it seems, is nothing other than restraint and avoidance; and a righteous person is one who does not act unjustly. The same applies to the other virtues. God, however, is good
not because he refrains from acting unjustly even though he can, but solely because of his help and gracious gifts. For this reason he alone is good. Among human beings,

however, goodness is established first through fleeing from evil. It was necessary that power over these things should be within a person's reach, so that whoever wishes to be good might have it within himself and his own agency not to do evil things, even though

For one who is perfect, the practice of good deeds is also required along with this flight from houses [?]. But this is the greater thing, and in it lies complete victory. Among human beings, no one can find a victory as excellent as this.

For abstaining from sins is difficult. A good deed is sometimes found even among those who are very wicked. It is therefore clear that a gracious gift has been bestowed on the human being in this power given to him to sin,
since it is by abstaining from it that he wins the victory, and not otherwise.
It is therefore through this freedom that the human being is honored: he has within his nature knowledge of the good and evil deeds that can be done. For before they are done, they do not exist.
For how can a deed exist when the person who does it does not exist? This is why evil both comes into being and disappears, according to whether it is done or not done.
Furthermore, God, who is good and knows only how to help and show kindness, does no evil whatsoever. Nor is it through ignorance that he abstains from evil.

Nor is it because of weakness that he is completely foreign to it and far removed from it. For how could he who teaches people not to do evil be ignorant of it? And how could it be right to suppose that God abstains from evil because of weakness?
For the one who is good is not good because he is too weak to do wrong, but [?] a complete inability to will it. Yet if we say that God cannot do any wrong, we speak rightly.
But we do not describe this inability as weakness; rather, we attribute it to the greatness of his unwillingness.

And because he does not change, he possesses this abstention: his will does not change so as to do evil. And therefore he could [?]. No, he does not do it, because of the nature of his unchanging will.
Thus evil does not exist with God, not only as a substance, but not even as an action. But among human beings, abstention from it is not unchanging,
even if someone rises very high in virtue. Evil is considered to exist only in the action, and it does not exist before the action.
Thus God honored the human being by creating him in his own image, so that, just as God is good through the freedom of his nature, so the human being too,
through the freedom of his will, might imitate God—not abstaining from evil because of the weakness of his nature, but honoring virtue through his freedom.
This very thing is fully and sufficiently demonstrated by the many changes toward virtue and toward wickedness that are often found among human beings, when neither of these
has been firmly established in them through long-standing habit. For in everything we do under the compulsion of nature, we do not admit any change from it.
But everything we do by the decision of our will varies within us from time to time, according to the wishes that arise in us and incline toward one side or the other.
It is therefore not in human nature to sin under compulsion, but to do evil by choice.

The very effort required by virtue also demonstrates and makes known that it depends on the will of those who possess it. Whenever they show even a little disregard for it, their possession of it is in danger and turmoil.
But if someone raises this objection to our argument—that there is a person who sometimes wishes to abstain from evil deeds but says, “I cannot”—
let him learn that even an illness that has been in the body for a long time cannot easily be changed and brought to an end. So too an unhealthy condition of the soul,
which has become established in it over a long time, cannot easily escape from the things in which it has become involved through long habit,
unless some powerful good impulse enters and drives out the one that preceded it. For often people have set out with a fierce impulse, unchecked, to perform some evil deed,

but one has seen the husband of the woman with whom he wished to commit adultery and has been restrained by fear of having his desire exposed, or has been held back by remembering the law. Another has wished to engage in robbery
and has checked his desire out of fear of punishment. Thus sins are the actions of passions and do not flow from nature. And we all love someone who has humility:
By the judgment common to us all, we have established laws for evildoers that allow no pardon or appeal, and by this very action we have shown
that they are not forcibly driven by their nature, but choose of their own will to commit evil, and we consider them deserving of punishment.
But since Mani’s disciples also attempt in another way to demonstrate and prove that we have two opposing natures, saying that we sometimes think evil thoughts and sometimes good ones,
let us tell them: Since knowledge of both is in our nature, it is necessarily toward thoughts of the things we know
that we are moved. We lose nothing by this; rather, we gain abundantly by choosing and honoring what is good and excellent.
For they choose virtue by their own will, although the thought of both injustice and justice is not in their nature. Knowledge was necessarily required for discernment.
Desire, however, [?] the things that have become known, and the will itself inclines toward whatever it wishes. These things are not separate parts of the soul, but are its activities.

For just as our eye has the natural ability to see the actions of others, sometimes evil ones and sometimes good ones, without itself being the cause of any of them—for it receives knowledge through sight
and distinguishes what is seen—so thought, like the eye, necessarily moves toward things that can be done. The soul is not forcibly driven toward them, but through its natural knowledge approaches
them. For if we wish, we can think about opposing things at the same time, but we cannot do opposing things at the same time. Thus the will distinguishes the action itself through its choice.
Thought itself bears witness to the knowledge of good and evil that is in our nature. For if we did not already know these things, we would not even think about them.
Nor [?] would we choose virtue, and we would be deprived of everything. But many people happen to take pleasure in evil because they have already become caught up in hateful ways of life.
For this reason people ought to take greater care over the upbringing of their children than farmers

take over the growth of their plants. To take this thought within us as evidence of two opposing natures is therefore like someone saying that sight is a mixture of all colors because it encounters them all.

What has already been said has therefore fully demonstrated that it was necessarily appropriate for a human being to receive the power even to sin, and that he was created this way because otherwise he could not have acquired the excellence of triumph and victory,

which God, because he is good and free from envy, placed in his nature. It has also been shown that there is no compulsion requiring us, because of injustice and sins among human beings, to suppose that there is evil matter without a beginning, opposed to God,
or even to suppose that evil exists at all as an actual, independently existing substance. Rather, it exists only in action.
And now let us speak, as far as we are able, about God’s governance, which is full of all wisdom,
and about those created things that the madman Mani groundlessly condemns as evil. For he objects to many circumstances among human beings, saying that they occur in a disorderly way.
He criticizes wealth and poverty, health and sickness, saying that they are not distributed equally. He also objects that evildoers often escape the punishment

of the law, while someone who is unaware receives punishment, and that sometimes even evil people hold leadership and authority over others. Let us therefore say in answer to these objections that a human
being was brought into the world by his Creator to gain nothing other than the worship of God and virtue. For by acquiring these, he would conduct his life here well and rightly.
But if he despises them, he will sink deeply into error. God gives him nourishment for his body, clothing to cover him, and other necessities,
not as the foremost and most honorable gifts, but as things required for his existence here, because he has a body, so that through them he may live and work and labor without hindrance.
so that he might acquire the things mentioned. He also made physical light for him, suited to his nature.
And also air to breathe, water, and the other things that are needed and necessary. For all these things are naturally available from God equally, for the common use of all human beings.

No one can say that a poor person has less use of light or a smaller supply of water, or less of this inhalation and breath of life that belong to nature, or even of the food that is necessary and needed.
For although it cannot be obtained without sweat, the manner of providing what is suitable and necessary for everyone's life is equal and common to all.
Gold, silver, and precious stones also come from him to those who possess them. But they do not greatly help with the business mentioned earlier; rather, they do not greatly help
with the business mentioned earlier, and indeed they hinder it even more. Nevertheless, this business that God previously set before human beings is not unattainable for those in poverty.

Nor is it easier for those with wealth. Rather, it is easy for both, for those who are diligent and concerned to travel this road laid out for them: in poverty through endurance and freedom, and in wealth through humility.
And by honoring his giver more than the gifts given to him, a person can accomplish what he is striving for. Likewise, a poor person does not succeed in this undertaking without [?] and toil.
Rather, he needs perseverance and diligence. If there is negligence in him, he must be angry with it and rebuke his own will for honoring the things given by God more than God himself.
Nor, again, can someone who possesses a great abundance of wealth buy reverence for God and virtue as though making a purchase. Rather, labor and much sweat
are required of him. For his mind especially seems to be in a great storm, divided in its thoughts and concerns between the things outside him
and the things within him and in his soul. Thus, unless he fully considers his wealth superfluous and despises it, and love for God alone becomes his master,
he is completely submerged in ignorant error, without realizing that he has abandoned what alone is the foremost good and has become a slave to lifeless wealth, which he leaves
to others when he dies. Equally, then, neither the rich nor the poor travel the course of virtue without labor and turmoil, nor is it unattainable for either of them.
They differ from one another only in things external to them, which offer no advantage for this course laid out for us.
1. God's wisdom has also arranged this very thing as a necessity. For the poor person is trained in endurance when he sees wealth in another's possession.
And the rich person's will is tested by the poor person's lowly condition. For wealth is of no use unless poverty is close at hand.

For to whom would he show kindness? Poverty, too, is not put to the test when there is no wealth confronting it. Nevertheless, a person is not blessed because he is rich, nor is he condemned and [?] because he is poor.
For only that person is blessed who increasingly has within his soul the true good deeds of virtue, whether he is rich or poor
in his circumstances. For this is also why the human being was created by God. It was fitting that he should receive his existence from God in this way.

But he should hope to become increasingly good through himself and his own efforts, with God helping him. For God wishes the human being also to gain possession of himself through himself and his own efforts, because he is rational, so that he may have praiseworthy confidence. Henceforth, then, we neither marvel
nor call a rich person blessed who prospers in wickedness. Nor do we doubt God's providence because someone of this sort is rich. For what advantage does a wicked rich person have?

And what does he not lack all the more? Does he not have sleepless nights and turmoil over his money, and anxieties over expenditures that are greater than his comforts over profits? For what is at hand does not comfort him as much as what is far away troubles him.
His desires continually grow along with his wealth, and so his mind constantly dwells, without respite, in unceasing turmoil. His body, too, is often wasted and weakened along with his mind.

And what seems to be a superior possession—the abundant wealth of someone who has acquired it—is worse than scanty possessions. For pleasures, worries, and luxurious beds bring together diseases of every kind from time to time.

But through the plainness of the food that is necessary and needed, the poor man gains abundant health for his body and profits from it. Now who can say that the body is not more valuable and superior to the things outside it? If, then,

those who use necessary things in moderation retain the healthy condition and strength of their bodies, while those who indulge in pleasure without moderation grow weak, and the strength of their bodies also declines and fails, how

is it not clear that in this respect too wealth is inferior to poverty? This is so unless someone is found who lacks even the necessities—something that never happens to a person who is diligent in virtue.
Moreover, the pleasure of costly food keeps diminishing through long-established habit, until those who enjoy it can no longer find anything further to offer themselves for their enjoyment.

For what is habitual is always held in little regard. But for the poor man, even a small amount is satisfying and pleasant because of his health. And if something costly should occasionally become available to him,
because it is unfamiliar and new to him, he receives it with pleasure and satisfaction. Thus, in this respect too, anyone who reasons rightly finds that the poor man is better off than the rich man.

In the same way, then, both health and sickness are necessary. Health makes the work and practice of virtue easier. And sickness, in turn, sometimes serves to discipline people and restrain them from sins.
For the mind is often helped by external restraints. Furthermore, the experience of sickness recalls the excellence of health, because [?] would be
greatly despised if a person always remained in it and nothing could disturb him. Now if a humble person is sick,
while an oppressive and arrogant person is healthy, the former is held in check by the help of restraint, so that the course of his life may be free from contempt.
The latter, however, gives himself over to wrongdoing, like someone who is careless, lets himself go, and neglects himself. But if, in turn, the oppressive and especially wicked person falls sick,
while the humble person is healthy, the former receives punishment not to be helped and brought to his senses, but to serve as an example for those who see him.
The latter, however, because he can conduct himself and live peacefully even without a restraint, therefore remains continually free from sickness. Both conditions are useful in every situation.
Truly miserable and senseless is the person who, because of these things, denies God's providence and finds fault with it. For this alone is the destructive disease that harms the soul's conduct,
turning it away from virtue. But any soul that remains unharmed in its understanding, whether its body is sick or healthy, perceives the help and usefulness
of each of these conditions. For even if sickness does not fully turn evildoers back and frighten them, since evildoers sometimes also escape the punishment prescribed by the laws,

can we really say that the laws do not frighten and discipline evildoers because their punishments do not reach everyone who does wrong? Or is it not also in this, as in everything, that there appears
the glory and wonder of God's wisdom? For if it were always evident that anyone who did something forbidden by the law could not
flee and escape punishment, the person who did not commit sin would be thoroughly counterfeit and untested.

For everyone would be restrained from wrongdoing by fear of punishment, rather than by hatred of evil deeds. But a diligent person ought rather to refrain from doing evil because he hates it, and not hold back because he fears suffering,
even if it happens unjustly. For this reason many evildoers escape the punishment prescribed by the laws: this is not the punishment for sin, but is only regarded as punishment
of evildoers, which no one can flee and escape. Yet many people escape this punishment, so that the very possibility of their being overlooked and escaping may test people's understanding and will.
And what has been said applies to them all: to thieves, to liars, and to those who dare to commit great evils.
18. But perhaps someone will say, “Human free will would be tested much more if not a single evildoer received punishment to discipline him.” But this very thing
would, on the contrary, become an encouragement to evil deeds, if not even some of those who do evil were caught and received the punishment
prescribed by law. For this reason both things are necessary and required: that an evildoer should be subjected to punishment as an example and a correction, and also that he should escape, to test

human will and understanding. For the human being, who came into existence from God in this way and was created free, was given authority to choose for himself, by his own power, both virtue and evil.

He was granted that his thinking should also be helped and supported from outside, whatever its condition, so that he might recall and remember the things that help him, through fear and also through freedom from fear,
through encouragement and correction, through sickness and health, poverty and wealth, and all those things that seem to be opposites. For they all work together in complete harmony

and contribute to this one purpose: to train and test human understanding and will, so that a person does not sleep too long, but, being driven and struck from this side and that, awakens to the practice and exercise of reverence for God and virtue.
But if it happens that someone [?] receives punishment, someone who is not only innocent and unaware of any offense, but is also an admirable person
and an example of virtue, let us ask: what harm comes to the person to whom this happens? For those who did this to him are subject to correction,

but the person who endures it suffers no harm, even if he endures unjust punishment to the point of death. For such a person has already trained himself to be dead to the world. A person who finds no pleasure in any of the things that give pleasure to others,

and whose only pleasure is something that gives no pleasure to the many—how is such a person not dead to the world even before his death? And he accepts as a kindness what seems to have been done to deceive and harm
him, because he expects great blessings to meet him beyond this world. To those blessings, from which he thought himself far away, he is quickly sent by his enemies; and as
benefactors he welcomes those who plot against him. Moreover, for another reason it was necessary and required that God should permit and overlook the envy that exists among human beings,
so that the choice of virtue might be tested and trained, to see whether it does not fear even death.

And when, again, we see wicked and oppressive people sometimes holding power and being entrusted with leadership, let us understand that this too is permitted within God's providence. For when the sins of those under authority become numerous, as a punishment

from justice, unjust rulers are placed over them, who inflict punishment for what they commit and do, [?] for what they do, so that it may become still clearer that no injustice goes unpunished. For a judge's uprightness is thought to consist
in his punishing those who do evil because he himself has done nothing evil. But if the very person who is judge is himself the originator of these things,
and he punishes those who act as he does all the more severely and abundantly, so that he may be thought to have done nothing evil,
it becomes clearly known that justice holds power and rules. Along with this, it appears all the more fearsome, since those people, because of their evil conduct and deeds, justly endure
rulers of this kind, rightly and [?]. For judgments of this kind, coming from God against sinners, are also plainly found in the Holy Scriptures.

Who, then, has gone so terribly mad as to embrace this teaching about the rule of an evil power without beginning, and its blasphemy against God? For there are many occasions when one can see even righteous people

who, because they sinned, came under the hand of the wicked. It is as if a freeborn son who will not obey his father should be beaten by slaves, so that, along with the pain of the blows, the low status of the person beating him may also put him to shame.

And change the one who errs. For, as we have said, there is only one thing, and it is truly what is required in the life of a human being who came from God: that he prevail through the discernment of his understanding.

And he should not act unjustly in anything, but should live virtuously. By looking to this alone, he will truly be blessed, even if he possesses nothing else in the world. So, if we bear this in mind throughout the whole
discussion of God's providence, nothing among the things governed by God appears to be unequal or confused. For if someone could find

that the path of reverence for God and of virtue was open and easy for one person, but obstructed and blocked for another, then it would seem that there was grounds for criticism in a governance that was unequal
toward that which alone is the source of all good things. But if that through which alone a person becomes truly blessed is placed equally within everyone's bodily power [?],

what inequality can anyone find, even if he is very fond of finding fault? Even those things that are external to us, in their abundance and quantity, are also found to be equal when considered with sound judgment.
For the poor person enjoys the food he receives no less, but even more than the rich person does. The same is true of clothing,
even if it costs less. This is the pattern of [?] with things familiar to it and to which it is accustomed, so that one person does not even notice the excess,
because habit dulls and impairs perception. Nor does the other notice the deficiency, because for him too, through habit, the lack makes no impression on his perception.

Look at the barbarians: although most of their bodies are bare of clothing, they sleep without bedding and sustain themselves with small amounts of inferior food, yet they have never been persuaded to abandon the customary way of life they have come to love.
For through habit they do not notice what is lacking in their way of life. That is, they could not abandon this way of life; otherwise they would quickly lose their health
and would also quickly lose their endurance against the cold and the heat of the sun. But as regards living, and living comfortably,
no one has any advantage in life over his neighbor. For the natural comforts of reclining and sleeping are common to everyone, as are the acceptance and enjoyment
of food, if someone wisely arranges its provision and examines its usefulness through his senses. Distresses of soul and body are also certainly shared, and not to a lesser degree,
or they are found in even greater numbers among those who are thought to possess much in the world.
Since these things are truly so, how can inequality be found in God's governance? For it is variety of every kind, and not
inequality, that is seen in human affairs. For the variety established in the world with beautiful and glorious wisdom is one thing, and confusion
in governance is another. For if someone could find some human beings free from suffering and others suffering in both soul and body,
and some living without food and others by means of food; or again, some who did not experience evils and others who did; and again, some who were mortal and others immortal,
he would rightly call this confusion and inequality in governance, as though God were governing human affairs by chance rather than according to an orderly principle.
But if the pattern and form of everyone's birth are the same, and the nourishment of nature is one and the same, and the provision of necessary and indispensable things without which one cannot live
is shared equally by everyone, then, in short, there is one equality alone toward everyone, which is clearly and supremely evident in everything.
Either the person who accuses God's providence of confusion is completely blind, or he looks at things with an eye of hatred.

No, no: it is not at all right to believe a lame person if he says of a rider that there is confusion in him [?], or in the things and the beauty of this variety, which is supremely fitting for an artisan wise in everything.
He is blamed for this; then let him also be blamed for the mixing of colors of every kind and for the varieties of foods and drinks that wonderfully overwhelm the senses
of those who receive them. From this arose those exceedingly wretched people who thought they could establish the inequality and injustice of fate through two
principles [?]. But it has been fully demonstrated to the wise that there is not a single inequality in human affairs.
Since they also maintain that wars come from evil, how is it that the separate fates of many thousands, in those very wars,

sometimes fall together at one time—that is, in a single hour? Does one fate gather them so that they fall together? And how is it that there is not always room for the severe sickness of these misguided people
in the facts themselves? For wars take their beginnings from aggression, but their occurrence comes through God's permission. Their actual cause, however, is evil.
I mean the desire for greed and aggression. This is human folly and wrongdoing, not God's, as was shown in what we said earlier.
Natural death, however, is not evil. For birth and death were ordained by God as a law of nature. Those who die do not perish; rather, those who are born are added to those
who already exist. For goodness does not consist merely in granting continued existence to those human beings who exist, but also in bringing into being those who do not exist and adding them
to those who exist, so that those who have come into being and have fully run the course of their lives may receive death as rest from their running, without its bringing them to destruction.
Instead, each is transferred in a different way, as he deserves, so that those who do not yet exist may receive an entrance into existence. Thus death, which is ordained by the law of nature, is not
evil, however it may come and happen. For we should not inquire into the different adversities that bring it about, but should know this: its general character is the same for everyone.

I mean that the soul does not depart from the body without some adversity and compulsion, but remains as long as its natural lodging and dwelling continues undissolved. Thus, in this very power inherent in the common nature

there is also a certain fear, which necessarily carries within it a reminder of judgment [?]. This is not for everyone, however, but for those who, through their ignorance, find sins easy, so that they may be restrained from them.
For whoever is wise and virtuous both avoids sins and is far from supposing that death is evil. But someone who loves sins, through the very ignorance by which he sins,
also fears death. His ignorance therefore necessarily has this fitting accompaniment: by fearing what is not fearful, he may acquire the fear that is truly fitting.
I mean that he should flee the harm and injury caused by sins. Thus, when sins increase among the various nations—one form of these sins being aggression—
the nation itself becomes the cause of this apparent punishment. It has been said that this is not truly punishment, because it is ordained for everyone by the common law of nature.
Yet it benefits both those who fall and die in war and those who escape and live.
For those, because it is ordained for everyone by the common law of nature. Yet it benefits both those who fall and die in war and those who escape and live.
For the former, it brings their sins to an end; for the latter, it provides an example that inspires fear. It also benefits the righteous, if they depart with the many. For just as
death becomes an end to the wickedness of the wicked, so also for the righteous, as victors [?], it becomes the beginning of a crown. And thus, wonderfully, through God's providence,
which is wise in everything, it happens that what appears to be punishment actually brings benefit, and not
only through the things he openly does that seem painful, but also through the things that people themselves bring upon themselves through his allowing them to act. Thus war is not the work

[?] of God, but rather his permission, which must be kept in mind in connection with the punishment of sins. In truth, however, it brings them to an end in battle [?], even if a righteous man falls and dies. But for a righteous man to fight

is not the same. Rather, he benefits greatly. For receiving and enjoying the fruits of the labor of virtue is greater than being restrained from sins. This is what awaits the righteous after their death.

But those who speak and argue against these things blame one part of death before demonstrating that death as a whole is evil. For if they say that wars come from evil, which, they claim, has an independent existence, and from a beginningless principle,
they ought to demonstrate that death itself is evil. For it is superfluous to ask about its causes when what happens necessarily and without distinction
continues. But how can they say that death is evil, when, according to that deceiver’s statement, it supposedly releases the soul from matter?
Now, according to the common understanding, death is not an evil at all. For what everyone must necessarily
experience is not an evil. They vainly blame death through wars, since it brings nothing except what is established in nature. But if someone says that the cause of war itself is evil,

whether it is anger, hostility, or arrogance, he does not go beyond what is right. But this is charged against human beings, who have become like this through the wickedness of their own will. That death is not an evil at all is also made especially clear in the following way.
For if it had not been decreed for everyone, the righteous man would have remained forever engaged in the labor of virtue, receiving no fruit beyond sweat and toil.

The wicked man, too, would have continued forever in the ease of sin. Both outcomes would have been very unjust. But death both puts an end to the sinful ease of the wicked and gives rest from the labor
of righteousness to those who do good. For this was necessary: that human beings should also be able to live [?], which is the reason they can also overcome. And this very
power was given to them by God for acquiring what is noble and good. Yet in many people it inclines toward the ease of sin. So that virtue, which is mingled
with difficulty, may be admirable, death benefits both the righteous and the wicked: it gives the former rest from toil and puts an end to the latter’s sins. Since death is therefore found not only
not to be evil, but also to be good—and not, as the madman Mani says, because it supposedly releases the soul from matter, which does not exist, but in the manner we have described—
why does anyone devise another principle for the evil of war, instead of blaming only the evil, unjust will of those who engage in wars? For what happens,
as one should rightly consider in the light of God’s providence, not only through war but in every form, is wholly good in its nature, and not merely free from evil. This is evident to the wise.

Henceforth, let us blame not the death that occurs in wars, which is appointed for our benefit, but the evil will of those who engage in them. It is all the more unjust to exclude, on this account, the one who governs through providence.

Again, the wicked madman Mani finds fault with other forms of death, and also with earthquakes, famines, pestilences, crop failures, locusts, and other things like these, claiming that they too come from a principle
opposed to God. Yet it is evident to everyone how, amid great ease and an abundance of everything, almost all

human beings, with few exceptions, habitually become lax in their minds, sink and fall under the passions, and surrender themselves to pleasures and desires. And remembrance of virtue, labor, or the fear of God
is found in none of them. This same thing happens in a similar way in any circumstance.

For when people have abundant food and drink without measure because of their great prosperity, and their bellies grow very fat, their understanding becomes dull, their thinking becomes arrogant, and their soul becomes heavy and falls into the passions

of ignorant error. But if one of the adversities mentioned above occurs, people concern themselves less with their bellies and less with their desires, and they improve and benefit in their way of life.

as it can do more when people are caught in these things than when they luxuriate in ease. Which things, then, are designated as evil, according to his statement? Those which, even though they distress the senses,
nevertheless help greatly through their effects. And which things are good? Those which bring ease, yet sometimes prove harmful.
And how does evil not appear to encourage and urge people toward virtue more than good does? For often those who were not turned toward virtue
by luxurious ease have been changed by the adversities and troubles that befall them.
For people always need these reminders too, so that their minds may be awakened and they may recover and escape from their great negligence. For if, amid luxurious ease,
they were found and seen to keep far from great wickedness and to commit only minor faults, there might perhaps be grounds for a complaint that these things happen undeservedly.
But if they take the continual provision as an occasion to forget its giver completely,

the provision that supplies necessities without begrudging them, it is fitting and necessary that they should sometimes be awakened through adversities and sufferings to remember God, to whom we ought to give thanks continually and without interruption for his gracious care for us.
Thus God arranges these things to admonish people. He is not gripped by the passion of anger; rather, in his care for those who need discipline in order to turn back, he appears

in this way. For it would not be characteristic of excellent and exalted compassion to cherish and preserve human passions through kindness and, by not becoming angry, allow them to grow. On the contrary,
is it compassion if, wishing not to depart from this apparent kindness, he neglects people like a deceiver, allowing them to be completely overwhelmed and fall under the assaults of evils?

Rather, in accordance with proper order, he necessarily brings distressing things too. For a father who beats a misbehaving son is not considered cruel. On the contrary, if he does not discipline him and turn him back,
he is thought not to act with a father's compassion. Nor is a physician who cuts and cauterizes the [?] of an ulcer cruel. Rather, insofar as he is concerned with the proper practice of his craft,
because he has compassion on the sick person, he offers him harsh and sharp remedies that cause pain. For the sick person will die from the malignant ulcers if, in this way,
help is not brought to him. And if it is judged that incisions and cauterizations should be applied to him, he is healed and made well. People bring painful things upon themselves more than God does—

those who, by their own will, first multiply both the need for these things and the occasions for them through the passions of their souls. For it is not the physician who creates the occasion and the need for cauterization, but the ulcer and the pain themselves

that lie before him draw the physician to them and call for cauterization. In the same way, human passions call down upon people the providential care from God that is appropriate for their healing. And it never happens to people
that he fails to care continually for his creation. For he has allowed people to choose virtue and good and noble deeds freely, and he also supports them in their weakness toward the passions

through those things by which he openly admonishes, rebukes, and reproves them from time to time. He does not bring these harsh things constantly and incessantly, lest he abolish their freedom through the compulsion of grievous blows.
Nor, again, does he let the headlong rush of their negligence run loose and unchecked, lest their advance in the passions be left without treatment.
And as these things develop, he guides people with wisdom beyond words. He knows the appropriate time for each of them.

For sometimes earthquakes, a lack of rain, or an invasion of locusts appear, and immediately they make everyone bow down in fear and approach in supplication the one who can change these things. And if
those things customarily considered pleasant and agreeable raise and exalt people's thoughts and minds, while distressing and painful things awaken them [?] to a proper fear of God,

how can anyone fail to recognize and say that the former occur for the body's sake, while the latter are arranged by God for the sake of souls? What, then, should we call those things that awaken souls to the fear of God and to virtue?
Those evils are not evils at all. For although they seem painful to the senses of those who endure them, they necessarily come upon people for their help and healing.
So Mani himself, who is truly mad, does not know that he is fighting against himself at every turn. For if the growth of matter is harmful,

who does not realize that the opposite of what he says is the case? For matter grows to people's detriment when they indulge themselves luxuriously, continually pursue pleasures, and enslave themselves to their bellies and to what follows their bellies.
But it is diminished especially through famines, disasters, and pestilences, which do not allow it to advance and proceed unchecked in its growth. Consequently, this man ought

to call those things good rather than evil, especially according to his own argument. And he would thus have seemed to favor a better argument, if he had not, in turn, called those things that bring ease,

which belong to the other [?], evil again in his argument, making the opposite accusation [?]. But both are good, since they come from the good God. Yet because he delights in sins, in order to demonstrate

the existence of what he claims and supposes to be evil, he is distressed by those things that clearly come from God for correction and instruction, and through which people are helped and become better.
And very often, even worthless people are transformed fully and completely into virtuous people, exposing the teaching of error and showing that it has neither foundation nor stability.
And along with all those things, there are those that God ordinarily gives to all humanity in common.
If no interruption ever befell them, people would attribute their provision to the unchanging course of nature. Even when receiving them, they would not acknowledge the goodness of their giver,

nor would they ask for them while they already possessed them. So from time to time they are deprived of them a little, so that they may ask; and they receive them again so that they may acknowledge the goodness of the provider and know that he is their giver,

and that it is not some other nature apart from God that provides for them indiscriminately and without change. God wants people to recognize the goodness that comes from him, so that they may be worthy to receive

the things that come from him, not because he gains any benefit from them. He also wants these same people to ask him for good things, so that, when they receive them from him, they may be conscious of his provision.
For he rejoices when he gives what comes from him, but he rejoices still more when he gives to those who are worthy. For mercy is, as it were, treated with contempt in this way,
if it is not shown to those who recognize it. And [?] is all the more apparent if, besides receiving, the recipients honor their providers above everything else.

And if cities collapse because of an earthquake that grows great and extensive, as happened a short time ago, in the days of the man who acted with great wickedness and revived the error of idolatry, sin is destroyed and error directed against God is diminished.

Nothing has happened beyond natural death. Discipline and correction from God are certainly not evil, unless we are to call the helpful divine dispensation evil and blaspheme. For the man who criticized the birth of children,

claiming that it is the growth of matter—if this same man calls the sudden death of many people evil, does he really seem to possess human understanding? He invents and says things that fight most strongly against him. But

neither is the birth of children evil, since it continually brings life and renewal to the mortal race and adds those who come into being to creation; nor is death evil, even if it comes suddenly upon many, since it was not for harm that God

imposed it upon humanity, but for an excellent benefit. It is decreed for the righteous and the wicked alike. For what naturally happens from time to time to one person or another, if it comes suddenly upon many,

comes as something natural, and there is nothing beyond that. Yet this whole event reveals the providence of the ruler much more than what happens from time to time to one person or another, since in the latter there is not even a single

demonstration of the condemnation of sinners. But this event, through fear of the wrath that is displayed, helps those who die in the manner described earlier, and turns back and disciplines those who remain alive.
But if someone says that, although many such things happen repeatedly, human life remains as it is, gripped and entangled in these sins,
it seems to me that he is like someone who, seeing fish in lakes and seas, supposes that the craft of fishing is ineffective, because the fish that are caught are not
seen, while those swimming in the sea are seen; or like someone who sees many sick people and supposes that the art of medicine accomplishes nothing. For although many are helped

toward reverence for God and virtue through those terrifying events that God brings about from time to time in his providence, the pleasure-lover denies this conversion and correction, and mocks the obstinacy of many
and reproaches their persistence in sins, although we too [?] that these things do not lead the many by force, but serve to turn discerning people around and bring them back from sins.

For this reason they come briefly, in small measures, and immediately cease: so that they may not lead by force, but bring people back through persuasion. Immediately, however, the customary course of things resumes, so that they may test the will of those
who turn back and change, and so that the mere memory of their manifestation may serve as a support for the weakness of discerning people. Let us also say this: if, even when
such things happen, those who take notice of them are few and small in number, how much more would people's minds grow and advance in wickedness
if discipline and correction did not come through them! And even if no one benefited from them—which would be foolish to say—it would be better for people to be reproved because they are not even

brought low and turned back in this way, rather than for God to be blamed for neglect, because he does not even employ discipline. Let him use this very argument against those who take no notice. For it is clear
to discerning people that fear not only brings a few to the transformation of complete virtue, but also secretly diminishes and reduces the eagerness and boldness of many in wrongdoing.
Let us now also come to the discussion of created things, which that deceiver maligns without cause. First let us inquire about darkness and night, which he especially said were evil—
he whose own mind is dark. For this empty-headed man supposed that the darkness seen at night comes from that Darkness, as he calls it, and he came forward just as he is: someone who does not
see except like a blind man, and as though he needed no argument at all to substantiate this false statement of his, since, he says, it took its name from this, from something hateful.

Let us therefore say that this is indeed called darkness, but it does not have a substantial existence. Rather, it comes and occurs every day, passes away and changes, being an accompanying condition. Like evil, it has no substantial existence at all as a created thing.

Rather, it is the shadow of the created world. For just as a human being is born within it, and his shadow also accompanies the solidity of his body, yet the shadow is never thought to have been fashioned together with him, but comes and falls upon him

and passes away and changes according to the movement of his body and the passage of the light over him, so night and darkness, too, are merely an accompaniment of the world because it is bodily. They were not, as created things with their own being and substance,

fashioned. Rather, of necessity, the whole interior of the world is shaded and lies in shadow, because what illuminates it is outside it. For God willed it so; we shall explain a little later for what reasons.
For in the daytime, too, the height of solid bodies casts its shadow on the side opposite the position of the light, and it shifts
with the light to the opposite side. Where the sun is until midday, there the shadow is after midday.

And where the shadow was before midday, the sun is afterward. The shadow, however, is—the shadow, however, is—a shadow in the daytime, but not completely [?]. The places where there is shade, it allows
to share in the radiance of the light. But if you close up a house completely,
whatever house it may be, so that you leave not even a narrow entrance for the light, you make it like night, because the sun changes its position. Thus night is clearly the absence of light.
But a person can learn this by knowing and understanding that even at night the sun exists and remains wherever it is, whereas during the day darkness does not exist at all.
Rather, it is completely dissolved and abolished. Thus light has had and has its own subsistence and existence, but darkness has none whatsoever.
But let us consider how necessary and indispensable night was, since it is, first of all, the common provider of rest for everyone. For sleep, even during the day, demonstrates
and shows especially that night was necessary and indispensable, since all this is its appointed season and time, not [?] to give rest to people's senses.
Not everyone, however, shares equally in daytime sleep. But the allotted rest of night belongs equally to everyone, without any
inequality favoring those who enjoy greater prosperity in human life. This itself bears no small witness to the equality that the Creator grants to the one human race.
33. Again, if it were continually daytime, with no interruption in its course, time could not be counted, since it would not be cut into portions
and divided. The daily separation and division of time into its portions makes it possible to count it. Without knowledge and discernment of time, human life would be without reason and understanding
in many respects. And this too is important: there would be no enjoyment of light if darkness were not placed beside it in this form

of night that has been described. For unchanging, continuous physical light would not even be recognized as light. It is through its distinction from darkness that it is called light and is light. Nor
would it be seen to be as wonderful in its creation as it is, unless this thing placed beside it, which seems to oppose it, revealed it. Therefore, in many respects, let us give thanks for the grace

of the Creator's wisdom, which fills everything, on account of night, and especially because it has produced in us both the perception of light and the enjoyment of it. Otherwise, light would not be known for what it is.

At this a person is amazed and marvels at God's inexpressible wisdom: although all these things, and still more besides them, are necessary and useful benefits that people receive through darkness, nevertheless,

because it is darkness, both in name and in reality, he did not establish it as something with an existence of its own. Rather, he made it an incidental condition [?], occurring and passing away, so that it might appear as though it existed, for the reasons already mentioned

and for many other reasons connected with it, and yet also as though it did not exist, so that its Creator might not be blamed at all. Night, then, is beyond reproach and is wonderful in every aspect of its usefulness.
But they say, 'The robber does evil at night.' What does this have to do with night? As though those who wish to do evil could not do it during the day as well!
The nighttime should not be blamed. Rather, the evildoer waits for the moment suited to the evil deed, whether it happens to suit his wishes during the day or during the night.
We should blame the doer's will, not the time. Indeed, if every evildoer obeyed the night, he would certainly sleep, for this alone is what it permits.
After these things, let us consider how light and darkness seem equally opposed to one another, as do truth and falsehood. For just as light is to the body,
so truth is to the soul; and just as darkness is to the eyes, so ignorance and falsehood are to the mind. For a human being is nothing other than soul and body,
and God provides for both. Through the body a person enjoys physical light, and through the soul, the truth found in knowledge. But just as darkness has no existence
of its own and is merely permitted to enter, as we have shown, so too falsehood did not arise from any independently existing being—that which presumption
calls 'what did not exist' [?], flows and comes. Nor is it any being with an independent existence and life. Rather, it is only permitted an opportunity to exist, occur, and pass away,
like darkness. This itself is especially useful and necessary. For if the opportunity for falsehood and its cunning were not permitted, there would be no testing among human beings,
and the choice of truth would be made without examination. Even its name would be empty, if it were given a name at all.
If he had not permitted the tricks and schemes of falsehood, no one would have been a lover of truth either, if this had not depended on him and he had not had the power
also to devise falsehood. I do not say this as though falsehood were preferable to truth, but because the choice of truth would not seem to exist

if the power to lie were not available alongside it. For it is fitting that a truthful person should also have this within his power, and be free to lie, so that by refraining and keeping away from it he may be truthful. For it is through this that

both the choice of truth and attachment to it are made available to human beings, since they are also free to lie. In the same way, the presence of darkness prompts the senses to recognize light. And just as,

then, light shines in darkness—for by its coming it dissolves and abolishes darkness, since darkness has no independent substance—so truth too, through its victory over falsehood, exposes it as something that does not, fully and absolutely,

exist. Rather, through the tricks and schemes made possible by the mind's freedom, it reveals its own choice. For how could anyone choose truth if it were not also within his power to choose its opposite?

If, then, it were possible for someone to see that darkness possesses being and substance, and is not merely something that happens incidentally and passes away, as we have said, existence should also be attributed to falsehood. But if neither
he nor anyone else can see that [?] this darkness is imperishable—it both appears and disappears in the form and shape of a shadow—and light, moreover, exists even at night, while darkness

does not exist during the day, it is clear that falsehood, which resembles darkness, likewise has no substantial existence. It is merely permitted to arise through contrivance, for the sake of choosing truth.
But because light possesses being and substance, truth too is clearly understood to possess being, so that their resemblance and comparison may be preserved precisely. What, then,
prevents us from thinking of God as truth and calling him truth? For if God is light—intelligent light, not visible light—it is clear that he is truth. For intelligent light
is nothing other than truth. That is, because God is light and truth, it is not because of weakness that he keeps away from falsehood. For he knows and does not lie.

And although he knows, it is not through weakness that he refrains and turns away from falsehood, but because he never wishes to lie. But whether he is also unable to do so, we ought not to say, since he never even wishes to.
For with those who may either wish or not wish under different circumstances, their ability is rightly distinguished as well. But with God, since it never even happens that he wishes this,

let us acknowledge that he cannot, in this sense: because he never wishes to, and not because he is unable through weakness or deficiency. For something created is fettered and bound by its nature. I am speaking,
however, about physical light. And it is not unreasonable to say that its being light comes not from itself but from the one who made it. But to suppose that the Creator himself is subject to

the compulsion of his nature is very unreasonable: to suppose that even his ability to [?] does not come from himself, but that he is governed by his nature under compulsion, when he simply is what he is.

In those whom he created, he established that they should necessarily be what they are by their nature. But no one established in him that he should necessarily be truth. Therefore he is high and exalted above nature,
he who established natures; and he is free even from the compulsion of nature. For in this way we confess that he is truly good. Therefore, for the reasons stated, he is not a liar.
For a liar is someone who lies: he receives the name from the act, not someone who does not act, from something that does not exist. For falsehood does not exist before the person who devises it.
In the same way, darkness too was not created as an independent substance, but comes in as the shadow of this whole world. Yet darkness is not merely permitted to run its course; there is also much

benefit in it. The possibility of falsehood, however, makes the choice of truth clear to human beings. But if falsehood is valued above truth, it is exceedingly harmful and unreasonable. For falsehood, the children of
People [?] are exposed. But bodily darkness was established by God. Therefore we ought to flee from what we know, and not revile this, which God established out of necessity.
But that inventor of a new blasphemy against God reviles not only this, but also the animals and creeping things that have received an irrational nature from the Creator,

and openly, like an enemy who finds fault with everything, he rises against all created things. But our argument will restrain his foolish blasphemy even concerning those things against which he brings accusations.

For he finds fault with all four-footed animals and creeping things. I think this man resembles a very wicked servant who loves foolishness: he would welcome all the other things in his master's house,
but hate and find fault with the scourge of discipline, even if it were seen only in a corner. Yet by this very hatred of it, he himself shows that it is necessary. They are easily [?].

If there were nothing in the visible creation worthy of their fear, they would separate themselves still further and withdraw from God of their own will. Nor would they rightly be blamed because, through something visible,

they were not awakened and stirred. For although we have this freedom in our nature, to choose virtue by our own will, nevertheless, because of our weakness, we easily fall into error when we are at ease.
There are therefore many things that necessarily awaken our minds through fear and direct them toward God.

Through delight and the enjoyment of good things, we are led to acknowledge the Creator's grace. For through both we are instructed and brought up: both through the things in which we delight as pleasant,
and through the things by which we are turned back as frightening.

An irrational creature, then, is frightening by nature, not evil and malicious. Since it was fashioned this way, it is free from all blame. But God, who has compassion on human beings, made them so that, through people's fear of

those irrational creatures without speech, their rational minds might pursue good and beautiful things. There is no evil in these creatures, not even one. For how can something that does not know what it is be blamed for what

it is? Yet the argument that the mad Mani invented about evil, which he called the primal principle, is exposed no less by these considerations. For he did not give it awareness and knowledge of its own evil,
so that it would not be found to possess even the good of awareness. For in this way it would have appeared not to be evil, since knowledge of good is evidence of a nature that is not evil.
And when he declares that it is without awareness and devoid of knowledge, he also takes away from it this knowledge of what it is. For if it perceives and knows its own evil,
it continually perceives [?] the goodness of its opposite as well. For through the knowledge that perceives evil, it also comes to know the proximity of good.

Where one opposite is not manifest and known, its counterpart is not manifest and known either. For every opposite bears witness to its counterpart through the knowledge that distinguishes them. But without

knowledge, neither of them makes the other manifest. If, therefore, evil does not even know itself and does not apprehend its own evil through knowledge, it is not evil either, and it is pointlessly blamed for

something that it does not know is in it, since it is free from knowledge of its own evil. For we are all accustomed to pardon a person who does not know what he is doing, whether because of an attack of fever or some other affliction.
Indeed, we are all the more inclined to compassion and mercy toward him, and we acquit of evil someone who strikes without purpose and, if a sword comes into his hands, even kills. And likewise,

this is evident to everyone, and this distinction and judgment are universal. It accords with nature that we should not name and call someone evil when he does not know what he is doing. If, therefore, not even something that knows the good is called

evil, and something that does not know what it is is not regarded as evil either, then it is not evil on that account. But as for his not even making this supposition [?], in this too he has made his assertion in error and outside the common understanding.

Likewise, none of the irrational animals and creeping things is evil, since it lacks awareness and discernment. A human being, however, is evil through wicked habits, and knowingly does those things that he understands fully.
For an increase in natural knowledge brings blame upon the evil that is already present and prepared, and what is being done is clear and known to it. But the absence of knowledge also removes
the cause. Thus, because a person knows both virtue and evil, he is named after whichever he chooses, since knowledge precedes discernment and choice.

But before he knows, while he is an infant, he is not called by either of those principal names. It is therefore clear from every consideration that both evil and virtue are attributed to knowledge and to the choice that follows knowledge.
Those animals and creeping creatures, then, which have no knowledge are not evil, nor do they come from evil. For even evil itself, if it is like this, is not evil.
On the other hand, it is often seen that even among creeping creatures there is something harsh.
I mean the bile that diligent physicians take for healing. Mixed with those substances that can combat it, it dissolves and at times also clears away severe ailments and pains.

The flesh of creeping creatures themselves, mixed with other roots and substances, becomes a beneficial medicine for the body. In the same way, certain parts of other animals and creeping creatures—their limbs and even their blood—by themselves

often help and heal the sick. How, then, can those creatures come from evil, when at times even their parts are beneficial? All these creatures, then, appear to serve a purpose solely for the sake of human beings.
Yet they are called neither good nor evil, because they necessarily produce fear in human beings, so that they may turn toward virtue. They also restrain the idle pursuits
in which people engage, and curb their idleness. For these creatures are placed like a disciplinary whip displayed in a house to inspire fear in its inhabitants
and those who pass through it. The idleness of human beings [?]. For these creatures are placed like a disciplinary whip, which remains unused if none of those in the house does wrong.
But if we can see even wicked people who suffer nothing from these creatures, let us marvel at the patience of the Lord, who bears with their wickedness. Yet let us regard the whip as no less

an instrument of discipline placed nearby. But if, on the contrary, even good people are seized by these creatures, let us know that the Lord also has compassion on a good person who does wrong, to bring him back, unlike the person whom he entirely
neglects and bears with. For the former commits offenses for which there is a cure, while the latter is being kept for a punishment that cannot be cured. For we can find very many examples like these
written in the Holy Scriptures. For God cares greatly for human beings. For this reason he has placed beside them, in every form, things that shake them and awaken them to fear, so that
not even their sleep may be free from persistent urging. Rather, even sleep itself is disturbed by those apparitions [?] and, like a goad, stirs, shakes, and awakens their understanding and mind.
There are many things that wonderfully help human weakness to remember God.

For through what a person suffers bodily, he is freed from the passions of the soul. And through what he may suffer, even if he does not suffer it, a person is necessarily turned toward fear and falls into it.
He is caught up in human sufferings so that he may escape what is truly the only grievous suffering, namely sin. For the person who is without pain is without discipline and without punishment.

And the person who goes unpunished when he sins is utterly ruined. For if, even when all these things are set close at hand to inspire fear, human beings are for the most part grievously sick with fearlessness,
how could they have regard for one another if nothing frightening hung before their eyes? For illness, too, softens and relaxes a harsh mind.
Often a storm that has wrecked a ship has changed a merchant’s deceitful conduct. Again, poverty has brought low and humbled someone who became proud through wealth.
The loss of children has shamed and corrected someone who acted oppressively because of his children. But if it has not shamed and corrected him, it has become an example to those who take notice.
