Those children, however, have suffered no harm at all. Rather, they have benefited all the more, since they have escaped the upbringing and conduct of wicked parents, and those parents’ oppressive behavior has been restrained. Again, if the children of others who are good should die,

children, or how they would turn out unlike those who fathered them: perhaps they would become an evil image and likeness of good people; or, if they were good, [?] when they grew older they would change and become evil.
And they are helped by not being left to their own devices, since God orders all these things through his foreknowledge.
Fears are very necessary and useful, and there are many causes of every kind, countless in number, for those things that God orders and provides
for. These things often happen together through intertwined causes of every kind. One person falls ill because he is being disciplined for his sins,

and another so that, because of his [?], he may be trained still further in endurance; and another so that, because of his virtue, he may be trained still further in endurance; and another so that he may be restrained in the excess of his wickedness.

The very same event has many causes of every kind. One person falls and is brought down from wealth because he did not conduct himself well with it; another, because he did not make good use of God's care.

Another is trained in virtue through poverty; and another voluntarily throws off the burden of possessions so that he will not be hindered in virtue. No one can easily understand each individual instance

accurately, among the things that God orders for human beings in his care. But the few things that can be understood serve as testimony that those which cannot be understood should be believed. For some of them he himself also

reveals and makes clear to human beings, so that the things they perceive may serve them as a step, and they may use them to rise toward him. But he conceals many things so that they will not be known, lest he become

a teacher against himself, teaching them not to trust him. For it is not right to demand a demonstration of every single thing that comes from God. Otherwise, knowledge of this kind becomes far worse than ignorance.
For this very reason knowledge is concealed, because it teaches [?]. Otherwise, none of the things that God orders would be accepted

as things he orders justly. For faith in God is excellent, and its perfection is this: even when knowledge does not see what is being done, it trusts the uprightness and justice of the ruler [?]. For approaching him in everything through demonstrations

is not faith—this is especially clear—and would not constitute faith. For many people do not even investigate and question their beloved friends, but, in their agreement with them and attachment to them, their pure love, without questioning,

they bring to fulfillment. For they are readily reproached for distrust if they only ever show their confidence in them after putting them to the test. So too God, who wishes us to be this way toward him to an even greater degree,

does not reveal and display the whole working of his providence and his ordering of our lives. For he wishes us to trust him more, not to distrust him. Yet he does not conceal his entire ordering of things either.
Rather, through a few demonstrations he gives our understanding support in some way. Those, therefore, whose wills are upright
and who fear God perceive these things immediately. They always preserve their memory and remain like the good soil that received the seed,
and rejoice in good things. Those whose understanding has been buried beneath the great weight of habitual sins, or through imitation of others who are outsiders
and opposed to God—such as those that I too have brought forward, which are also found among others [?]—have their understanding assailed, and they drive away from themselves the perception
and help that come from these demonstrations. Let these things be added to what has been said about the providence of the God of all over everything.
The question we were asking in our discussion concerned all animals. It has been shown, through reasoning about nature, that they are not evil, nor do they come from any evil [?]
whatever, and that they are very useful to human beings in awakening fear in them. For if everything in creation were only gentle
and full of delight, and there were absolutely nothing that silently inspired fear, it seems that human beings would be badly nurtured and brought up without fear.
But these creatures also have fierceness mixed into their nature, and beauty is blended with their fearfulness.
Alongside these there are also others that are not suitable as food for human beings, nor do they provide coverings for clothing, nor again are they savage and frightening, but only

They speak of the diversity of things in the world. It is clear how all animals, both tame and wild, and those that are variously colored, are subject to the creative power and will of one, and continue to exist, and are kept from harming

one another. They are equipped with a rich variety of endowments of every kind. Some of them possess invincible strength, while those that are weak prepare escape for themselves through the agility of their nature.

Others are equipped in other ways. Those that seem to be without weapons have some other form of protection that provides a means of preserving them: either they have been given a [?], or they hide underground.
Thus the Creator has enhanced the world's beauty through variety. Among creatures that differ in their characteristics, he distributes help to them all, so that not even one of these species
should succumb and perish through the weakness of its nature. Likewise, against the changes of the seasons, they are clothed in coverings of their own thick hair and in tough skins sufficient

to ward off the harm of winter and heat and to cover them. They are also made so that they can easily lie down and rest on the ground, since they seem to have bedding of their own beneath them. Some of them have been allotted the bearing of few
offspring, either because they are not easily caught or because their lifespan is long. But those that are easily caught and handed over for daily use are able, through abundant reproduction,
to preserve themselves. Different foods are also prepared for each of them, and generous provision is made for them all. Thus even those roots that are thought to be deadly—
not one of them is destructive by nature. For what harms one species helps another. How, then, can the very same thing be both destructive and helpful by its nature?
The diversity of the species that use them required a varied provision of things of every kind, so that even among creatures without reason, a trace of reason might be seen through the Creator's law.

For there is not a single one of them that does not know what is suitable for it. Nor, because they are animals and their nature is without reason, does any one of them take something deadly as nourishing food.
Instead, each approaches what benefits and nourishes it. For if all roots and all grasses were suitable for all of them, the Creator's law would appear deficient,

as though it had no hold even over creatures without reason. But when something lies before them that is harmful to some, while that very same thing benefits others, this clearly proclaims the wisdom present in everything, since even

creatures without reason can distinguish between the foods before them. For if this ability were not present in their nature, someone might find fault with [?] in these harmful things, as though they came from evil.
But if discernment of what they need is already present by nature even in animals, and each of them chooses and gathers what is suitable for it, then clearly
all roots and grasses are useful, even if not to all animals. They are set out in variety before creatures that are themselves diverse in every species.

Thus let this accusation of the mad Mani also be restrained and brought to nothing in this way—his accusation against the roots that are called deadly. He has contrived to find fault with everything. For in the same way he also speaks falsely about iron and

fire. Yet even in these matters he does the opposite of what he intends. For while he accuses Matter, which he has groundlessly invented in his madness, he appears once again as its patron and as an advocate pleading its case.
For he hates those who destroy Matter as though they were evil. Iron and fire were sown in the earth by the Creator, and were discovered through human knowledge with God's guidance.
Without them, human life would have suffered severely. For although Mani considers them harmful because they destroy
the bodies that fall into them, they prove far more beneficial and helpful because their use is essential and required for everything.
Human knowledge discovered them from the beginning. From whom, then, does this knowledge come? Is it, as he says, from [?], or from the Good One? But it is clear that the wisdom of knowledge
is good and is a gift of the Good One. Against whom has iron ever leaped of its own accord? It is placed solely at the disposal of knowledge, and serves and benefits every craftsman. But
“A person,” he says, “killed with it.” And what connection does this wickedness have with the craftsmanship of the one who used the instrument? For if there had not been someone using it in this way,

iron would not have been thought evil. For if a murderer wishes to commit murder but refrains from the deed, is it not clear that it is the will that performs the act, and that the iron is innocent? So even if he commits the deed, the iron is not the cause,
but rather the person who used the iron unjustly in this way. And if he strikes with a piece of wood, throws a stone, or strangles someone with his own hands,
he calls these things evil too. Everything is especially blamed by the mad Mani, while he does not blame what is truly the cause: the mind.
For all those things mentioned along with iron are neither good nor evil. They are directed and drawn toward whatever is desired by the person
who uses them. They are placed before him merely as instruments and serve the person who uses them. If these things had not been entrusted to human beings,

a person would not have practiced any craft, nor would he have had those many useful things supplied to him without stint. More importantly still, he would not have been able to examine and consider virtue, since he would have had no instruments placed ready before him

that could be directed toward the practice of virtue or of evil. He would not have had within himself and of himself the distinction that virtue brings, and in this respect especially he would have seemed deficient
and disadvantaged, falling short of this victory [?], if it were thought that his only reason for not undertaking evil deeds was that he lacked the things with which to commit them.
For someone who does not act fully is idle and deserves no praise. “But look,” he says, “at what happened!” Yet what happened beyond what necessarily occurs?
For death did not originate through the murderer; rather, it was decreed by the Creator. But if someone takes care to rebuke iron, wood, stone, fire, water,
and things like them as though they did evil, let him leave aside their use, since they are instruments, and blame only what happens through them—I mean death.
Let him first refute and demonstrate that this itself was not decreed justly and fittingly by the Creator. Only then, finally, let him call those things evil
that assist evil. But if no one can demonstrate that death is evil, and if, on the contrary, as we have shown in many ways,
it is beneficial, how is it not pointless and futile to accuse the things through which death occurs as though they were evil by nature,

when they do not know for what purpose they are being moved? They are moved by others to whom they have been entrusted, and they are free from all blame. It is right to blame only the person who moves them when he ought not to.
Thus it has truly been demonstrated that nothing in creation is evil.

Only human understanding and the mind have necessarily received this authority. Sometimes the mind sins and is reproved for its sins, merely for honoring something hateful and evil. Yet it cannot bring about anything contrary to nature,

nor is it in its power to make what is above become what is below. Rather, it does only things that belong to nature, even though it is accused of doing them unjustly. For example, in murder it brings about death, which belongs to nature,

and does nothing beyond what belongs to nature. Yet this brings reproof upon the person who does it. Likewise, in adultery and other things like it, the mind is accused only of making improper use of them.

But it is entirely unable to bring about anything contrary to the nature decreed by the Creator, so that the boundary and order established for nature by its Creator remain unchanged, enduring and untransgressed.
Sins operate within these things that belong to nature, introducing nothing new. They merely bring reproof upon the person who commits them, because he sins by his own will.
For otherwise he could not have been victorious, unless the opposite course had also been within his power, so that by willingly fleeing from sin he might acquire virtue and become virtuous.
Hence it is an act of folly and fundamental error for us vainly to blame iron, wood, and other things like them, rather than blame only the person who uses them unjustly.
But if someone asks why a human being is killed, the answer already given many times is repeated: why, then, does a human being die at all? This very thing may be seen [?]

to be evil, and responsibility for it rightly falls upon the one who decreed it. But if death is not evil, there remains only the permission of the one who, through his providence, directs human affairs.
You may ask why a human being meets death through murder, since death is not evil by nature. This is found to happen for many reasons of every kind.

It happens for reasons that it would be pointless for us to enumerate. For the very same thing happens both to the righteous and to the wicked for different reasons: not to the righteous for their harm, nor to the wicked as punishment. For
what belongs to nature is not punishment, but serves as a demonstration or to prevent greater evils. There are many reasons why God allows a human being to be killed. Yet it is clear how

nothing beyond what is decreed by nature happens. For even if the opposing forces are at peace [?], whether those of fever, excessive fullness, or, on the contrary, hunger, or cold, or heat, or burial, or

stoning, or the sword, or fire, or water, nevertheless, in all these cases, what happens and is undergone is one and the same. And what is this but what the Creator decreed, well and providentially, for our entire race?
Thus, in many other ways too, it is evident that nothing in creation is evil.

Nor is anything in God's governance blameworthy. Rather, everything came into being and was created through glorious, inexpressible wisdom, and is governed through inexpressible providence, so that it should not be
easy to attain knowledge of those good things and of those things that seem painful. For it would not, it seems, be fitting for the signs and purposes of God's wisdom to be grasped in everything,

and for that hidden, incomprehensible knowledge of God's wisdom to be recalled [?], and for that hidden knowledge, which cannot be recalled or expressed, to lie completely exposed before human beings in everything. For even a human being who is a king
or a governor often has many hidden thoughts and intentions, so that even when something is done, it is not openly apparent on what grounds and for what reason it is done. It is therefore no wonder

if human beings cannot give an account of God's entire governance. They ought to submit and remain silent even without extensive investigation, and not rebel at all against his hidden, inexpressible governance.
For often we do not even question a skilled craftsman, whether in building, shipbuilding, or metalworking, because we feel shame before him,
when he performs each individual task within his knowledge. Instead, we trust his experience and wait to see the finished work itself. And it is possible that sometimes, even if we are deceived [?],
we do not notice. What, then, shall we say about God's wisdom, which is high and exalted above all knowledge? Whether we know and understand it,
or whether we do not know and do not understand it, we ought to marvel at it, wonder at it, and honor it.
But if someone, because he does not understand the explanation of the many things that come from God, is overthrown and falls into an evil, erroneous attitude toward God, he is more miserable
than anyone and utterly senseless, because he uses the very blindness of his ignorance as a guide. In this same way, this Mani too devised a harsh and bitter madness against those
who are persuaded by him. Because he did not understand how our human affairs are governed, he invented and proclaimed a sovereignty of two beginningless principles of evil [?],

so that he might stumble even over the things above in the heights, and not allow them to understand the things below. He invents all these things and blasphemes against the God of all, thereby proclaiming his goodness and his patience,

with which he has endured his wickedness. For he divided the things belonging to God and attributed many of them to that evil which does not exist, so as to blaspheme the Creator completely in every respect.
He says that proper prayers coming from God exist in the composition and well-being of evil [?].
What, then, does he say about the primary nature of bodies? For there are four things that people customarily call elements, those four which are opposed
They belong to one another, yet they are strongly opposed to one another. Not one of them, however, can accomplish anything independently, all by itself.
For what is the dry without the moist? Or what is the hot without the cold [?]? If, then, the mingling of these opposites produces and completes the finished state

of bodies, let him specify which of those four belong to evil and which belong to the Good. For if he invents and asserts a mixture of good and evil in everything, he must necessarily divide those four into two groups.
He must divide these either equally or three against one. But whichever of them he assigns to the Good, that very thing is found to be capable, in and of itself, of causing harm and injury.

For there is not one of these four that is not harmful when unmixed. Thus, even in their mixture, whichever predominates becomes a cause of the body's destruction, as those who understand these things say.
If, then, the hot burns in and of itself, the cold chills, the dry dries, and the moist moistens, which of them does this deceiver assign to God?

For every body contains a mixture of them, like a lump, and for this reason it is compounded and has an individual existence. But each of those things from which the mixture comes into existence cannot itself be found to be mixed.
Consequently, there is no justification for dividing each of these elements between two opposing principles and supposing a mixture in each of them. For what composition can this deluded man contrive
for the dry? And what mixture, again, for fire, which is unmixed? Or what mingling for the cold, which is cold throughout?

The same applies to the moist. For these clearly have a single form and are indivisible. Furthermore, none of these has an independent existence all by itself; rather, they have their existence together.

He therefore raves with great and terrible madness when he says of fire that part of it belongs to the Good and part to evil. He is necessarily compelled to do this same thing with the other elements too, dividing things that do not admit division.
For the dry is dry through and through, and dryness is pure and simple, having only one form. Nor can the cold even admit a means of division, since it is one, pure, and simple throughout.

The same applies to the moist. And what opposition from evil can there be in something that does not even admit division [?]? For it has not admitted mixture either, since it is itself unmixed. A body that is mixed can also, in principle, be divided.
But how can an element that is unmixed be supposed to be mixed and compounded from opposites? And what opposition can anyone
conceive of in fire, which is unmixed? If, then, each of them is entirely harmful in and of itself, and not one of them, according to that madman's statement,
is appropriate and suitable for the Good, then all of them must be assigned to evil. Bodies are therefore not compounded from both of them—a conclusion foreign to Mani's teaching.
How, then, does he suppose that the healing and nourishing part of fire comes from the Good, while its destructive and burning part comes from evil? Unless he has also invented a mixture
of bodies from good and evil and asserted it in his madness. Because of this opinion, he is compelled to set apart for the Good whichever of those four elements he wishes, whole and undivided,
as they are by nature. Thus he is evidently admitting that even from God there is something unmixed that is harmful in and of itself. Yet this senseless fool divides
the indivisible nature of fire, saying that one part of it heals and another part burns. The barbarian does not understand that the distinction lies in its use,
and not in the nature of fire itself. For proximity to fire without moderation is harmful,
while a measured distance from it provides a beneficial interaction. In another respect, even the burning power of fire by itself is necessary and required to exist.
For fire bakes and melts the things necessarily brought to it for use. Thus fire is nothing other than burning, and nothing else
is necessary or required except this. But he insults fire without reason, because he is utterly ungrateful for the benefits that come from the Creator of all.

But if someone supposes that all four elements belong to evil, how can those that are opposites be considered to come from a single nature? For if heat comes from this side, cold comes from the other side,
or conversely, the other way around. The same applies also to the other pair. Consequently, the mixture of the elements cannot even hold together according to an account such as
this. But if we attribute the formation and invention of all four to the resourcefulness of evil, it turns out that evil is exceedingly wise—this evil
that possesses neither knowledge nor understanding! It would even deserve great admiration and the status of a creator, if it knew how a body could hold together.

But because he praises the sun and says that, as he supposes, it does not participate in the mixture of evil, let us approach the subject of the sun too with a love of truth and examine it. For it turns out to consist of one of
the four elements: I mean the hot substance. For it not only harms the things placed beneath it, but also heats this surface so that what seems like a hot iron is
its surface beneath the feet of those who tread on it barefoot. Many times people have also fallen under the sun’s scorching heat and perished from its great heat, because they did not
find nearby anything with which they could obtain relief. It also blackens and burns bodies, and plainly performs the work of fire. Indeed, it produces fire [?],
if someone holds water in a glass vessel facing it. For through the purity and transparency of the water
and of the glass, the force of the sun’s ray is concentrated and forced out. When it comes close to something that catches fire easily, it immediately produces fire.

It plainly convinces anyone who is not excessively eager to argue that the sun is like fire, and that it is foremost among the luminous works of creation. For the nature of fire, too, is found to be finer than anything else.
For all the other elements move downward, while fire alone leaps above the things that are burning. Its course is upward in everything, since its fineness makes it light.

It also demonstrates that the air is dense by passing through it, so that this too shows its fineness, because it is of the same kind as the sun. Mani, therefore, who made the sun his god, claiming that it comes from the nature of the Good,
finds that it resembles fire. That is, he plainly introduces the Good as being like this. For since the sun consists of the hot substance, it differs in its formation
from fire, but in its activity it does exactly the same thing. If the extent of its lofty distance did not save the things lying before it from the harm of its activity—but
it would even be considered destructive to all animals and plants, if the Creator had not provided other protective things along with it, through which there is help against the sun
both for us and for the other animals. These are hollows and coverings. For plants, too, the supply of water and the blowing of the wind provide help. Consequently, even
those who have supposed that the sun is a fifth element dispute what is evident. And this very Mani, the madman who raved violently and blasphemed against the Creator of all, should by no means
be believed when he compares the sun to God and says that it comes from God’s own being. For everything visible, because it is a body, is by nature the opposite of the one
who is invisible and incorporeal. It is his work—indeed, it is an especially wonderful work of his—but it has no resemblance whatsoever in nature to its Creator.
It would therefore be a great task to enumerate all the wicked things that this deceiver put in his writings. For he insults everything that exists as though it were evil.
He also condemns all the fruits of the earth together, claiming that they nourish matter, while he expresses great admiration for the sun and says that it comes entirely from the Good.
And he is not ashamed to attack bitterly the plants and seeds that it nurtures with its heat, which could not exist at all without the sun that comes from God. For just as the sun would be of no use
if the provision of rain did not also water the plants, and the blowing of the winds [?] did not stir to help them, so too rain and those other things would provide no help without the sun.
So here too this man vigorously fights against himself: he bitterly condemns as evil the fruits of the earth, which are nurtured by the very sun that he admires so greatly and honors.

As for the rains, he says that they are superfluous. He explains that they are the sweat of the rulers of Matter, who in their lust throw themselves against the power of the Good One, and so grow weary, toil, and sweat.

He also tries to show that they are superfluous and unnecessary, as he supposes, by saying that rain falls even on the seas and on uncultivated wilderness, like someone who has come forward to draw up an account

foolishly against God, alleging that he spends his wealth of water uselessly and wastefully. Because of his madness and unrestrained stupidity, he does not see what is fitting and proper for God: how,
if God were poor in water, he would give it carefully and in proportion to the need for it. But since he is rich—how rich no one can even say—through this very

abundance he shows his generosity by watering even the sea, from which [?] water rises into the air by means of clouds. In the wilderness and uncultivated land, water is necessarily stored underground to provide for those within it
and for those who sometimes pass through, so that they too may find pools of water for their needs. In short, for the most part he does not leave land unwatered, to be
burned by the sun’s heat alone. For either through rivers or through rain, all of it is refreshed with moisture by God. So if there is no rain, this man and his disciples readily
blaspheme; and if there is rain, he does not stop making empty accusations and speaking against God. Even when they hold bread in their hands, those who are disciples

of blasphemy first curse, and then eat their fill and are satisfied, these ungrateful people! Though they enjoy created things no less than anyone else, their tongues are sharpened for nothing but attacking creation,
that is, its Creator. Like wicked enemies of God, they receive what comes from God and then complain and scoff about this very fact: that they need created things. And the bearing

of children they dishonor, wishing their sexual union to take place without it. They are servants not of procreation and fruitfulness, which God ordained by law as necessary, but of their lust. And they are enemies

at all times of everything belonging to true and pure virtue and reverence for God. They complain, as it were, about the continual life of the human race, wishing the course of their nature to halt and stand still. They lay down

a law for God, and grow angry and complain about God’s goodness, through which he bears with their wickedness and blasphemy. Yet it is precisely for this reason that he naturally kindles sexual desire in the body, so that with little effort,

as though compelled by the impulse of nature, living creatures may proceed to the work of procreation and fruitfulness, through the wonderful wisdom of the Creator, who established this too. For the pains of childbirth are hard on women,
and raising those who are born is hard on both men and women. But fruitfulness and procreation are necessary and greatly needed. Desire is therefore stirred naturally and, as it were,

leads by a kind of compulsion. Yet the mind and understanding, acting reverently and rightly, clearly carry out procreation and fruitfulness rather than merely gratifying desire. And fruitful desire is blameless, if

it holds to the knowledge and law of the one who made it. But those who constantly take pleasure in their lust hate its fruits, which are necessarily needed. They advise women who transgress and fall outside their vows
to use some means to destroy and expel what they have conceived, rather than wait for labor and childbirth at the proper time, as though this alone were hateful and evil. They are enemies of nature,
that is, of the one who created nature. And they have learned great peacefulness toward everything!

“Why,” they ask, “is sexual desire present in the body?” But how could the beauty of chastity have been seen in any human beings unless they experienced desire through their nature, and through their understanding and their will

They were victorious. And how could women have practiced virginity, or men have refrained from experiencing and knowing sexual intercourse, through a chastity superior to ordinary chastity, unless in their minds and wills they had acquired a love of holiness and purity

by which they struggle against nature and are seen bearing the prizes of victory—those who have nobly resisted and conquered the desire implanted in them, not to dishonor nature, but to train themselves in endurance, purity, and holiness.
Likewise, although we find relief in food and drink, we do not indulge ourselves in blameworthy ease, for this too belongs to nature. Yet we train ourselves through fasting,
and in this practice, which is above nature, we are not training ourselves against nature. Rather, we love endurance, and through humility we plead with God. It would not have been possible

for us to undergo the discipline of fasting if there were no hunger in our bodies. Everywhere, then, desire is directed toward both moderate use and the victory and praise that come through abstinence according to
one's strength. For using natural things does not dishonor them; rather, sin does that. Wine in moderation is helpful, but the evil of drunkenness enters through sin.
In the same way, the moderate use of food in accordance with nature is blameless, but indulgence in an unjustified excess is condemned. Likewise, the desire
for sexual intercourse, when exercised lawfully and with a sense of moderation, is entirely blameless. But its unlawful and immoderate exercise brings the blame that attaches to reckless conduct.

Neither Mani himself nor his disciples, then, saw or understood anything with knowledge and discernment. He treated everything with madness and contempt, saying that all desire is evil—this desire whose moderation

within the law is blameless, and abstinence from which, as far as possible, is a marvelous victory of virtue. For if someone is praised before God for abstaining from it and renouncing it, this desire is not evil

in its exercise of power, since abstinence from it is a victory that brings virtue to perfection. For it would have been a great loss if a person had no power over it, because he could not, through renunciation and abstinence,

have shown himself good. For unless he refrains from doing the opposite evil, which he has the power to do, he cannot be considered to have done the corresponding good either, as we have shown many times.
But Mani himself dishonors both goodness and virtue and condemns the power to choose and freedom. Nor is he ashamed to say that stones have a soul, and to say of everything that it has a soul.
He invents this about things that plainly have no soul, claiming that some of that power is still held captive even in stones. All this brings the one he honors into dishonor and degradation,
since he says that the nature of the Good is bound even in lifeless stones—the very things about which he argues that they are so [?]. What
greater expression of madness is there than this? For if the one sent by the Good is held captive even in stones, then the opposing evil has already conquered,
since the one who came to bind it has himself been bound. And he makes the sound that a stone releases into the air a sign and proof that there is a soul in stones and wood,
as though he had ever heard distinct, articulated sounds from them! Yet even within us there is thought and the soul's own speech, which is entirely inaudible.
What is audible comes about through the striking of air by a bodily instrument. This is found, apart from the [?] of reason, even in irrational animals, which cry out with a sound [?] without

articulation, because they lack reason. Thus every body that exists, even if it has no soul, has this property of producing a sound when it strikes the air. For what is without a body [?] does not utter intelligible things aloud,
because it does not strike the air, having no instrument with which to strike it. Otherwise, even the incorporeal powers would be considered soulless, because nothing audible comes to us from them.

So the very thing that ought to have been made a sign and proof that those things are entirely soulless—because they strike the air under external compulsion, something that belongs to a body alone and not to a soul—he has taken as a sign and proof that they possess a soul.
And here again he is very severely at fault concerning those who slaughter four-footed animals and birds that are useful as food for human beings, as though
the power that comes from the Good One, he says, holds their souls—as someone intent on thoroughly insulting in every way the one whom he calls good. But let us ask him by whose permission [?]

these very creatures were handed over from the beginning as food for human beings. Was it perhaps by evil, to insult the Good One? But evil could not have contrived this whole affair, since it possesses no knowledge.
For it is not even a creator, he says. Rather, as he said, God is the creator, who also, he says, sent a power from his own nature to arrange and order matter.
It has therefore become clear that all animals came into being by the Creator’s will, both those suitable as food for human beings and those unsuitable.
And no one else permitted these creatures to become food for human beings except the one who made them. For human nature itself would have known absolutely nothing
that was useful to it, had its maker not established this law for it. For this reason these creatures were also made naturally prolific, so that the supply of them would never
run short. And the more of them are consumed for use, the more numerous their offspring are.

Some of them merely provide human beings with nourishment, while others also clothe them, and still others provide other benefits, having been fitted by the Creator in their very nature for the service of human beings.
For this reason they submit to service, and even those with large bodies readily obey. Those in the air are caught through knowledgeable skill, and those in the water are brought up.

This is especially true of all those that meet human needs. Thus it is clear that human beings did not themselves forcibly subject irrational animals to their service against their Creator’s will. Rather, the law of the one who created them subjected them to human beings.
But let Mani himself say that it is not even right for an ox to be subjected to a farmer for working the land.
So that, he says, the soul sent from the Good One should not be thought to labor greatly in servitude! How, then, would our cultivation of the land have been maintained? And how would
the human race have survived without food? Thus Mani, who is insane in every respect, stands outside ordinary reasoning, utterly alien and opposed to creation.
For tame animals are by nature fitted for human service and are handed over for human use. Wild animals too are intended for service, although in other senses of the word,
in addition to the reason already given: insofar as human beings conquer and capture all irrational animals through knowledge. Yet by God’s permission, for many reasons of every kind,
it is not only a lion, which is a powerful animal, or another such animal, or a creeping creature, that overcomes a human being.

For even a gnat or another of these small creatures overcomes him. Moreover, wild creatures, as has been said, also serve another purpose: for human beings to observe and sometimes to experience. For various reasons they cause distress and are useful.

But since it seems wearisome to speak against each individual thing that he babbles and invents, and to answer him, let anyone with understanding consider, even without an argument, how everything is held together by a single word, and one

law of the Creator embraces everything. Nothing among existing things is in conflict, nor is any sign of war or division seen among created things. Rather, they are all at peace with one another, apart from the human being who sins.
It is as though they receive from one source the aim of peace and tranquility—from the one from whom they also received their existence in the beginning. For the things on earth are in harmony
also with the heavens, which give rain when the season requires it, and again withhold their rain when only warmth is needed for the fruit to ripen. The sun too, in its movement according to the law
of its maker, brings about seasons and times without ever altering its appointed times. It displays one inviolable order for them all, differing only in its arrangement. And one
and the very same harmony is clearly seen between the things above and those below. Night together with day has continued without conflict throughout all time since the beginning.
And it does not hand over to the day in a disorderly course, but according to the Creator’s wisdom, with measured increases and decreases. Nor do these things themselves
differently at different times. But the time of increase is clear, and the time of decrease is also clear. Nor does the sun find it burdensome to hand over to the night.

Nor does it consider the Creator’s law a disgrace to itself. Instead, like good servants, when it has completed its daytime course without resting, it goes where the law directs it and remains hidden at rest until
the night has received its allotted time. And what can anyone say about the earth and the sea—how each is enclosed and confined within its boundary, and neither takes even a span from the other?
Sometimes the sea is seen rising with its waves, but the law prevents it from crossing its boundary. When violent winds drive it against the land, it turns back out of fear of the law,
although no wall of adamant helps restrain it from flowing over the earth and disobeying its Maker. Rather, its Maker’s word is sufficient help for the earth against the sea, and sand holds it back.

This same law also restrains the force of the vapor outside and the flow of [?], so that no part of the earth is flooded. Created things are friends, like brothers to one another, and they show that their Creator is truly one.
Who has ever seen a star in heaven rise up against another star, or one species of animals on earth fight another species [?] to wipe it out, or, conversely, to be wiped out by it? Rather, even those

that attack one another individually—even these, under the law of the Creator’s wisdom, are taken for use from whichever species among them is more numerous. Both their existence and their being consumed for use are for human beings.

And if someone goes on in his discussion to the origin of bodies and points out the four elements, which blend into harmony despite their opposition, he will marvel still more at the concord of these things, which have their existence as though from one

alone. For their opposition is the cause of their friendship, and the fact that their natures contend with one another is itself the cause of their excellent peace. Although they are four in number, they are one in their mixture.

That is, they depend on one another for their existence, and through their very opposition they help one another. They are hidden in one another and are revealed through one another. It is a small thing to speak of how the hot is not cooled by the cold

or extinguished by the moist, and how the dry is neither burned by fire nor flooded by the moist. For they sustain one another and dwell wondrously in one another. You think that you have seen fire alone,

but it is not apart from the moist and the dry, through which it is nourished and gives light. Likewise, the other elements exist in one another, and their opposition is apparent only to the touch. They are such friends to one another that not even a single

division can be thought to exist among them. Even in their silence they proclaim the inexpressible wisdom of the one Being who created them, from whom they came into existence and were blended together. For a body did not come into being from just one of them, a single unmixed element.

For a body exists through a mixture. But what mixture can there be of the dry alone, or of the moist, if it is to exist of itself and by itself? Thus, intermingling was necessary and appropriate for the mixture

of a single body. Indeed, the opposition of those elements that hasten toward a single completeness was also most necessary and required, so that their Creator might be wondered at and admired. These did not first, of themselves,

on their own [?], and then come into existence, and then become mixed. Rather, they came into existence and were mixed simultaneously, receiving their existence together. At the very moment they came into being, they became distinguishable to the senses. For when the body came into existence,

reasoned understanding distinguished them through the senses. Through the senses of the body that came into being, it was found to be compounded of them, although they did not precede it in existence but received their existence simultaneously with it.

Who, then, can marvel as he should at the Creator’s power and at the concord and harmony of the things that have come into being—how they are all without conflict and at peace, apart from the wickedness of humanity?
Thus the whole creation endures, moving in an orderly way in its own motion and keeping the unchanging law laid upon it by its Maker. And who is this who has chosen for himself?

If he is sound in his soul’s perception, when these things are so, and there are also countless others that are exalted and lofty and surpass all knowledge, would he invent another sovereignty [?] in his argument and set it against that one, the sole Being and God?

For to invent, as though in a dream, another sovereignty that is harmonious and not different is superfluous, since that one is sufficient for everything. But to suppose it opposed and hostile is utter madness, when every

thing exists in harmony and peace, is adorned with variety, and displays its Maker’s wrath and kindness, and his splendor together with his severity. For all kindness that is wholly unmixed is harmful

and disorderly. Severity and harshness, on the other hand, left to themselves and deprived of kindness, are close to savagery and brutality. But the two together discipline and soothe; they entice and also frighten,

promise pleasant things and also threaten terrible things, hold out hope of gifts and also display the storm of punishment, so that the mind and understanding of those on earth may be guided and trained,

and may not sink through the slackness of ease into boundless contempt, nor again be broken and blinded by incessant terrors, but may be instructed by both in due measure and grow in the fear of God and in virtue.
The second discourse against the Manichaeans is finished.
The third discourse against the Manichaeans.

Now the things already said, drawn both from the realities themselves and from the thoughts within everyone’s mind—perhaps even the minds of those outside the church—give warning not to be carried away altogether and accept the blasphemy of that mad Mani against the Creator.

But because he contrived another harsh and wicked device against those within the church, forcibly dragging statements from the Holy Scriptures themselves after his lying argument, it is now time for us also to bring forward a refutation from

the divine Scriptures in opposition, to warn those who believe in them and are sometimes led astray by his disciples through foolish interpretations that never have any persuasive force. For by every device he contrives

to enrich his error with Satan’s assistance, and he strives to gain a hold among the pagan Greeks, not by dissolving and overturning their beliefs, but by extending their lesser evils into greater wickedness

and magnifying them. He teaches a [?] art of pagan customs, in matters in which he continually accommodates himself to everyone and agrees, as has been said, with their agreement in evil opinion; and to the teaching of error he adds an invention
of his own, introducing and imposing it. But among Christians, the things that belong to Christians

he pretends to accept. By making use of the name of Christ, the words of Scripture, and an appearance of humility, he covers the wolf that he is within, wrapping himself outwardly in a lamb’s skin, and becomes a deceiver of the flock.

Thus he brings down and injures those deficient in knowledge. And because he resolved to circulate and introduce a new wickedness, both from himself and from another, so that none of those who had learned of Christ would even
dare to inquire about the novel evils circulated by him, he calls himself the Paraclete. By using a name exalted and raised above not only human beings but even angels, he conceals his deception,
so that, because of the dignity and glory of the name, those who are otherwise senseless may accept what he says without examination. There are also times when
he even writes his wickedness in letters as an apostle of Jesus Christ—this barbarian, who is a barbarian both by birth and in his thinking. But we shall speak about those things at the end.

As for the Scriptures themselves, he attributes those belonging to the Old Testament, the Law and the Prophets, to that evil principle called [?]. But the Gospels and the rest of the teaching of the New

Testament, he said, were supposedly given by the good principle, as he believed. Yet even these, he claims, are not entirely pure of the opposing principle, as that inventor of blasphemy declares and boasts. For, he says, there are also
in them, as in some mixture, many things from what he calls matter. These things, he says, must be removed, and only those things that are reckoned to belong to the good principle

should be left in them. Yet the madman did not himself undertake to produce an established correction of the Holy Scriptures. All the more because of this, he dared to claim that he was the Paraclete, and he erased many things from them.

He left a few passages from the New Testament, however, which, through their mutual affection, seek out and indicate their agreement with those kindred statements that were erased. Yet he thought that he had exercised all this care,

leaving only those passages that could be forcibly dragged into agreement with the things he invented in his madness, and nothing less. We will show these things too, very clearly indeed, in our discussion.

First, however, let us show how foolishly he committed blasphemy against the ancient holy Scriptures. In this very matter he agreed with those wicked men before him who were denounced and expelled from the church, and in his wickedness

he surpassed them all. Now, if, like the pagan Greeks who do not fully believe the accounts in the Scriptures, he too had disbelieved and had said that, either altogether [?] or as though by chance, there happened

the things written in them, we would not bring any objection against him about these things, nor would he incur any great condemnation on their account. But since he too acknowledges that, yes, they really happened,
yet says that their cause is evil—which does not exist—let us now proceed and show how he attributes great deeds and astonishing wonders to that evil which he condemns,
and does not perceive, because he is blind in his understanding, the wondrous providence of God, the Creator of all, which is found in the scriptural account.
In his own words, either he or someone belonging to his party says this, writing a chapter entitled: “On the First Formation of Humanity.”
“For because the rulers knew that, when that portion of light which had once somehow fallen among them was taken away, death would quickly come upon them, the descent of the soul

into the body was their contrivance. They wanted to ensure that it would not run upward at all; and if it did ascend, it would be found unworthy of the dwelling there, since it was held fast in the body’s impurity.”
And again, a little later, he said: “For this reason, each one of the rulers of matter, in the manner we described before, because of that disturbance
which occurred, and because of what first appeared at the soul’s [?]—when the gates were first opened involuntarily in their alarm—each one sent

out the power within him and fashioned his own person beside the soul. He formed his likeness on earth, so that souls could be snatched away from it only with difficulty, because of the compelling force of the enticement of error.
“And their creation is the first Adam, the vessel of desire and the enticer of the souls from above, a device by which these souls fall into the body.”

Let us therefore consider first how much wisdom he attributes to those rulers of matter, as he supposes them to be—that matter which he so [?] condemns as being without knowledge. For, he says, so that they should not be deprived of that light

which had mingled with them, they devised the soul’s descent to them by means of the body, and they do not allow it to run back upward again. And if it does run upward, he says, it will be found unworthy of those above,

because, he says, it is defiled by the body. Thus the Good One cannot fully redeem the soul that comes from him, in its entirety and completeness, because he is defeated by the cunning of the rulers of matter. To say anything further about these things

would perhaps be ridiculous. But since he said that the first creation of the rulers of matter is Adam, the vessel of desire and the enticer of the souls from above, we have now learned that he explicitly said

that humanity was formed from that matter which does not exist. Everywhere he gives preeminence and honor to matter and to evil, while imagining that he is condemning it. And now too he has said of it that it made humanity,

which is king and head of all those living creatures that have bodies and inhabit the physical world. For humanity alone among them is rational and remarkable in its natural powers of thought, its skills, and its resources.
He also raises doubts about the whole world, asking why, he says, [?]. And concerning humanity, he even dares to claim that it is not God’s creation.
He thoughtlessly raises other objections too, saying: “How could God have given Adam a commandment? For it must be one of two things: either he knew
that Adam would transgress it, and not only gave it in vain but himself became the cause of the disobedience; or, he says, he did not know—and it is not fitting
that God should be subject to ignorance.” And he says that the commandment was given to humanity to deceive it, by evil, as he supposes, and not by anyone else; and, he says, he was greatly helped.

And that man was set free through [?] his compliance with the serpent’s advice—the serpent who, he claims, is the messenger of the Good One. For, as he says, the man had been blind, and when he tasted some of that
which he had been forbidden by command to eat, he saw, he claims, that he was naked, and used the covering he found. He also knew, he claims, both good and evil, and thus, he claims, all the more

he benefited by transgressing the command of the one who had deceitfully formed him. And how, he asks, as he puts it, is it fitting for God to say, ‘Look, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.

And now, lest he stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life and eat and live forever’? For if, as he says, it was possible for him not to lose his immortality, it was envy, he claims, that drove

the man out of paradise and prevented him from partaking of the tree of life, since, he claims, by receiving from it he could have remained immortal forever. Again, he also reproaches him over Abel’s murder.

And when he comes to the flood as well, he speaks abusively, claiming that it could not have come from that Good One against his own creation. Again, he also brings up the burning of Sodom and says that this too is the work of that ruling power, against whom he has reckoned all those things.

Again, he does not leave the righteous men’s taking of many wives without criticism. Nor does he exempt from criticism all those things that happened against the Egyptians, claiming that they display savagery
and great bitterness toward the Egyptians, and unjust partiality in favor of the Hebrews. The Good One, he claims, would not have commanded them to ask the Egyptians for articles of gold and silver

and, through the deception of borrowing, have made them owners of what was not theirs. Along with all these things, there is also the fire that appeared on the mountain, as though he thought that not even a word
was needed for his criticism of it. And Moses, he says, states plainly that God is a consuming fire. Along with what appeared, he also takes this statement as evidence for his criticism.

Therefore, through all these things and others like them, he dares to make the Old Testament opposed to the New, although he cannot understand even a single matter, and through the wickedness of his will
he is deprived of discernment and understanding, like those before him who did this very thing. In the end, he uses only those passages from the New Testament that he left

out of the many, supposing that they bear witness for him to the things he has said. He says in his own defense that it was not without reason that he dared to reject many things from the New Testament as well.
Thus, as we have said, this man’s foolish babblings are very numerous. His disciples take care to conceal his writings and do not put them openly before the public at all.

It is clear that they were instructed by that man himself to do this. From this he is plainly exposed as not daring to reveal and display the things he has fabricated. For error loves to hide and deceive, entering unnoticed

and slipping into souls; but truth is proclaimed openly and confidently. They, however, conceal their writings because they are ashamed of their deception, even before they are caught by those who are going to judge what has been written

by them. But although we have taken into our hands what is called the Treasury of his madness, we continually present for dispersal with a breath those few things that need it. And as for [?] speaking without end, all

his foolishness—we do not restrain it. For it is clear that when those great and well-known claims, repeated everywhere, receive the breath of argument that disperses them, they necessarily carry the lesser ones away with them as well.

There is therefore no other cause whatsoever for the world’s coming into being—this is his first piece of nonsense—except the Creator’s goodness. For he is Creator by nature, and he does not take counsel,
nor does he learn through experience, nor does he create under the compulsion of his nature. Rather, being good, he shows kindness to the things that come into being,

things of which he has absolutely no need. Rather, in his kindness he grants existence to those that do not exist, and grants that they should exist in a good condition. For as for what does not exist,
unless it is granted existence, how can kindness be shown to it—to something that does not exist? And if there is nothing to which kindness is shown, where is the goodness of the Good One?

For it cannot be what is proclaimed if he turns only within himself, from himself and toward himself. Rather, it is so when he provides for others and carries out what belongs to his nature. And henceforth

If it belongs to the nature of the Good One to help and show kindness, but no one is found to receive help from him, the Good One ceases to function. Therefore he is a creator, and it is not the things that belong to him that

help him and show him kindness; rather, he helps those things that come into being. For he is the one who brings them to completion, and thus he needs nothing—not even to be seen and known through the things he has made.

As for the things that come into being, unless they have a maker, they do not exist. Since, therefore, he is good, it is necessarily required that they exist—that is, those toward whom kindness is shown, since he is good.
And his goodness is beyond expression, and he is the one who never neglects to show kindness.

That God created and made them. For what greater kindness could there have been for those who came into being than this: that they should come into being from nothing? This reveals at once the maker’s inexpressible power
and his kindness: unlike a human being, he did not even need any matter to accomplish his will. Nor did he neglect to act, so that his goodness would remain inactive, for that was not even possible.
But now is not the time to speak against those who are uncertain and ask how something that comes into being can come from nothing. We say only that God, being good, granted existence

to the things that came into being. And, being wise, exalted and far above every mind, he composed everything that came into being completely and perfectly. Through their combination, and by adorning them as well, he fashioned the world.

Thus everything that came into being was collectively and rightly called “the adorned,” a fitting name. The adornment was not their own, for they did not adorn themselves; it belonged to the one who made them, because they also make him known.

And hence the things in heaven are evident, existing in their ordered arrangement, and all the things on earth are evident too. But whom would the usefulness of these things have benefited if humanity

had not existed? Apart from humanity, Mani’s madness finds fault with none of the things that came into being. For he does not seize upon anything in heaven as though it were at fault; rather, he especially

praises those things, saying that the sun and the other things belong to the Good One’s portion, as he supposes. Nor does he find fault with the earth or the sea, if he relaxes his great love of faultfinding a little.

For what fault can be found in these things? Thus all those other things, he says, belong to the Good One’s portion, as he supposes. Nor does he find fault with the earth or the sea, if he relaxes his great love of faultfinding a little.
For what fault can be found in these things? Thus all these things, those in heaven and those on earth alike, would be left to be regarded as superfluous, and necessarily
would be so if humanity did not exist. Consequently, humanity is indeed the chief part of the world. For humanity, the sun makes daylight at the command of the one who created it, and the moon also
marks out the seasons. The stars also show the routes over land and sea, along with the beauty that they impart to the heavens, like lovely blossoms among its flowers.

Thus the error of Mani’s wicked madness is especially apparent in these things too. For if God himself prepared the useful and necessary things, as Mani himself says—the sun, the moon, and the stars—but Matter itself

brought forth the one who uses them, humanity, through Matter’s rulers—they did not receive [?], but fashioned him—then God seems to have worked as a slave for the household, in that he prepared all those necessary and suitable things for what Matter fashioned.
For those things would always have been idle and would have existed in vain if the one who uses them had not necessarily existed.

Thus the whole creation was first put in order, and then humanity entered it, as though entering into the prepared use of the things made beforehand, when God said, “Let us make humanity in our image,

according to our likeness, and let them rule over all those creatures without reason”—those in whose likeness Scripture reckoned them. Thus humanity was established by God as the head and governor of all living creatures:

the rational being over those without reason, the one guided by wisdom and discernment over those without reason, and the one guided by wisdom and discernment over those bound by the compulsion of nature; the one who, according to the principle
of nature, also has his own nature under his authority. For he can restrain and check the activity of nature—that is, eating and sleeping—even though he cannot rise above it completely, but

Amid abundance, he deprives himself as much as he wishes, through the exercise of endurance and the authority of reason. Furthermore, he can submit to nature’s need without being governed by nature’s compulsion like those creatures that lack reason,

but knowingly, as though dealing with something else, he habitually supplies it with whatever it needs, after exercising endurance to the extent of his strength. The human being is thus shown to have been entrusted not only with authority and dominion over

those creatures that lack reason, since he too possesses their needs, but also to have authority over himself. For [?] reason, as the head exercising authority over his nature, belongs to his nature, so that, from himself and within himself, he can become either

the helmsman or the shipwrecker of himself, depending on whether he makes use of the reason within his nature. For this reason Scripture also says that he was created in the likeness of God, on account of his dominion, his rationality, and the freedom of his nature. He is not

therefore a slave to nature’s compulsion, like those creatures that lack reason, but is free through the reason belonging to his nature. He possesses dominion over those creatures that lack reason, and in these very things he preserves and displays the likeness of God.
For this reason, then, those creatures that lack reason were not deemed worthy of a command or an admonition, since they did not possess reason, which is what receives a command.

But the one appointed head and ruler of those creatures that lack reason, through his participation in reason in the likeness of God, is especially and preeminently honored with a command. For the honor

of the one who was made is that, through some form of reason, he should participate in the one who made him. A command and the admonition of reason bring the Maker’s fellowship to his creature. For the one

who receives a command knows, as far as possible, God who commands; and the one who gives the command reveals knowledge of himself according to the capacity of the nature of the one receiving the command.

The statement that he is the work of his hands is also made to honor his formation. For although the scriptural account itself says that he took dust from the earth and formed the human being, in this manner
visible in material things it indicated an action that is invisible. For everything is an act of will, not something fashioned by hands.

Nevertheless, he was called the work of his hands to honor his nature. Likewise, the statement that he is in the image of God does not refer to a likeness of nature—for it is not even possible to say how deficient and inferior it is—but to the image and likeness of dominion, authority, and freedom.
Thus that first man received a command. For he already knew, before the command, that he ought to obey his Maker. But for the testing
of his knowledge and also of his freedom, he additionally receives a command. It is as though someone had acquired an understanding and knowledge of some craft,

whether medicine or carpentry, within himself, and were then led to put into practice and action the knowledge he possessed in his mind, so that what he had learned and knew would not remain fruitless within him. So too the human being was not merely fully equipped in his freedom
to obey or not to obey, but was also adorned with knowledge of both, and through the command came to put into practice
those excellent capacities within his nature. The command frees him from compulsion [?] and teaches him obedience. Thus God, who gave the command, knew what would happen, but he did not deprive

the one who had been made of his freedom or abolish it. Nor did he withhold the command so as to nullify what depends on freedom, which from the beginning he had seen fit to grant him, so that the human being might thus be in God’s own likeness,
as befits the one who made him. For withholding the command would abolish obedience. But perhaps someone will say, “See how disobedience harmed the human being—a disobedience that was not unknown

to the one who gave the command.” Whether it harmed him or not, through the punishment [?] that was brought upon him, we will discuss shortly. For now, however, this freedom of his greatly helped him toward the excellence of his subsequent conduct.
For if he had not received a command, he would have had neither obedience nor the power of virtue leading to triumph and victory. Nor, indeed, would he have been considered obedient if he had not had
the authority also to disobey. For in being given the command, on receiving which his awareness increased, through disobedience his obedience [?], through an experience that taught him obedience.

For it is not possible for someone who has neither experienced nor known something to be persuaded beforehand, before putting it into practice. Rather, he must either accept it through the demonstration of others, or have it increased for him through his own experience.
For he acquired caution through disobedience—the caution that comes after experiencing disobedience, either one’s own or that of others, as an illustration applying similarly to every virtue.

Perhaps, then, someone will say, “The will of the one giving the command was defeated by the disobedience of the one who received it.” Yet it was certainly not defeated at all; on the contrary, it was not even left unfulfilled.
For by warning him through a command rather than leading him by force, he revealed and showed in this way that he wanted that person himself to be capable of disobeying as well as obeying,

so that this would come from him and depend on him, in keeping with the freedom of his nature. Consequently, the first disobedience of the human being who was created makes clear the will of his Maker.

“What, then?” someone asks. “Did he want that person himself to disobey?” Rather, he wanted him to have the power to disobey, so that through his obedience he might distinguish himself. For even if his disobedience first brought him humiliation and disgrace,

the disobedience was not caused by the one who gave the command. Yet he did not entirely prevent it either, but directed it toward the glory and greatness of the one who, through his freedom, was afterward destined to live in virtue. Thus he encouraged him all the more

toward that which was also fully within his power. For someone who has learned through actual experience how he can do both learns, from himself and within himself, to choose what is better than his former experience.
[?] necessarily revealed his freedom and the authority belonging to his nature. For [?] experience, nor full knowledge of disobedience. For even when the human

being disobeyed, he did not immediately perish or put himself beyond healing. For then it would have seemed that his own Maker had failed to achieve his will. Rather, he was only reproved so that he would become aware

of his power and the freedom of his nature would become clear to him. Nor, once he had become aware, did he receive another command and law by which to conduct himself. For he knew that he had discernment in his nature,

and knowledge of what he should do and what he should not do. Nor, when his Creator reproved him, did he advise him to repent. For this deed did not require healing, since he was not remaining there either—

the one who had disobeyed—in the place where he had disobeyed, so that he might thereafter be restrained from what he had wrongfully approached. Rather, he was making a beginning of his subsequent life and conduct, having experienced his own freedom.

But perhaps someone will say, “Look how much his disobedience harmed him! It made him mortal instead of immortal, drove him out of a paradise of constant delight, and brought him to land that must be cultivated

and worked with toil.” In response to these things, let us speak plainly. For I also promised a little earlier to say this: God himself, being good, in his goodness made the human being in the beginning

to exist and to be free by nature. He made him capable of choosing both virtue and evil. And since he was also fashioned with a body, correspondingly, so that he might live in the bodily world, he wished

it to be within his own power to choose either life or death. He did not impose the sentence of death upon him without a cause, but pronounced this sentence upon him for his disobedience, which he clearly
foreknew. He did this necessarily, and in a very fearsome manner. For it is impossible for a human being who has power over virtue and evil to be entirely without sin.
Indeed, his Maker did not demand this either. The freedom of the one who came into being bears especially strong witness that he also has the power to sin.
For this freedom alone also enables him to perform righteous deeds, as has been said many times. Death, then, carries with it the notion of punishment, but it is a wonderful and great gift

from God to the human being. What, then, is this gift? Although it has already been explained in another appropriate place in our discourse, it is this: that even someone who has already become accustomed to sinful conduct should not forever

live deathlessly in the evils he has freely chosen, increasing them greatly, but should afterward have some correction following death. Nor, again, should someone nurtured in the contests of virtue endure sweat and toil that never cease, forever.
Rather, both receive the end of their lives through great and exalted grace.

But simply because it bears the name of death, although it is a great and wonderful gift, he allowed the human being himself to become its cause. It was certainly not so that he would not be thought to have created him mortal.

But he took the fact that man possesses free will as an occasion to show himself truly a benefactor even in those things in which he seems to impose punishment on him. Yet human disobedience is not therefore to be regarded as acceptable to him, in that he wishes

it to be within man's power to choose death for himself. Rather, since this very thing is necessary and fitting for him, it is appointed for him by God: he also needed this providential care, so that, because he had received a beginning, he should also have an end.
For even if it had been possible for everyone to live without sins, yet they attained victory in this only through toil and effort, death would still have been necessary as a rest from the toil
of virtue. But if we acknowledge that virtue is acquired only through toil and effort, how could everyone together have reached a victorious conclusion, since their freedom necessarily
has the power to make them travel along varied paths of every kind—even those who have resolved to pursue only triumphs and victories for the sake of a victorious outcome?

If, then, the one who disobeyed was also transferred to lowly toil, anxiety, and sweat in the various necessary crafts, take from these very things that are written an indication of the foreknowledge of the one

who formed him. For before this man's disobedience, he said that they should rule over all these irrational creatures. But how would they have needed this authority over irrational creatures if they had always

remained in Paradise, where they would have been free from needing them? For neither were the irrational creatures accustomed to Paradise from the beginning, nor were they fit to remain there continually with man,

But the one who said, “Let them rule,” indicated the multitude and fullness of humanity, although at that time there was only one man. And this man did not first have intercourse with the woman who had been formed from him before

he went out to the place outside. For practicing the procreation of children in Paradise would have been unnecessary; it was necessary for the one who was destined to die, for propagation and succession. Where,
then, after his disobedience, he received a suitable place and a fitting occasion, there he also began to father children, so that from these very things it might be clear and known that

God himself, in his foreknowledge, prepares and orders everything beforehand, as it pleased him that the whole earth should be filled with humanity, and that those descended from that first man and the woman who came from him should not live in Paradise alone.

For it was God who, by way of blessing, said before man's disobedience, “Be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fish in the sea and the birds of the sky.” How, then, would they have

needed these things if they were destined to live continually in Paradise forever? And this saying, “Look, I have given you every plant that sows its seed on the face of the earth, and every tree that has fruit containing seed that can be sown;

it shall be food for you”—how does it not indicate that from the beginning we were formed for this way of life in which we now live? It was not disobedience that changed our constitution, as though the arrangement had been different at the beginning.

Rather, because disobedience was evident in God's foreknowledge, he prepared and made ready beforehand the things appropriate to it. For he knew what, because of the inexperience of the one who transgressed the commandment, would necessarily happen in one form or another.

And he allowed it to happen so that disobedience itself might also provide a beginning, without harm, for learning through experience to guard against harmful things. This would serve to establish man, as God himself had wished from the beginning, together with

making it clear that he wills this for man's benefit. For man was assigned not only the toil of virtue but also that of a craft, so that he might pursue the former victoriously and carry out the latter by the sweat of his brow,

so that through the endless continuation of life he might not be driven into incurable evil. For this very thing happens to no small degree even within a limited time, even when his toils do not cease.

God, then, did not act under compulsion because of man's disobedience when he clothed him with death and separated him from Paradise. Rather, it appears that they draw their grounds from his own providential ordering,
since this, then, is what he wills. But [?] God himself did not act under compulsion, nor did man suffer loss or harm by entering this way of life, which had been prepared for him beforehand by God.

the one who made him. But a testing of his conduct was necessary and required for the excellent life from which he had come, so that his return there might be gained through the labor of virtuous and God-fearing conduct.
with great honor. But what that one man experienced through testing is known to all of us through knowledge.
Therefore, whoever doubts whether God knew of Adam’s disobedience or not,

let his mouth be shut by this [?] form of the divine arrangement that has been described. For this reason, even the wickedness of disobedience itself seems very slight. For something that brings no loss
upon him does not seem greatly blameworthy either, whereas the very punishment that came upon Adam made his disobedience appear much worse. But if that punishment involved no

loss, let us consider what it was that was decreed against him. For from this we marvel all the more at the care shown in the account of him: in Paradise God set it apart, so that he should observe it and not approach it—

the human being who had come into existence. It was not that he should avoid approaching it as something evil, but so that he might exercise the freedom of his nature. For there was nothing harmful in Paradise. Rather, the command not to approach just one

of the things there was for the training of the freedom of the one who had been formed. Therefore he calls the tree the tree of knowing good and evil, not because it itself knew both, but because this alone had been established

through the command not to approach it, as a demonstration that the human being himself knew good and also evil [?]. For all the other things were set before him without fear, and they were not withheld, even by a word, from
Adam, nor did they testify that he knew good and evil. Rather, this tree alone was called the tree of knowing good and evil, because a command concerning it had been laid down as a law.

For through it, by means of the law he received, he was clearly shown to know good and evil. For every command is given to someone who knows both. Thus knowledge precedes the command, just as the eye precedes the sight of visible things.
The command therefore involved only training in obedience, and not a danger of sin. For what opportunity for sin did Adam have? He had no occasion for theft or adultery,
