nor did he have any occasion for murder, false testimony, or oppression. For this reason God did not forbid him any such things or give him commands about them—not merely because there was
no temptation for him toward such things in that place and at that time, but also because he had no need to hear them. For knowledge had already been implanted in his nature that, even if
he should have an opportunity, he ought not to do such things. For even the tree concerning which the command was laid down testified that he knew good and evil, since it was given this name.
He was trained only through food, for this alone was what he needed. Thus, for every person, testing and training alone are a constant need. He was therefore trained through
food, which itself was not naturally destructive and did not bring death, for there was nothing of that kind in Paradise. But [?] it was right that, in whatever

was among the things set before him, he should obey his Maker, whether he commanded him to approach and take it or not to approach it. It was simply that he did not obey the command. Nor was he blind: it was visible to him.

For it says, “The woman saw that the tree was pleasing to the eyes and desirable to eat.” Therefore, if he saw it before tasting it, he was not blind. And if it was beautiful to look at and its fruit was desirable, then certainly
the tree was not evil, and only their disobedience was exposed. In this way we can show that the very same actions may be both performed and forbidden, according to the difference

in the intention of a promise made by each person’s own will. For if someone promises, out of a love of endurance, not to do something that is permissible, he thereby restrains himself from exercising his freedom to do it. And it is not

the action itself, as it is in itself, that is then called into question, but the will of the person who made the promise, who has given the action a different character through the intention of his promise.

It belongs to him, and [?] and the commandment that restrains everything over which he has authority. He prepared and made ready a contest for the one who accepted it. But they both saw their nakedness; they saw themselves and felt ashamed after their disobedience. [?]

For this is what is remarkable: before he had experienced evil, he did not look at nakedness with discernment. But the experience of disobedience took away from him the innocence that had not experienced evil and cast

shame upon him. It was not, therefore, only when they ate that they saw: they had also been seeing before they ate. But [?] experience of evil and discernment [?] because they had transgressed the commandment.
As for the statement that the eyes of both of them were opened and they knew that they were naked: this is because every eye is so described when the mind directs it toward the things it sees.
For the eye has no knowledge or understanding in itself. Thus, often, when our mind is occupied with other things, we pass by someone like blind people,
even someone we know very well. And when we are reproached, we excuse ourselves by pointing to the preoccupation of our mind. So it was also with that couple.
They were moved to look with conscious awareness. For the statement, “They knew that they were naked,” refers to the discernment of knowledge, not to the sensation of sight.
For they could have known their nakedness even without seeing. Where there was no covering, they did not need sight
to know that they were uncovered. Indeed, the statement, “They knew that they were naked,” indicates a revelation that occurred in the mind, not the sight of the eyes.
One might also say this: before their disobedience, because it was not yet their time to have children, God had not given their union
an awareness of nakedness. Rather, they lived like beings without bodies, since the time for bodily activity had not yet come for them. But because disobedience, without
experience, happened in some manner [?] and brought mortality, and because decay entered on account of mortality, succession and reproduction were now granted to them by God.

With these came modesty toward one another, as they finally recognized the difference between their bodily forms—a difference that their Maker had foreseen for the reproduction and succession that would be fitting and necessary.
When he brought the woman to him, Adam said, “This is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.” And this is clear:

because he could see and was certainly not blind, he named what he saw. And when he had prophesied a little, the narrative says, “Both of them were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed.”
For if they did not see one another, what would it mean that they were not ashamed? How can someone who does not see feel ashamed before someone whom he does not see?
They could therefore see, but it was not yet the time for shame. When Adam was reproved for his disobedience and offered an excuse for having hidden himself,
he was afraid because he was naked. God said to him, “Who revealed to you that you are naked?” He did not say to him, “Who made you able to see?”
“Look, have you eaten from the tree from which alone I commanded you not to eat?” From this it becomes clear that no one had spoken with him or informed him that nakedness was disgraceful.
Rather, they knew it of themselves and within themselves, since shame had come in its time: from then on they would see one another in bodily activities, and from there they would depart to the earth
from which they had been formed in the beginning. Nor was it out of envy that God prevented them from making use of [?] life, as those disciples of the mad Mani suppose.
Rather, because living without death and in great ease would not help them to be without sins, on account of the freedom of their nature, and lest their sins too should be immortal like themselves,
God, for their benefit, prevented them from making use of what would have produced immortality in them, since it was seen to be good for the human being to be mortal.
But what God said—“Look, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil”—indicates the original formation of his nature, not that he had gained
knowledge of good and evil through his disobedience. For he had made him beforehand; and it is clear that, since he was formed in the image of God, this was already present in his nature.

Knowledge had been implanted in him, and God commanded him, as someone capable of understanding, about the things appropriate to his needs. This is also why the woman answers the serpent with understanding.

“He whom the followers of Mani praise is the one by whom I was deceived. For it was by a misleading statement that I, who also shared in reason and knowledge, was led astray and deceived.” How, then, can he fittingly
be praised—the one who advised the woman not to obey the commandment, lying and saying, “You will certainly not die”? For concerning those who were certainly and inevitably going
to die, the one who said, “You will certainly not die,” is a liar, like the madman Mani. But perhaps it is unnecessary to say at length that these claims are false.
But if someone says concerning this [?], from which Adam is said to have eaten and incurred blame, that it was such as to produce in them a lasting knowledge of good and evil, perhaps he has not

said anything improper. For the human being was free, rational, and capable of understanding the force of his Maker’s commandment. Nevertheless, he did not receive from the beginning the whole knowledge of virtue and evil,

but in simplicity, through the soul’s conduct and a quiet life free from care, he had previously received from God in Paradise something less than complete knowledge. Through that eating he came to complete knowledge.
For what is improper about there being such a tree in Paradise, one that produced knowledge of good and evil? And what, moreover, is improper about that disobedience,
which God knew beforehand would be of this kind, and which he allowed to happen to the human being, so that the toil involved in knowledge might be of great benefit
to the creature in attaining what is better? For “the one who has set knowledge before himself,” as Scripture says later, “increases
pain.” Instruction thus fittingly served to bring knowledge and discernment of the things that can be done and of their opposites. Therefore, no less evil
is the one who advised them not to obey the commandment—not only because he lied, something that is always foreign to an upright will,

but also because of his deceitful advice. For he framed his advice in this way because he thought it would cause harm. But he was mistaken and did not know God’s providence, just as it is said concerning God’s later, great act of providence: “If they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.”
For God often makes use of the evil one’s impudence to accomplish his own will, as we explain toward the end.
We also bring forward the events themselves, showing in what way the evil one also [?] in this manner, and we demonstrate this as far as our account allows.
From this it follows that he rightly received a curse from God on account of that first human being, because of the intention behind his advice, which, as he conceived it, was deceitful.
For he wanted to lead astray. That is why he spoke with the woman, regarding her as easily swayed and weak.

But even if God approached the couple as though in anger, this necessarily served to demonstrate the seriousness of the matter. For disobedience in itself is no small thing, even if it involves some discipline under divine providence.
Yet there was nothing beyond what was seen naturally in the woman and also in the man. Thus, then, and in this manner,
the person who has no love at all for faultfinding, but instead loves God, receives and considers the things concerning the first human being and the things said there.

But Mani and his followers have laid the darkness of error upon their souls, and they seek to increase it still further over themselves. Through matters that are unclear and require extensive interpretation
and knowledge from God, they thought they could confirm things resembling their blasphemies. Thus they read the Scriptures with an erring mind and find fault with God
even over Abel’s murder, although he reproved Cain, exposed the deed, and in many ways laid it upon Cain’s own head. Through his envy, Cain brought evils upon himself, while his brother

he did not harm at all. For if God had approved of the one who murdered deceitfully, they might plausibly say whatever they wished. But if he both reproved him and imposed upon him trembling and relentless, unceasing fire, and with a great and surpassing curse
confined him, how is he not good—the one who hated and rejected what had been wickedly done? “And why,” they say, “did he kill?”—as Cain himself said. “How did this very thing come to him? How?”
For Scripture did not say [?] out of love for truth, but he brought another accusation on every pretext. From [?] he plainly showed that he hated the deed.
But let it be said that, because of the evident envy and jealousy that arose in Cain through his own choice when he presented his offering and it was rejected,

God did not forcibly restrain him against his will from the treacherous murder of his brother, although he could have restrained him. Rather, it was so that, through the first pair of brothers, this rule might be established: that they should humbly endure—

the righteous, that is—the violence and mistreatment inflicted on them by the wicked. Thus Cain himself introduced the thought of murder into his own soul through his envy. But the rule of obedience and righteousness consists in the righteous being entirely unwilling to depart

from it, even if the wicked bring death upon them with iron weapons. Yet what loss did righteous Abel suffer by being murdered, when he quickly gained a return to the place from which his father had fallen?

For if his father suffered loss by leaving Paradise, Abel gained far more by receiving Paradise itself. It was also fitting, for another reason, that a righteous man should be the first to approach death, since it is a great gift

from God to human beings. It was also necessary that Adam should see it before experiencing it, so that, having tasted God's sentence through another, he might learn the sentence through actual experience and guard himself against sin,

in hope and expectation of the end. For it was possible for Abel to die in another way, even if he had not been killed by treacherous murder. But that death which comes through enduring mistreatment and violence is more excellent for the righteous person, for the exalted order and way of righteous living,
and as an example and pattern for those who are willing to endure this very thing because of their fear of God and their righteousness.
And if those against whom our argument is directed also condemn the flood as savage, making the one who caused it out to be evil, in accordance with Mani's fabrication—if,

by bringing the waters, he suddenly destroyed humanity, which they regard as matter—this act does them a kindness according to their own fabrication, because they say that it was carried out by the rulers of evil, just as

they themselves suppose. In this very assertion they do not realize that they are praising those rulers for their hatred of evil deeds: they introduce evil as hating evil deeds and describe it that way. For when
human beings were committing great acts of depravity, and a life of lawlessness and injustice was being lived at that time—which is why God said, “My Spirit shall not dwell in human beings,
because they are flesh”—how can the one who washes away the evil of depravity with water be considered evil? For if he is seen to hate a life of pleasure and unlawful desire,
how indeed can he be considered evil? But he says, “This deed is savage,” although it is evidently an act of mercy, the opposite of savagery. For it would have been great savagery not to frighten

and restrain those who were corrupting their nature through great recklessness and unrestrained desire. And those disciples of Mani would themselves have had much greater grounds for just criticism [?], because he did not

wish to discipline them, that God became the cause of the ruin of those living in depravity. For all of them were destined to die individually by their nature. If he suddenly wiped them out together with their entire race,
and their sin as well, to provide a fearful example, how did he not act like a judge wise in everything? Yet he did not bring the punishment by water upon them suddenly.

Rather, he first set a period of a hundred and twenty years, during which the ark was being built, to give those who saw and heard an opportunity to repent. He first expressed a sigh over his sentence. Then, because habitual sin overcame fear of the threat,
its actual execution followed; and he had also preceded it with a fixed period. But a chaste and righteous man was spared, together with his beloved sons, as a life-giving leaven for our race.
This itself is no less a demonstration and testimony that the one who punished those who were perishing through unrestrained desires is good and righteous.
For he restrained and silenced those who were behaving dissolutely, while he loved and preserved the righteous man who lived chastely.
For this is the demonstration and pattern of a righteous and good judge, and is not at all like that madman's fabrication about those rulers of matter—matter which does not exist.

For there is this saying of God: “My spirit will not dwell in human beings, who are flesh.” And it is as though he were finding fault with the flesh—something that even those without understanding find fault with.

In keeping with their foolish argument, they ought to have seized on the saying as something spoken by the Good One. But they have nothing to do with it. For although both belong to him, they perhaps praise the saying while dishonoring the deed.
Even if they accept the saying of the one who said that they are flesh, they nevertheless do not think that he spoke from a superior standpoint

about this, although he spoke rightly. For he does not find fault with the flesh, which cannot do anything by itself or for itself, but rather because they had extinguished their understanding in everything, and in everything their flesh

was being comforted and delighted through desires. They did not guide this understanding at all toward helping the flesh, but abandoned it to be thrown down and fall as though from a cliff, and turned their thoughts toward the passions of the body.

And if we still see the passions of desire holding human beings captive, let us not suppose that this punishment came upon those people for no reason—if indeed it was punishment and not God's great providential care.

And we should not call it [?]. For he knew that purity and chastity would have been completely extinguished among human beings if this example had not been set before them appropriately and necessarily. And again, from a man
who was righteous, our race was renewed. And it is clear that through this man abundant help was provided by God for the people who came after him,
especially for those living at that time, when the suffering was still fresh and new among them. But if it had not happened, God would not have done what was fitting for him either.
This same argument of mine also applies to the people of Sodom. Since the subject is similar, if we say the same things again, we will weary and tire the reader in every

place. For whenever the understanding sinks deeply and falls away from the thoughts proper to its nature, and through evil conduct willingly collapses beneath the passions, so that its nature is corrupted, God, who cares for human beings,
restrains and puts an end to what is being done unjustly. First he helps those very people who, in disgraceful practices

that are not right, have already become entangled, graciously giving them a swift and immediate end to their evil way of life. Then, for those who come afterward as well, he restrains [?] and checks them through

the example. For those who are readily willing, he fosters and increases the fear of him. Nor does he give those who refuse to be persuaded any grounds for questioning [?], so that they might freely continue their deeds.
Where, then, the things being done can be healed through the will of those doing them, and they have not fallen under the domination of wrongful wickedness, he guides them differently in his care
for them. He allows them to live and to enjoy fruitfulness and offspring, and in whatever other way is suitable for them, he acts for them so that they may escape and be delivered from evil.
For those who, after the flood, devised the tower made by human hands and planned to reach a path of ascent to heaven, and went far in their rashness, were not wiped out by punishment.

For their insolence was senseless, but they had not corrupted their nature through the passions of desire. Rather, through the wisdom of the one who cares for them, they were helped by the punishment they received. For each one

of them appeared to his companion speaking a different language, and they abandoned the agreement and harmony of their speech, which had been harmful to them. Each and every one of them became a father of nations, since separation from one another

was forced upon them through their knowledge of the distinct language given to each of them by God. For because of this they no longer shared one language: that separation affected them all. And in this way alone they received

punishment, so that they would no longer take pleasure in the association with one another through which they had wrongfully become arrogant. Those who came afterward, however, were greatly helped. Thus God, in his wisdom, even through the things

by which he punishes, everywhere helps and delivers. Through his providential care he turns even the rashness and insolence of sinners to the benefit both of those people themselves and of those who come afterward, by his own governance.

But let Mani himself show whether he considers these very things, and things like them, to belong to that Evil from which he said he had come into being, on whose behalf he spoke, and whose burden he took up.
This makes it strikingly apparent that this is a wondrous dispensation: he supposedly gave it, as though from himself, what it did not possess, and it became superior.

If he had openly been its messenger and had testified to this and those other excellent qualities in it, rather than our supposing that he despised it and called it evil! Everywhere in those earlier statements of his, he grants it priority, power, and wisdom.

What, then, can he say about those miracles in Egypt, performed through the agency of both those who opposed one another—Moses and Pharaoh—in their wills, though not in the power of their deeds? For Moses was higher and more exalted
than Pharaoh, so that he was regarded as his god. Which of those beings did he say it was? From which of those two principles did he declare that he had been sent? Was it

really of Pharaoh that he said he belonged to the Good One? For he also describes the ruler of matter in connection with the Old Testament [?], the one who resembled Pharaoh in his thinking in every respect. For just as Pharaoh said,
“I do not know the Lord,” so this man too, through the things he has invented, is condemned and reproved for not knowing the Lord fully, since he wickedly reckoned those miraculous deeds
that came from him as evil, like someone who shares Pharaoh’s anger at the rightful liberation of the Hebrews—or rather, because he was unjustly enslaving those free people.
Pharaoh inclined toward great hardness of mind, although, according to that man’s statement, he is supposed to belong to the Good One. Or if anything of this kind
is not said by that madman, it necessarily follows that Moses is God’s servant. For this is indeed the truth—not according to that man’s madness, but according to the order of the fear of
God, in which there is no opposing being equal in existence that is supposed to fight against God. If, then, Moses plainly belongs to God, it is God who brought those plagues upon the Egyptians,
not out of unreasoning anger, but for the instruction and training in the fear of God of that free people whom the Egyptians had subjected to slavery with great brutality.

What, then, is this Mani doing here? Has he perhaps taken both parties and, in his great generosity, given them to matter, as he always does for it? And how can those parties, which fight so fiercely against one another,
be regarded as belonging to one side, as he said? For it was not through the craft of the Good One, as one might put it figuratively, that matter here was being crushed by itself and within itself.

Yet even if he is bold enough to say precisely this—that killing, death, destruction, the changing of water into blood, the coming of hail, and the bringing forth of a mixture of creatures of every kind

should be regarded as having been set in motion against human beings by the thought and [?] of the Good One—if, on the other hand, he had no concern whatsoever for these things, but matter itself was moving against itself, by itself and within itself,

how did it contrive, through its rulers, to entice the souls from above by forming the body, as his book, or that of one of his followers, records? It devised all this against the Good One, yet it forgot this and did not know how terribly it was destroying and ruining itself!
But who, then, was standing on Moses’ side? For if both parties had been receiving similar blows together, perhaps, in keeping with that man’s madness,

this supposition would have been persuasive: that matter was acting against itself by its own authority. But if, while the Egyptians were being struck by plagues, the Hebrews were being kept entirely free from
harm and plague, who was it that, with all this wisdom and diligent care, stood on the Hebrews’ side? Was it
evil itself, or, as they are taught to say, like [?], its rulers? Then evil too evidently knows how to save and to destroy, to protect and to injure, to help and to harm.

And it is clear that, since it knows both alternatives distinctly, it appears to act deliberately in the very things it does, employing fully developed reasoning. It also knows justice, since for this reason it had mercy on the Hebrews, either because they belonged to it or because

they were being forcibly led away unjustly. And it did not have mercy on the Egyptians, either because they did not belong to it or because they were forcibly leading others away unjustly. But if it was capable of showing mercy,
Did it, then, also have compassion? Did it also have love? Did it also have mercy? And what becomes of that essential character of evil which, they say, has no share
of evil which, they say, has no share in even a single thought or understanding, if it was moved on behalf of the Hebrews and against the Egyptians? And how is it supposed that great zeal
for its authority was displayed by matter toward those [?] concerned with the righteousness of the Hebrews? In all this it appears not only helpful but also just.
But if we attribute the whole affair to the confusion and disorderly disturbance of matter, so that it knows absolutely nothing of what it does,
then those rulers of matter are no longer thought to do anything evil or to act maliciously against human beings deliberately.
But let us inquire again how such diligent and complete care was undertaken for the Hebrews, so that not even one of their irrational animals, much less a single
human being, fell amid this whole calamity of affliction and adversity. And who was it that, like a wall, diligently kept the Hebrews' portion entirely free from injury and
harm from the plagues that struck the Egyptians? For these things do not indicate confusion and unjust disturbance, but care that is diligent and wise in everything.
For while the Hebrews were in the midst of Egypt and lived there, how could anyone suppose that through confused disturbance it was day among them and night among the Egyptians?

And again, since the river has a single current, how could anyone maintain that through some chance event or disorderly confusion the waters retained their nature for the Hebrews, while for the Egyptians both

their color and their appearance were changed into blood? For if there had been separate springs, there would have been room to explain the provision for their needs otherwise than by supposing that these things occurred through diligent and wise care
But how is this not evident, and how is great diligence not visible in it, when the very same current of the river was blood for the Egyptians, but for the Hebrews was available according to

its nature, with its appearance preserved? And so it was with all the plagues, down to the killing of their firstborn: not even one of the Hebrews' firstborn fell, though he might perhaps have died in some other way,
had not the wisdom and diligence of the one who cared for them kept the Hebrews entirely unharmed.
And how, again, can those things that happened at that time be attributed to the confusion and disorderly [?] of matter, when Moses brought the plagues through his prayer and removed
them, so that at the very moment he prayed, the effect of the approaching plague was set in motion together with his word, and likewise the relief that it brought? And when Pharaoh was contentious,

he would tell him beforehand of the assault that would take place in this way, and through his prayer the effect of the assault came immediately. And when Pharaoh repented and made a promise, he would tell him beforehand

of relief and release, as though under an agreement, and through prayer he immediately brought the plague to an end. And it was not once or twice, but up to the full number of ten plagues, that he displayed such a
form of authority. That these things did not happen without providential care, nor through confused disturbance, I think not even the mad Mani himself can deny.
Who, then, was the one to whom Moses prayed, and who did such things against the Egyptians?
For who would not say that evil would not have listened to a prayer for the rescue and liberation of those who were unjustly enslaved by force? Moreover, even the magicians who opposed Moses plainly

made the power of the one who acted through Moses visible. For by means of magic they imitated Moses as far as the fourth miracle. But because they failed completely with the rest, the pretension of their magic was exposed.

They finally acknowledged concerning Moses, “It is the finger of God.” Those magicians, who served evil spirits, plainly said that they recognized that it was God who was performing miracles through Moses.

But Mani, who is far worse than the magicians, insults and despises the one who performed those miracles through Moses. And so, since Moses also invoked a certain living power, while the magicians appealed to someone else
[?] For neither Moses nor the magicians did anything by their own hands; rather, they called upon a power. Of which of them would someone say that it was good? And how is this not clear?

The magicians called upon the power of evil demons and received from them the ability to perform deceptive deeds. God openly permitted this and let it happen, so that, through their opposition to him and their matching of the things done by magic,

Moses would not be thought to have performed the things that were seen merely through some outward appearance [?]. For because they opposed him and were thought, in some of these things, to have acted like him,
yet failed completely in many greater things, it became apparent that the manner of the things happening through them was different from that of the things happening through Moses,
when they were plainly compelled [?] to testify about Moses that his deeds could not be matched, and said, “It is the finger of God.”
But if those disciples of Mani say that the evil demons themselves—that is, those who obeyed the magicians—were overcome in their power by Moses, then it has become evident [?]

that he is a prophet of God. Where the demons come from, however, and that they do not belong to another principle, we will explain in its proper time, when the discussion of Satan is appropriately taken up.

Whichever side of those two principles mentioned above Mani wishes to assign Moses and the magicians to, his tale is completely nullified and destroyed, since it is exposed as untenable from both sides. And how

does he dare to say that the magicians belong to the Good One, even if his disciples delight in the magicians tens of thousands of times, when those very men openly confessed, against him, that the finger of God was with Moses?
And along with this, let Moses again be supposed to belong to the opposing principle, as he said. How, then, does it both help and liberate those who belong to it, and perform wonders in every way,
and listen to the prayer of a righteous man, and show this pity and compassion toward those who belong to it? Not one of these things, according to his account, which has no foundation or stability,
is appropriate to it in any way. For there is absolutely no room on either side for supposing such disorder, confusion, and unruly disturbance, even though Mani’s followers are utterly shameless.

With all this diligence, care, wisdom, and distribution of the plagues, and the distinction extending to each individual, both among those who suffered and were being disciplined and among those who did not suffer, in accordance with Moses’
earlier words, down to the smallest details concerning each individual plague, as we said before—thus, to demonstrate at length against Mani, by these things, that equally from both

sides his argument consistently fails, is unnecessary and pointless for us. For we do not undertake to persuade his followers, but, as far as we can, to keep anyone else from being led astray after them.
46. The Hebrews were commanded by Moses that each of them should ask his Egyptian neighbor for articles made of gold and silver, and that they should depart in this way, so that justice might also

be fulfilled for them, and they might receive their wages for their slavery and the labor they had performed for the Egyptians. Yet does Mani himself dare to reckon the Hebrews’ crossing through the sea as the work of evil?
And was it evil itself that held it back and made it stand on both sides, [?] as though firmly established, and a dry crossing—on both sides, [?] as though firmly established, and a dry crossing

did it make [?] for human beings, and give the Hebrews a passage so that they could cross? But against the Egyptians it turned the waters back upon them, as though enraged. Why, indeed? Was it perhaps
because they worshiped magicians and [?], the serpent and the crocodile, and, along with these, the hawk, the dove, the wolf, and the raven? Then, it seems, matter avenges reverence for God.

And was it Moses’ song of praise that his followers composed and recited after the crossing? But why do I say that it was his followers? For it was his sister Miriam, a woman, and no one else, who composed it.

And if it had not been God’s grace, how could she have said openly, “Sing praise to the Lord, for he has been gloriously glorified,” when it did not belong to the Lord, as he said, but to the opposing power, matter? Yet she was praising the Lord.
And it was called “the Lord,” when Matter had conquered and the power belonged to Matter.

Yet the praise was offered in the name of the Lord, the one who had been defeated. And how, then, does Evil perform all these things, through which—if only we acknowledge the righteousness of the just and good Judge—these victories are displayed?

And how, again, through Evil’s activity, was the comfort of light provided to human beings at night from its own resources, while by day it refreshed and comforted them beneath the cloud’s shade, away from the sun’s blaze?

It is therefore clear that it also knows how to show mercy and perform miracles of this kind, even if someone assumes that it is Matter. And again, even bread came not from the earth, but from heaven:

Evil rains it down, changing the law of nature established from the beginning, and supplies bodies with what they need, not from the earth but from heaven, although, as Mani said, it is above everything.
“How much,” he says, “then, from their portion [?] Matter was bringing down bread.” Oh, the madness of that man and of those who think they ought to believe
him! And for forty years Evil sustained this entire people in the wilderness, carrying them and teaching them the law and an inheritance in every good thing,
and instructing them in everything good. And how is it evil, when everywhere it counsels and cultivates righteousness and does not allow anyone to harm a neighbor?
Consider: Moses fasted for forty days twice and brought the law. From whom, then, did he bring it?
And was it really Matter’s doing to write on stones, in its own writing, “Love the Lord your God, and your neighbor as yourself,”

and “Do not kill,” and “Do not steal,” and “Do not give false testimony”? For if Moses himself had decreed and laid out the law on his own, it could have been supposed, according to that man’s argument, that because there was also something of the Good in him,
he commanded and said such things. But if he remained forty days without food—something that human nature cannot endure—this was instead the work of God’s providence.
While he was on the mountain, he was openly receiving it; he was not writing the law from his own thoughts. And [?] the one who placed the Ten Commandments in his hands.

For the power that handed these things to Moses was not itself a mixture formed by the union of good and evil, so that they could then recognize what it was like from the character of its words. But are these words really fine
and good, while the one who established the law is not good? How is that possible? If, then, he is good, he is the same everywhere—the one who administered and gave the old covenant
of the law and the prophets. For it is not even plausible that Moses was sent sometimes by the Good and sometimes by the Evil. For if, as I said before, he himself had established

the law from his own mind, they could have said that he appeared to be a mixture of good and evil, speaking these things in one place and their opposites in another. But if some power was handing him the tablets,

the inquiry concerning him and his own nature should be dropped; instead, inquiry should be made—the inquiry concerning him and his own nature should be dropped; instead, inquiry should be made—into what this power was: was it good,
or, on the contrary, evil? But from the things written there, it is evident that it is very good, exalted above all wisdom and power; and it did not exalt Moses.

For he says nothing of his own. Rather, the entire establishment of the law, the history, and the miracles that took place there were openly accomplished through Moses by that very one who also, concerning the people who had gone astray and cast an idol for themselves,

told Moses beforehand, before he went down to the people, and hated what they had done. In the end he also brought it upon their heads for their help, salvation, and common benefit—both of those who remained and of those who died. If, then, from the history
and from the things laid down in the law, the power whom Moses served is shown to be good and fully powerful, how can the law be condemned
as though it had been given by Evil? For absolutely none of the things said or done in it fails to reveal goodness [?].
But because they do not understand or know the teaching about sacrifices, they suppose that the arrangement governing them is evil. For those who offered them were not meeting a need of God.

[?] But for themselves, in this worship, they used whatever form they thought proper. God, however, accepted the intention with which they made their offerings in the fear of God, and not the offering itself. For look:

he turned Cain’s intention in sacrificing against him because of his wickedness, since it was an act of contempt rather than honor. He rebuked him for the distinction he had made, acting wickedly and honoring himself above God,

offering the inferior things and keeping the better things for himself. Thus he accepted only an intention marked by righteousness, and accepted whatever was offered out of love for him, whatever its nature.
For nowhere is there found a command given by God to those righteous people of old to offer sacrifices.
Rather, those early people offered the firstfruits of what they possessed of their own free will, and God rightly accepted them.
But if God explicitly commanded sacrifices through Moses, it is all the more fitting to marvel at the mercy of so kind a lawgiver: for those who thought that there was absolutely
no other way to worship him, he stooped and humbled himself so far as to appear to need what he did not need, and to accept what he did not require.
For those who had been brought up in Egypt, according to the custom there, he did not wish merely to change the form of worship, since they were unable to rise to spiritual realities,
but rather their understanding of whom they ought to offer sacrifices to. And if, indeed, it was the very things they had wickedly worshiped in Egypt
that they were commanded to sacrifice, you should regard this as a means of turning them away from their wicked custom.

We have shown from what was said earlier that these very things were provided by God from the beginning for people’s necessary use as food and for other needs. Moreover, in another way he also explains the reasons

why they were commanded to sacrifice them everywhere: God himself was bringing about remembrance of himself for the help and salvation of those under instruction. For if they had been able to remember God on their own,

it would have been enough for them to please God through the willing intention of their own minds. But because they were very prone to forgetting the fear of God, bodily worship was also necessary for them as a reminder of God.

Moreover, it was also fitting that this should not happen all at once, but through a progression of instruction from small things to great things, and from the first things to those that followed. For those who were seen [?] did not grasp even the very small things, because their will was not good.
As the scriptural accounts clearly rebuke them, how was it fitting that those who had come out of Egypt in their wickedness should enter upon those perfect ways of life, in the contemplation
of knowledge? For such a form of teaching and legislation would have seemed to show that the lawgiver was self-loving and concerned to preserve his lofty honor, and not
the benefit of those being instructed and brought up. But because, over the course of a long time, they were unwilling to turn away from their sinful habits, and through ordinary sacrifices
with an intention [?], the unjust thought they could wash away their wickedness, there was henceforth added to them, from that
instruction and from the wearing effect of a long time, without faith and without love, a certain foundation of obedience [?] could readily submit to perfect instruction.
We can now consider what God said through the prophets to the unjust Jews concerning sacrifices.

For through Isaiah he said: “What use to me is the multitude of their sacrifices? says the Lord. I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fattened animals; and the blood of bulls, lambs, and goats
I do not desire. When you come to see my face, who has required these things from your hands, to trample my courts? Stop bringing worthless offerings. Incense is detestable to me.”

Again, through the same prophet he said: “Whoever slaughters an ox is like someone who kills a man. Whoever sacrifices a lamb is like someone who kills a dog. Whoever offers frankincense is like someone who blesses idols.”

Again, through this same prophet, he said in another place: “It was not I whom you called upon, Jacob, though I called you, Israel. You did not bring me lambs for your [?], and you did not honor me with your sacrifices.”

I did not enslave you with offerings or weary you with frankincense. You did not buy fragrant cane for me with silver, nor did you satisfy me with the fat of your sacrifices. Instead, you enslaved me with your sins and wearied me with your wrongdoing.
And through Hosea the prophet he says these things: “My judgment will go forth like light. For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings.”
And again, through another prophet, Amos, he said: “If you bring me your sacrifices—did you present offerings to me in the wilderness, house of Israel [?]?”

Along with these, Micah also said: “With what shall I come before the Lord and please God Most High? Shall I come before him with whole burnt offerings and year-old calves? The Lord does not desire thousands of rams or tens of thousands of streams of oil. If I give my firstborn, it is wrongdoing for me,

and the fruit of my womb is a sin against my soul. I have shown you, human being, what is beneficial, what God requires of you: to love justice, practice righteousness, and be ready to follow your God.”

And again, through Jeremiah he said: “Thus says the Lord, the mighty God of Israel: Add their burnt offerings to their sacrifices, and eat meat. For I did not speak to their ancestors or command them on the day

when I brought them up from the land of Egypt, either about whole burnt offerings or about sacrifices. Rather, this is what I commanded them: Listen to my voice [?], and I will be your God, and you will be my people.”
And one can learn many other things through this same man when he voices his complaint.
And through David the psalmist it is said, as though in his own person: “You did not desire sacrifices and offerings,

but you pierced ears for me. You did not ask for whole burnt offerings for sins.” And again: “Listen, my people, and I will speak to you; Israel, I will testify against you. I am God, your God. I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are before me

at all times. I will not take bulls from your house or goats from your flocks, because every wild animal is mine, and the livestock on the mountains, and the bulls. I know every bird of the sky, and the wild animals are mine.

If I were hungry, I would not tell you, because the world and everything in it are mine. I do not eat the flesh of bulls, nor do I drink the blood of goats. Offer thanksgiving to God as a sacrifice, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.”

And afterward, in another place, he said: “For you did not desire sacrifices, nor were you pleased with whole burnt offerings. The sacrifices of God are a humble spirit, and God does not despise a broken heart.”

Thus God himself plainly rejects sacrifices. Yet because of the weakness of the Jews, he accommodated himself to them from the beginning and appeared to accept sacrifices, so that through these things, in which they found enjoyment, toward him
the minds of those people might be lifted and raised. But the disciples of Mani cannot say that even those through whom God spoke these things and rejected sacrifices do not belong to the Old

Testament. For they belong to it, both in their ancestry and in their way of life. And the Spirit who worked in them was the very same Spirit who worked in Moses. From this it is clear how God, in the time of Moses, saw to it that his arrangement

would be solely for the benefit of those being taught. In his great mercy, he appeared to accept the things offered for his praise, willingly, like someone who lowers his own nature, without neglecting or despising those

who cannot, through the understanding of faith, attain knowledge of the incorporeal nature. His purpose was to ensure, by every means, that they would not cease to remember him continually. For they could not preserve this very thing

unless they pursued something tangible and bodily through the things they performed with the law’s permission, in accordance with their inclination, insofar as they were able to be taught and trained in the love of God.

These things, then, have been said about sacrifices. But an arrangement like this also exists in other forms for the Jews, in many things and throughout the entire ordering of the Old Testament, so that through these images they might be firmly directed toward those things which, through them,

become known to the minds of the wise. In this way, through visible things, as though with milk, he might nurture and raise those who are still infants in their understanding, while through the things made known by them, as though with food

that brings maturity and strength, he might delight those who, through faith and love, are sound and mature in their understanding. Yet even those things that were given in images, types, and mysteries, before the dawning of

Tradition, and let the form that is fitting and suitable for [?] and for the knowledge of God be explained clearly. These things ought always to have been observed without being transgressed. For it does not belong to those for whom

the law was established to change what was decreed for them. Rather, it belongs to the lawgiver to make additions to the law as appropriate to the circumstances established at each particular time. This very point is clearly stated in what follows.

But if some people at various times possessed knowledge and righteousness and endured the inadequacy of commandments that were beneath them, these people, through their faith, made up what was lacking

for them in the legislation, while lacking nothing for their [?] through the observance of bodily commandments. For it is love arising from reverence for God that is required. When this was present in them,

they were highly acceptable, so that they did not despise even the lesser things because of their confidence concerning the greater things. For the sake of the latter, it was necessary for them faithfully to observe the former as well.
Nor should they set these things aside altogether before the appropriate time, so that those who had thus been raised through their love toward the lawgiver might be regarded

as not inferior to those for whom the law was established and who observed the lesser things among what they had been commanded—what they had been commanded—even more necessarily for them, for the completion of their righteousness.

Those who possessed this, who had excelled through their faith and [?] those others, were also to be perfected by giving many people an example in the observance of, and careful attention to, such things,
and so reach perfection. Such were the prophets through whom God readily explained the things previously laid down concerning the setting aside of sacrifices; and before them, Moses, through whom God

established the law for the Jews. He had already been upright and righteous before God through his love and faith. But some of the laws he established were not continually for himself, for he had no need of them,

since he was righteous before the law. Rather, they were necessary and useful for the many. Nevertheless, he himself was the first to observe what he commanded. So too Elijah, who offered a sacrifice on another occasion, did not even

ever, from the time he arose, [?] upon it. For through his faith he was above the reasons for which it was appropriate to offer sacrifices. Nevertheless, he sacrificed to expose the poverty of the priests of Baal

and of the Sidonians, so that the comparison might show where the true God was. And indeed, it was necessary that those who were without knowledge because of their unbelief should be led through a bodily demonstration,
as though by the hand, toward the account of God. For in this way fire too was sent of its own accord to receive the sacrifices and lift their eyes toward faith in the God who is invisible.

On the mountain in the wilderness, burning fire was visible to all the people. The terror of smoke and thunder was appropriately sent upon those who saw it, since they were not at all inclined toward reverence
through words and [?], unless some terror sprang before their eyes through visible things. For the fire that was visible was not God. Nor did the statement made by Moses,
“Your God is a consuming fire,” mean that God's being was fire. Rather, as an astonishing addition to the fire that appeared, this too was said to terrify them,
so that something greater than what their eyes saw might be understood to exist and stand before their eyes and in their hearing, serving to frighten them as they were trained like little children.
Thus, in the history of the Old Testament, many things can be seen: sometimes as an arrangement that especially accommodates itself to those being taught, or as things established out of necessity;

and sometimes, as mysteries and patterns, they also announce beforehand what is going to happen. There is also another reason for them, for the sake of those who receive them. Some of them, through God's evident forbearance,
were practiced at that time even by the righteous without distinction—things that today are counted as sins. At that time, however, for the maintenance of the circumstances that had been established,
they were necessarily permitted. Such was the practice among the ancients of taking many wives. And because they were not altogether forbidden by the law, it was not yet an act

the law; and at that time it was permitted by God that they should flourish through the abundant production of upright and righteous children—those to whom God had granted, as an honor, that they should be fathers

of nations and should also be called so. For when it was necessary that the earth be filled with inhabitants, how was it not especially fitting that those who were noble in their character and conduct should be made numerous

by offspring born from them, just as cuttings from a good tree are planted and established throughout the earth’s many open spaces? In this way both things would result from this: honor for the parents, because they are called fathers of nations,

and a good upbringing for those who shared in their union. One can [?] the history of the Old Testament, that this was indeed the case with them to a remarkable degree. What I have said shows that it was much more

fitting that those who lived in the fear of God should multiply through abundant offspring, if continually from both of them [?], and not that this inhabited world, in which there are nations of every kind,

should be called something [?] from God. But now that this inhabited world has received its due measure of inhabitants, a limit on marital union was gradually introduced through an addition to the law.
And even now we see that some people are permitted to do the very same things that others are not permitted to do at all.
For example, for men to take wives lawfully, and for women to marry men, is free from sin according to the general law of nature, which was given by God.

Apart from that exceptional case, it is left within everyone’s authority. But those who promise chastity are no longer permitted to do so: their promise has gone beyond the common nature, and, having gone beyond
the law, it goes beyond what the law permits. Why, then, are we surprised if, for those upright people of earlier times, taking many wives—which was neither forbidden by law nor rejected by nature—

was far removed from blame? For those who came afterward, however, it was made subject to great reproach by an addition to the law, when a limit on marital union was introduced in its proper time. Otherwise, what shall we say about

marrying their sisters, which we believe those born from Adam practiced out of necessity? For even if someone should suppose that permission for this did not continue until many generations afterward,
nevertheless, even those born from that first man had no escape from this compelling necessity. Without making a distinction, they accepted this as something necessary
to them. Yet this very thing, which was not only permitted at that time but which they even accepted as necessary, was considered a detestable violation of the law in later generations.

The restriction was added because offspring had multiplied through the generations. For someone who has a single vine is unwilling to cut it back and reduce it by pruning and trimming, lest he greatly reduce its fruit and grape clusters.
But if he plants and establishes its many branches, making many vines instead of one, and fills a very broad tract of land with vines for a vineyard, confidently
and eagerly he undertakes the pruning and cutting of its shoots, because he will no longer lack its fruit, owing to the abundance of the plants propagated from it.

65. Thus, then, let us recognize how those people of earlier times, because they were very distinguished and adorned [?], honored an abundance of children because their race was small. The dignity of marital union extended to the continuation of the family, because this was necessary.

66. But Mani himself, although he spoke very contemptuously of the body, does not examine these matters intelligently. Instead, like a slave of the body, from which both righteousness and wickedness, both good things and
bad things arise, he has assumed and spoken without knowledge or thought. He ought to have understood how, in each action, the intention of those performing it determines its character. For example,
taking nourishment is natural and common to everyone, while [?] completely is blameworthy; but doing so not altogether without a reason is considered [?] on certain days,

according to a decision of the will made at a particular time and the initiative of each individual. This too has been stated many times in the preceding discussion. But he does not intelligently understand these things,
because he is very uncultivated: just as we must provide people with suitable foods according to their bodily stature, so also we ought to provide teachings suited to the condition of their souls.
Let the things appropriate for their benefit be offered to them. For who offers bread to those who have just been born? And as for those who have already become strong in body,
who would now offer them their mothers’ milk? For both these foods are always harmful and destructive to both groups when given at the wrong time, but at the proper time
they are always helpful and healing. Or how can someone suffering from a fever and someone in very good health receive food in equal quantities and [?]?

That misguided man, then, was completely unaware that, for those Jews who were born and raised in an immature condition, the complete teaching would evidently always have been superfluous, useless, and inappropriate. This very thing, when

they had been trained over a long period, they finally came to understand through the teachings they had received under compulsion. It is like setting food, against their will, before people who are entirely unable to receive it. But it is proper, it seems,

for the person who teaches and speaks to demonstrate and explain what is appropriate for those who have just begun their instruction, so that he himself will not be, as it were, beating the air, and those who listen will not fail to receive his message.

That thoroughly deranged barbarian did not consider these things and all the other things like them that accord with God’s attentive providence. Instead, he was eager to show that the Old Testament contradicts the New,

so that, by demonstrating that the two do not, as he claims, have one author, he might seem to have grounds for his impious invention and persuade the thoughtless that the first law was established by Evil and its rulers.
Others before him, whom he followed, had done this very thing in their audacity. For Marcion attributed the

Old Testament not to Evil, but, as he said, to another, just being distinct from the good one. He held this belief mistakenly and with great impiety; nevertheless, he refrained from attacking the justice of its commandments. Basilides, from whom those called Gnostics derive, also

dared to attribute the Old Testament to Evil. Mani differed from this predecessor of his only concerning the manner of creation; in other respects, both expressed the same blasphemies in complete agreement.
Valentinus, along with these, and still others who disagree with one another and with those previously mentioned on certain other matters, agreed with those

previously mentioned. They specifically criticized and maligned the Old Testament, and set passages from it against one another, claiming that they conflicted with the New Testament, because they thought
that these clearly demonstrated a contradiction. From this point onward, this chapter on the subject is directed against all those together who disparaged the earlier commandments.

But before we set out those statements on whose basis all the heretics supposed there to be this division between the old things and the new, this first point must necessarily also be made against those
pagan Greeks, even if we seem to be departing a little from the subject before us. Whenever we tell them and demonstrate that the teachings of the pagan Greeks do not stand, because

because of the conflict between the divisions they themselves have established among themselves, they immediately try to silence us, saying, “You too have many divisions.” This is found among the heretics previously

mentioned. Yet, without making any distinction, and without knowing how great the difference and estrangement between them and us is in these matters, they vainly [?] reproach us with their own disease and turn their own wretchedness against us.
This is an accusation answered with an accusation, not a way out of the difficulty.
For among the pagan Greeks, all the philosophers who are considered worthy of honor oppose one another, yet all alike are honored among them as pagan Greeks and receive that designation

and praise. The teachings that conflict with one another equally [?] have no acceptance with one another. Thus, whenever someone honors the teaching of one of them as true, he does not dare entirely to exclude any one of them from the number

of the Greeks or from the praise accorded to philosophy. It is clear that he acts with a certain indiscriminate partiality, according to whether he favors the school of Crates or someone else, choosing one for himself from among them all.
For from this [?] they seem [?] to be saying, all of them, something that has no foundation and cannot stand. For not even one of all the others has any superiority in doctrinal opinion.

For they are all equally Greeks and philosophers. It is therefore absolutely necessary to set against their thinking and opinion the things on which they are divided and opposed, rather than those on which they agree.
For the overturning [?] and dissolution of their opinion is a rebuke to them all, insofar as all the Greeks grant them all equal standing in philosophy. For in it

they give them all their strength in their discourse concerning those first principles. For in it, in their discourse, they have expended all their strength against one another concerning those [?]. And its strength

in their books—each of them directed it against his opponent in the same way that he overturned it, by setting his fellow equally against it; and he suffered from him, in equal measure, precisely what he had done to him.
But the heretics were immediately, on the spot, denounced and rejected from the ranks of Christianity and the church, being censured for introducing foreign teachings. This was because

the divine Scriptures openly restrain and curb their audacity. When they realized that they had been exposed by these very Scriptures, they were compelled to cut away much of them, because they could not have

both: to be thought disciples of the Scriptures and to say whatever they wished. Instead, they were compelled to choose one of two things: either to despise the Scriptures, so that they would no longer
be called Christians at all, or to depart from their own teaching. For the catholic church never names any human being as its teacher, except the Christ of God,
who is the Only Begotten, God, who spoke in the Old and New Testaments. And in this it is plainly and indisputably evident that he, through those shepherds who were always simple
and heretics [?], and finally also through fishermen who received the Holy Spirit, set forth those great things concerning the glory of his Father and also his own, in plain words
as his teachings. It seems that not even the highly educated could have known and grasped these things, much less those people who not only did not know how
to read, but had not even received an ordinary education, because of their great simplicity and the purity of their conduct. Their custom was to speak openly without deceit and to take care
to write. And thus the church should earnestly obey them as it obeys Christ, who alone is its teacher through the holy Scriptures, and not any human being.

But all those about whom we are speaking made themselves strangers to the Scriptures through their firmly held teachings. They dishonored the Scriptures themselves, and deliberately cut passages out and erased them,
thinking that they would thereby also abolish the rebuke directed against them. From their own thinking and their own contrivance, like certain pagan Greeks, they introduced new teachings
of wickedness, so that those who obey them are not even called Christians, but are named after them—for example, the Manichaeans, against whom we are now speaking,
and the Marcionites after Marcion, and the Valentinians after Valentinus. But the whole catholic church, which from the beginning, through those in whom Christ spoke, throughout the inhabited earth
was planted and firmly established, absolutely refuses to call and name them Christians. Instead, it regards them as completely alien, not merely like pagans, but more than pagans
it considers them to be. Thus, only in the church are those teachings of truth and reverence for God contained in the Scriptures neither cut away nor impaired, nor is any portion of them
corrupted. Without conflict, openly, without dispute, and peaceably, they are diligently preserved among everyone throughout the inhabited earth, among both the educated and ordinary people.
But those who established and put together foreign teachings for themselves were completely rejected and expelled from the membership and ranks of the church, so that, by the common decision of all

Christians, they should not share even in the name of Christianity. For their innovations were not devised against a human being, whether against one person or against many. Indeed, the equality of their conflict would not at all have prevented them from

sharing the common designation, just as among the pagans they are all called philosophers and Greeks. Rather, they introduced innovations against Christ himself, the Word of God, and fell away both from fellowship with him and from his name.
But if anyone reproaches us over this present inquiry, and also over the division that has existed for some time now in the catholic Church, although the Scriptures remain intact and none

of us dares either to cut anything out of them or to alter anything, let that person learn that this division has not arisen among us over the realities themselves, as to whether or not they have individual existence,
but that we consistently acknowledge those realities themselves and their individual existence, in accordance with the [?] of the Scriptures, which all of us alike believe.
Rather, we disagree about their manner of existence: how any one of them exists individually. This is because of the excessive arrogance of those who first devised an inquiry
of this kind. For it is possible to become even more perfect in the fear of God without troubling ourselves to undertake an inquiry into these matters. Let us approach the divine Scriptures
with a clear mind, and accept that those things which have individual existence truly exist; but out of humility and fear of God, let us not investigate at all how they exist.
For this reason especially, we do not tolerate a deficient and feeble conception being applied to any one of the things that exist. We are rightly indignant and reject
those who introduced this inquiry, because they raise it not as investigators but teach it as demonstrators, and through contempt for the Scriptures, which are especially [?].

And [?], on the evidence of these, they impose a deficient and degrading conception on some of the things that are equally believed by the whole community. Yet those realities themselves are neither diminished
from what they are nor increased; rather, the whole community equally believes in them through all these things, and we all unanimously acknowledge that one sovereignty without beginning.
We have no dispute over doctrines except this one primary question: how much honor should be given to the Son? In this matter, it is clear that those who diminish the measure

of his honor are not free from blame or danger. Our concern in this very matter is his incomprehensibility. For these are his own words: “Everyone should honor the Son as they honor the Father.” On this point, then, we agree. Therefore, just as

the Father’s honor is incomprehensible to everyone, so too the Son’s honor is incomprehensible. For Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God his Father. For this reason, it is not without concern for them that we rebuke those people.
But those heretics who are entirely outside the Church, including those against whom we have [?] this, have devised nonexistent notions and novel realities according to their own
wishes, and are certainly not Christians at all. Their innovations therefore do no harm to the integrity of the catholic Church or to the established testimony to its truth. For the authority of each

one of these people is not equal to that of the holy Scriptures, against which they exalt themselves. Thus, everything said above makes it clear that Christianity consists in diligence and care for the holy Scriptures,

down to the stroke of a single letter. But those who have dared to hold opinions contrary to the Scriptures, and deceitfully to cut out and erase various things, or, conversely, to add things, plainly expel and distance themselves from Christianity.
For their dispute is not with a human being, as the Greek philosophers dispute with one another, but with God, who spoke to human beings through the holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments.

We have necessarily departed from the stated aim of our discourse and said these things calmly and at length, out of love for truth, in response to the pagan Greeks, who groundlessly reproach us over the heretics,
thinking that they are thereby refuting us too, just as the philosophers among them are themselves divided.
We also digressed into this because it was right to speak generally against all the heretics alike who deny that the giving of the law of the Old Testament
came from God, and to confront them on this one main point, showing how it is one and the same God who is the author of both the Old and the New Testaments.

Although they disagreed sharply with one another about sovereignty and the first principles, they nevertheless spoke in complete agreement on some matters, borrowing falsehoods from one another. One of these is their disparagement and criticism of the ancient history contained in the Scriptures.
They say that it is not in agreement with the new covenant, and they quote from it: “Our Savior himself said, ‘It was said to the people of old, “Do not commit adultery.” But I
say to you that everyone who looks at a woman and desires her has committed adultery with her in his heart.’ And again: ‘You have heard that it was said, “Do not swear a [?] oath,
but fulfill your oath to its Lord.” But I say to you: Do not swear at all. Instead, let your word be “Yes, yes” and “No, no.”’”
In all these things, someone may indeed say that there is a distinction and a change; but there is absolutely no conflict or contradiction in them.

As for this distinction, then, who is so senseless that he does not understand that it involves growth and addition, not a reversal of the earlier commands? For he did not say, “It was said, ‘Do not commit adultery,’

but I say, ‘Commit adultery.’” That would clearly have been a contradiction, and he would have seemed to be overturning those earlier commands at their root for an evil purpose and uprooting them. But the one who also cuts off and abolishes even the thought
of the act through an additional command is a helper, not an enemy, of those earlier commands. The same applies to the things that follow them: to speak briefly, he introduces and establishes [?]
that is earnest and complete, and bears witness to the superiority of the new covenant, which was necessary. Christ himself, who wished to come, came to fulfill what was lacking in the old covenant.

That deficiency was necessarily left in it because of the weakness of those for whom the law was established, as has been said and is said again. Thus, the deficiency in what is good—the part of it that was established earlier—clearly shows that it is good.
For that to which a good addition brings completeness also has this earlier-established part belonging to the same kind as the addition, with which it is joined in harmony,
and it produces and brings to completion one complete and perfect whole. But if the earlier part too is good, there is one, and he is the same good one: the one who sent also brought to completion.
“But what shall we say,” they ask, “when he said, ‘It was said, “An eye for a tooth,” but I say to you: Do not resist an evil person,

but if someone strikes you on your cheek, offer him the other’?” For they say that these words contain not a distinction but evidence of contradiction: “How is it that the statement of the old covenant counsels harshness, while that of the new teaches gentleness?

The former commands people to meet the violence of wrongdoing with an equal response, while the latter commands them to heal evil with goodness.” In these matters, then, to speak briefly, one should all the more marvel,
both at God’s merciful ordering of things in the old covenant and at the earnest and careful cultivation of patience in the new. For both come from one and the same.
God himself also spoke those words appropriately, in keeping with the habits of those who heard them.
He was not opposing himself or fighting against himself. Rather, at different times, in keeping with the differences in human conduct, he spoke what was suitable and right.
Let us again consider the habits of those people of old for whom the law was established. For if they had been such
that, through the excellence of their faith, they could humbly endure the abuse and insults of those who dishonored them, the law would have been harsh,

and its medicine would not have suited the wound. But because God knew the harshness of those for whom the law was established, in his great mercy he established a law and commanded that, with an equal response,

the person subjected to violence should obtain redress, so that there would be a limit to the injuries they inflicted on one another, and they would not, over a small wrong, be stirred against one another with anger so unrestrained as to lead to death.

Thus, by decreeing and commanding this equality, he restrained and abolished inequality. Moreover, that very sentence was, in another way, a restraint from the outset upon the person who committed violent injustice.
For he established the law of an eye for an eye. Was this really to catch the person who committed violent injustice as though in a trap, and bring him to punishment?

Or was it so that people would not commit violent injustice in the first place? For the one who strikes beforehand and announces punishment restrains sin; and the one who states the threat beforehand prevents the carrying out of punishment, because he has already restrained its cause.

Thus, with very great mercy, the lawgiver both frightens through his word and, in actual practice, through a demonstration, restrains those who are under him and obey him from excessive violence and wrongdoing.

For how was he not good, when, because he did not want people to behave contentiously toward one another, he devised a remedy for the sickness of those who readily commit violent injustice, and foretold

what would happen to them, so that those who committed such acts would suffer and would not commit them in the first place? For if at that time he had handed down to them perfect patience and teachings about enduring
evil, and had said to those who were very harsh in their conduct, “If someone strikes you on your cheek, offer him the other,” who would not have taken this freedom from fear of punishment
as permission for an abundance of violent injustice? And who would not have preferred to inflict suffering rather than suffer it? This would have been
an especially harsh and savage teaching, containing patience at the wrong time and encouragement for wicked injustice.

Therefore, those who were instructed under the new covenant were, first of all, chosen out of everyone, having been chosen because of their outstanding virtue. Moreover, they were also sincere enthusiasts for patience,

and they were able to hear perfect and complete teachings. They were honored with the perfection of the commandments, so that by suffering and enduring they might show their strength against those who inflicted suffering. Consequently,

these teachings are not opposed to or in conflict with one another. Rather, they correspond to differences in the customs of civic life. The one who taught both was one and the same. For there, in mercy, through retribution
accompanied by fear, he guided them; here, however [?], he handed down the testing of patience through enduring evil.

Consequently, both are good: the former, because in his mercy he restrained violent injustice through fear of imminent punishment among those who would readily have committed injustice if they had had nothing of this kind; and the latter, because he taught patience

to those who had already practiced and been trained in humility. These commandments are not opposed to or in conflict with one another at all. Rather, they are a differentiated way of governing, according to the habits of those who were instructed.
For they would clearly have been opposed if the one set had always been harmful and the other entirely beneficial.

But if both offer a distinct benefit to those who received them, neither should be criticized or blamed. Rather, through both let us admire the one who fashioned suitable teaching according to their habits, giving the lesser teachings to those who were less advanced,
but reserving the greater teachings for those who were mature. To make their distinction clear [?], let us consider how the law was established for the Jews to sustain a life
within the order of this world. They received laws for worldly conduct so that they would not quarrel and behave violently toward one another. The law itself served entirely to establish
worldly conduct in justice and the fear of God, according to their capacity. For Christians, however, laws were laid down for training in virtue. The former received regulations for life here

in orderly dealings with one another, while to the latter was handed down training in endurance and diligence for the sake of the life hereafter. For this reason, the former received promises of the land
and also came to possess it, while the latter have promises of heaven. And how do they have promises of heaven? Just as he proved faithful in deed toward the former

and fulfilled the promise he had made in words, so he himself remains faithful to fulfill also the second and greater things [?] that he promised. For the former, because of their unbelief in the reality

of punishments that are not seen, were called to account for their injustice and their transgression of the law through punishment by the visible sword. But the latter, because of their maturity in faith,

were threatened with the fear of future things—fire and Gehenna. For it would not have been appropriate for the former to be made to flee from evil through a threat of fear concerning what comes afterward.
Since they did not believe the things that were being said, because those things were not visible, they would have thought the whole teaching ridiculous.

Nor, again, would it have been appropriate for those who live in purity to be thought to turn away from sins through the fear of visible punishment handed down to them. For the form of such teaching would have contained an insult to them rather than honor for the message.

In this way, then, he also allowed those men to divorce their wives, so that, because of their uncontrollable anger, they would not take revenge on them by killing them. He permitted them this lesser thing so that they would not commit
