that greater evil. The women, however, are commanded not to agree to their wishes at all, except on grounds of adultery.

They learned this humility of outward conduct. There, the whole arrangement was continually adapted to those who would not submit to discipline and whose habits were very difficult. It offered a certain approach that gently brought them toward the practices of faith.
Here, however, the Teacher gave his commandments openly, as to men who had reached the level of virtue.

Again, the mystery of worship is also seen there through symbols, but here openly, through the truth itself. For example, there is the blood of redemption both there and here; but there it is the blood of sheep without

reason, while here it is the blood of the Word of God, who took a body. Without redemption through blood, there is salvation neither for them nor for us. Again, there is circumcision of the body there, but circumcision of the heart here.
For they have the earthly Jerusalem, while our way of life belongs to the city in heaven.

But since the followers of Mani apparently also compare other things from the Old Testament with the New, supposing that they do not agree, let us give, from a few examples, a taste of the refutation of their madness
to discerning readers, and show the difference. For they also hide their books and do not give them to those who can examine and expose the worthlessness of their madness.

It seems that they also bring forward the failings of the righteous in the Old Testament for enemies like themselves. They do not speak against those who committed them—for their wickedness was slight—

but against the Scriptures themselves, in their habitual madness, although in this they deserved [?]. For this reason we should marvel all the more at how Scripture displays the face of truth everywhere.

It never consented or agreed, out of partiality or flattery, to conceal what had happened if one of the righteous did wrong somewhere. Yet there would have been no one else to accuse him if Scripture itself had not
exposed him. In both respects God helps those who read: he proclaimed the victories of righteous people in the fear of God as a pattern and example, and also how one of them
did wrong. For he recounted this too, as a rebuke and a warning to flee from sins. But they speak against God because of the sins that human beings committed, whereas they ought
rather to see from this his patient endurance of evil, and not regard his governance, as presented in the holy Scriptures, as evil at all. For how can it be that they
themselves should accuse him of wickedness and ridicule him for bearing with those who sin? Yet the patience of the God of all is immeasurable and incomprehensible. It is evident even from
the scriptural history, but still more from their blasphemy against him: he bears with them and is patient toward them even while they openly dare to blaspheme and insult him.

Let us therefore take as an example one sin of a righteous man from those earlier times, and diligently explain, as far as we can, God's righteous governance. Let us leave the rest to those who are able
to understand, so that through comparable cases they may assess others like them. More than anyone else, these people are accustomed to reproach blessed David.

“He openly committed adultery,” they say, “and arranged for the woman's husband to be killed.” But they are unwilling even to read how greatly he excelled in his faith, or how he was a man who loved God.

They cannot even bear to learn this through the accounts. They look only at that one thing and accuse God, who, because of his unsurpassable and boundless mercy, set opposite one another, as though in a balance,
both people's achievements and their sins. And if the good deeds are found to be greater, even then [?] he does not leave even the unjust deeds without a remedy.

Nevertheless, he does not dishonor and reject the many good deeds because of the few sins. If, then, David sinned and he did not rebuke him, and the case came before the Judge, as he is accustomed to act

toward righteous people, let him be blamed—not in this case for wickedness, but for immeasurable mercy. But if, at the very moment when the sin was committed, contrary to the righteous man's own habitual conduct,

God himself immediately rebuked the prophet through a prophet, and at the same time exposed and declared his hidden sin. And when David groaned inwardly and repented fully and completely, nevertheless, no less
did he lay great adversities and afflictions upon him, allowing them to come upon him. How much more, then, should those disciples of the mad Mani, from David’s story, also

be silenced concerning God’s justice and his goodness alike, rather than, because of the sin of the man who was rebuked, prepare and sharpen their tongues against God, who in his goodness patiently allowed the man who had stumbled to feel remorse,

and in his justice dealt with him through outward afflictions. For God knows which will accepts of itself the healing that comes through repentance, and which, on the contrary, without any inward awareness,

proceeds from its sins to other sins like them. Therefore, because of the immeasurable greatness of his mercy, which is without envy, he grants repentance to wills that are readily disposed to healing—that is, he also helps them
toward it through the painful things he brings upon them. As for those who sin without repenting, he does not immediately deprive even them of the freedom and power to sin, but grants them

time of his own for repentance. Yet, in his foreknowledge, he abandons their wills to neglect, without rebuking them, as unworthy—that is, because they are unwilling even to feel remorse for their sins.

But he also knew how great David’s righteousness had been, his leadership, and the greatness of his reverence and love for him. It was not right that, because of one wound, he should neglect that accomplished man and let him perish, like a body otherwise entirely sound.
For this reason he healed that part too, and once again preserved the whole man in health.
83. Concerning God’s judgment in this matter, anyone who is not quick to become agitated says these just things and very many others like them.

84. As for David, what would anyone not say in greater admiration of him, whether because of his remorse or because of his former righteousness? For when the man, who was a king, was rebuked by a man who appeared inferior, he immediately humbled himself on the spot and bowed down.
His mind bent down to the ground, and he was crushed in his thoughts and threw himself into confession. He did not sleep at night, nor was he negligent by day.
The cares of the kingdom did not draw him away, nor did the authority of his leadership distract him. Instead, he did this one thing continually: he shed tears and pleaded with God,
and sought forgiveness for his sin. What I am saying is an important point, and especially true: through this very story he greatly helped those who came after him by the fact that he sinned once,

rather than by the righteous deeds he performed on many occasions, because he became an example and a model for them to confess their sins and repent for the life that followed, so that no one who sins should despair of himself,

since he has before him, through David’s example, the healing medicine of confession and repentance. Throughout all his psalm singing, continually and without interruption, before his enemies, he himself, even before the end,
sang of his sin. It is clear from his words that he did not speak without tears, for because of them even the person reading them cannot bear to read them without tears.
So if his words draw others to tears, how could the man who spoke them not himself have been moved to weep?

85. Hence it is not right that, following the insolence of those who belong to the mad Mani, that blessed man should be called an adulterer because of a single act. For just as no one is called an archer because of a single shot

with which he hit the target by chance rather than by skill, nor is someone else called a physician because of a single cure that happened to him without skill, so neither is someone who, as though suddenly seized, like
the man who sinned once, named after that sin, when the deed itself was earnestly wiped away rather than committed [?]. For this reason one greatly admires that blessed man himself:

how he fell and rose all the more swiftly, and did not fall again. For with someone accustomed to winning, it is nothing remarkable if he does not fall before his adversary; nor is it clear whether, if he falls, he will raise himself again.
But someone who became entangled [?] after being accustomed to victories, when by skill and abundant strength he wins victory for himself again, has fought swiftly in his contest.
The one who endured defeat is admirable and excellent, rather than the one who was accustomed to winning; and this very man displayed all the more a contest of struggle and wonder.
Thus they are criticized for the very things for which they ought to be admired. They also groundlessly wrong many other righteous people, because they do not consider the things
written about them. For if we were to prepare a truthful account of each one of them, we might perhaps become tiresome to our readers.
But if they also insult that judgment written by Moses as savage and unjust, and criticize the law for threatening punishment for the fathers’ sins to the third and fourth generations,
once again they fail to consider how much mercy is hidden in this statement. For the fact that punishment was not exacted from those first people who sinned and transgressed the law,
but that, with forbearance and patience, he gives time for repentance both to them and to their descendants together, and begins inflicting punishment with the third generation,
proclaimed the abundance of his mercy. For it is clear that even these would not have experienced punishment if they had not become followers and imitators of their fathers

in injustice and transgression of the law. From this it is clear that they are punished on their own account, and not because of their parents’ wickedness. Punishment is inflicted on them so that the inheritance

of evils may not continue far through a long succession. He assigned to his zeal against the parents’ sins the designation of punishment, to inspire the necessary fear. Thus that judgment contains fear in its wording, as is fitting,
but in its actual workings very abundant and perfect mercy is seen. Consequently, the law is very good, and the lawgiver is merciful: he began with statutes and signs, and gently leads toward

instruction in the fear of God. He did not cut off hope for those who do not advance, while to those who are perfect he generously gave perfection in a mystery. For it was not compulsory, when someone received a blow on the cheek, to give

one in return, or, if someone suffered injury to his eye, to inflict an equal injury. For they were permitted to deal with all such things in a spirit of humility. What was commanded was a concession for those who

were sick, and there was no compulsion to undergo treatment; they were permitted to go beyond the law. For the law is not laid down for the righteous, just as the preparation of medicinal remedies is unnecessary for those whose bodies are healthy.
Foolish, then, and very foolish is the blasphemous howling of all the heretics who have run wild like dogs against the Old Testament, and even against their Lord. For without
the narrative of the earlier Scriptures and prophecy, the teaching of the New Testament has no continuity. For from there the prophets announce beforehand the coming of Christ

and, through the hope and coming of the one they await, prepare the proclamation of the heavenly teaching in the Gospel. Yet those against whom our argument is directed are no less estranged from these things, and they are also exposed by what follows.
End of the third discourse against the Manichaeans.
The fourth discourse against the Manichaeans.

After the demonstrations we have offered to the best of our ability in defense of the Old Testament and the divine and wonderful providence within it, which is assuredly God’s, for those who, according to their capacity, are able to understand—
we have presented these briefly and concisely, since those quick to perceive do not need many words about matters so entirely clear—it is now time also

to use our argument to rescue the New Testament, which endures the attacks and assaults of the mad Mani, and to deliver it from his madness, and to show that he is utterly alien to it. For it was this, especially,

that he insolently dared to insult through his culpable exercise of power over it, more than the narrative of the Old Testament, which he attributed in its entirety to the rulers of that matter from which it takes its name.
For he left its entire body, both its subject matter and its words, intact and complete, and displayed [?] his hostility toward the divine Scriptures, he who is everywhere alien to the truth.

But he corrupted the New Testament in every respect, cutting it apart limb by limb like a body. He erased much of it and selected a little for himself, and in doing so displayed his destructive faith even more than his unbelief.

But as for the Old Testament, even through the passages he selected—which are fewer than those from the New—and which he forcibly used to support his own fabrication, his insolence toward God can be plainly seen.

For these very passages, through their binding force, require not only the context and completion of what he wickedly suppressed and removed in his madness, but also disclose and display a clear rebuke of this insolence.
Therefore he had no need of that [?], nor even of the New Testament. For why would a liar need truthful words? Or how could he use them for fabricated teachings that have no foundation?

And why would he wish to disclose a few passages from the divine Scriptures, unless his scheme and his device for spreading his error were something else? For since he intended to carry sheep away from the church, as food

ready at hand, this deceiver thought he would take upon himself the name of the true shepherd. In his writings he calls himself an apostle of Christ and the Paraclete, so that the revered name of truth might become
his helper in stealing the rational sheep. For even with the pagan Greeks, whenever he wishes to spread and set his snares, he distances himself from the Christians, as though they were strangers

to those people. He employs a different device for his deception, presenting himself to them as someone who agrees closely with them and belongs to them, just as he also deceitfully assumes an appearance before the church.

Therefore, since he first makes deceitful use of the name everywhere he writes, saying, “Mani, an apostle of Jesus Christ,” let us consider how even this name alone completely dismantles and nullifies his entire argument.
For it was not the New Testament that first revealed both Christ’s name and his person—the New Testament which this man proclaims and pretends to agree with. Nor, indeed, was anyone among
his disciples entrusted with bestowing this name upon our Savior in this way, or with calling himself by it. Rather, from the beginning, the Old

Testament had already revealed the name beforehand through figures, mysteries, and prophecy. Moreover, Christ himself did not openly proclaim himself in this way by that name, for it was fitting that he should be made known not chiefly by a name, but through the deeds themselves.
And those Jews who had long been waiting for him recognized him through the trustworthy evidence of the deeds themselves.

They called him by it and brought him his true name from the earlier prophecy. For the sun, too, when it rises, does not call itself the sun; rather, once it is seen, it is enough for it to be called so by those who see it.
Thus the name itself precedes the coming, since it was truly given and proclaimed in the Old Testament. From it, those awaiting his coming had grounds to expect the one who is so named.
Therefore, anyone who accepted even the name of Christ alone as glorious and true could find that the entire Old Testament plainly agrees with the New, and is a true teacher and a disciple of Christ,

just as the law is a [?] and an educator, bringing the pupil who is being instructed to the teacher. I mean the force of the name itself and the statement concerning it. A little later we shall explain this as well as we can.

But for now let us speak about what lies before us. Let Mani, who finds fault with the ancient prophecy, be consistent with himself by also fleeing from the name of Christ, through which Christ was known even before he came. For in this way, when he takes off the sheepskin,
he reveals himself as a wolf, and he has no means of deceiving those who come from the church, so that not a single one of them would wish
to incline his ear to him, any more than to any of the pagan philosophers among the Greeks. Or, if he praises the name, let him also praise the book
from which it comes, in which one Creator of all and one sovereignty are proclaimed—the sovereignty from which those things came into being well and wisely out of nothing.
All these things were pronounced very good by their Maker. That is, unless Mani, shamelessly and insolently, as is his habit, should say that in prophecy those rulers
of matter, as he claims, proclaimed Christ’s coming and spoke his name beforehand, so that after the events had come to pass they might establish a false belief that the prophecy had come from God.
Yet this very claim would produce an even greater [?] of his insolence. For if they speak beforehand, it is clear that divine knowledge also exists beforehand in those who announce in advance what
Finally, afterward, he acts as he says: “This is the good.” But they seem to have proclaimed the truth beforehand. Moreover, they also become messengers of the faith and heralds of Christ

and helpers toward the salvation of those who believe in him, so that they may help them all the more and not harm them. This is inconsistent and entirely foreign to the argument that this man previously put forward.
But if he says that the Old Testament also has some share in the good, then it is time for him to take some portion from it as well, and not cast it all out and reject it. Moreover, it appears
from this statement that all of it is attributed to God, and everything fulfilled in it according to the law given through Moses is credited to him. For in it he is called Christ, and also priest,
and also king of the Jewish people. Everything that happened took place in accordance with the conditions and fulfillment of these things, and apart from them nothing at all was

happening. Thus, in this way too, the whole body of legislation that was laid down must be regarded as coming from God, provided that one accepts the name of Christ. For the anointing that, in the law of God and by the word,
was prepared with spices through Moses was the sign of the appointment of both the high priest and the king, when they received this anointing, when they sought it. This was,
however, a pattern and shadow of what was to come. For the leadership of the Jewish people was divided between the high priesthood and the kingship. But when the outcome of these things came about,
and the likeness and shadow were fulfilled, both were to be united in one reality, which is Christ. For he is king from before the world, and also high priest on behalf of everyone before
his Father. Those who received anointing bore his likeness and were called anointed ones among the Jews. Without anointing, no one was either high priest or king.
Furthermore, those who were subject to them were called Jews, not Christians, because what was maintained at that time was a mystery and a pattern,
which prepared and made ready for the reality. For Judah [?] was one of the twelve tribal chiefs.
He was appointed to reign over his brothers, and it was never permitted to appoint kings from another line, but only from this tribe. Thus, from that Judah who reigned,
they were called Jews at that time. But the man who became king was not automatically worthy of kingship merely because of his descent, for there were many

from that line, but only if he participated in and received anointing. From then on he was raised and exalted above his own people. This was a pattern and a mystery. But when the reality came, of which that was the pattern and mystery
that had prevailed among the Jews, Judah ceased to exercise his leadership, in accordance with the earlier saying of the common father
of the twelve. In its place came the authority and leadership of Christ: the spiritual in place of the visible, and the heavenly in place of the earthly. In this way also
the Jews too, by receiving and sharing in the more excellent name, were called Christians—not to dishonor or disparage their former designation,

but because they received and shared in what is higher and more excellent, in accordance with the hope announced by the prophets long ago. They foretold these things to them and openly proclaimed beforehand: “My people will be called by a new name, which will be blessed throughout the whole earth.”

It is clear that it is new together with the new covenant. For when the one who reigned was replaced—the one from whom those within his kingdom ought also to have taken their name—they changed their designation as well. Yet the name was not new,
for it had also held sway over those earlier people symbolically, so that everything might be reserved for the reality.

Thus, in our dispute with the Jews too, we have no other main subject of inquiry than the Christ who has come, whose coming they had expected from long ago. They still await him even now and invoke his name,
mistakenly thinking that he has not yet come. In our argument we refute them from the Scriptures they themselves accept, from the earlier legislation, and from the evidence of the events themselves.

But what will the followers of the mad Mani say? They reject Scripture itself, yet accept the excellent and supreme name derived from that very Scripture as divine and glorious, so that this same Mani writes: “Mani, an apostle of Jesus Christ.”
The name Jesus is translated “Savior,” and in the New Testament itself it remained in Hebrew, as did other words in which it became clearly evident how the kinship with
[?] and of one kind is the message of the Old Testament and the New. Thus, even by the name alone, that deceiver is exposed, for the whole Old Testament names Christ.

It names not only the one anointed figuratively and symbolically, but also the one whom he symbolized, the one in whom it was fulfilled. Anyone can come forward, read, and gather testimonies to this very thing. This is not an urgent task for us.
But we must also state the reason and meaning of the name Christ, in which Mani has not even the slightest share. He has no part in it at all.

Anointing with oil is a sign of going out to a contest and into the athlete’s arena. For no one strips to face his opponent without being anointed, and no one enters the contest without anointing. Therefore, because the contest against the desires

of nature for the sake of divine virtue was undertaken by those who fear God, and against those who were going to persecute them, so that they might persevere in the fear of God even to the shedding of blood—for the contest of godliness is greater than all others—
for these things they needed not a bodily anointing but the spiritual anointing of the Holy Spirit. For their contest too is spiritual and belongs to the mind. Its symbol was

that bodily anointing of the priesthood. Together they become worthy of this and share in it, so that they may enter the contest; and they are anointed for that very contest. For this reason their king, the first of these,
alone was truly called Christ as the archetype, not by chance, but was anointed by his own Father with the Holy Spirit and with power,

as Scripture says. He was the first to endure persecution on behalf of everyone and the contest of the suffering that brings salvation. Moreover, he was also an example of the toil and struggle for virtue, although
it was not for himself—for he had no need—but for all others that he endured, and he became a model for human life, so that all [?] who look to him, through participation
and acceptance of the contests forced upon them, might share his name and be called Christians, followers of Christ. Thus the name Christ signifies holiness, persecution even to the shedding of blood
for the truth of godliness, and struggle. The Christian himself is a contestant and an athlete of both godliness and virtue, through participation in and the anointing of the Holy Spirit
he is such. The blessed Paul also makes this clear, saying that their struggle was not against flesh and blood, and what follows.
What, then, does this mean to that madman? First of all, he shows that it is pointless,

even if he does not openly acknowledge the exercise of virtue, since he introduces the invincible supremacy of evil. According to what he says, anyone who has more of this in his mixture—namely, evil—
cannot attain virtue, even if he earnestly desires it, so that such a person does not even need [?]. Conversely, the one who has more of the good would be a lover of virtue even without effort.

For both of them, anointing for the contest is pointless, since neither of them can enter such athletic struggles and contests. Consequently, even the name itself is pointless for those who introduce a nature governed by compulsion in place of effort.

Again, he does not say, even as though in a dream, that you should stand firm to the death against those who oppose the truth of godliness. Why, then, does he need, in any case, this very name, which teaches that one ought

to suffer persecution even to death and be anointed against the deceit of persecutors? For that teacher’s doctrine says that one should even offer sacrifices and adapt oneself to everything. To support this, he forcibly twists the apostle’s statement,

where he says, “I became everything to everyone, so that I might [?] everyone.” Otherwise, he says, it is unnecessary for us to struggle to the death against those who command us to sacrifice to evil demons and idols.
Consequently, this too makes it clear that, when the meaning of the name is explained, Mani is found to be wholly alien to Christ himself,

by whom he said and wrote that he had been sent. For through what is visible, what is spiritual is understood in its image, and through that bodily anointing, the incorporeal anointing is made known to us, although first in truth and power

is that spiritual reality in relation to its image. Yet he too is the one who is anointed. Consequently, even among the Jews there was no completeness in bodily anointing apart from spiritual anointing; nor did this

He accepts the Gospel, so that its mystery [?]. For when someone insults the king’s image, his wrongdoing is plainly directed against the king, and his insolence reaches him. For this reason Christ himself also made his appearance among the Jews.
For there was also an image of his kingdom, which had previously been revealed through prophecy.
For this reason this deceiver made it his aim to say that the creation of God spoken of in the Old Testament is evil.
Everything he found in the New Testament that was said in praise of it—that is, in praise of the one who made it—he erased and removed.

He acted just like those before him who dared to do this very thing, except that he openly admitted that it came from himself [?]. For he says, “I have come and have been sent to correct and purify the Gospels, because [?]

in them too, he says, from the admixture of evil, as he calls it. But let us consider and see, in this matter too, how he speaks foolishly in his insolence, and the immeasurable stupidity and confusion of those who believe him.
For he says that he was sent by Christ, and falsely claims to be his apostle and his Paraclete. But which Christ, then? Clearly, the one who came among the Jews.

For no other has been revealed and appeared. His birth in the flesh took place during the reign of Augustus, while his suffering and his ascension into heaven took place in the eighteenth year of Tiberius.
From then until Decius, who fiercely persecuted the church, two hundred and thirteen years passed, and Mani was still completely unknown. But how is this clear and known?
We say that Origen, who was both a teacher and a priest of the church, lived until the time of Decius.
He wrote no discourse about Mani, although he left not a single one of the heretics opposed to the catholic church without speaking against him. Thus Mani himself appeared after this man.

Yet he says that he came to correct and purify the words of our Savior. What, then, can be said about all this delay, neglect, and carelessness—that those words were not purified at once, if they required

any purification and correction? And why did he not guide them from the beginning, so that they would be spoken without the admixture of evil, as this man says, and without alteration? For the Old Testament was shown to be without alteration.

It was, however, incomplete because of the weakness of the Jews, and was awaiting perfection. Yet what had been established beforehand was not evil because of what it lacked. Rather, it required this to be added to it as something of the same kind.

But this man says that there were words originating from evil among the things the apostles said about Christ. Furthermore, according to what this man says, God himself is accused of having suffered compulsion from evil, since those things which he did not
wish were said about him. Did Christ himself, then, leave his teaching stained and impure throughout this whole course of years after his coming? Did he choose disciples for himself in vain?
And was it also in vain that he promised to send them the Holy Spirit immediately after his ascension, and called it the Paraclete? For if this man is the Paraclete, as he falsely claims
in his madness, whom Christ promised to his disciples, then Christ plainly lied about his promise to them. For he said, “Look, I am sending you the Paraclete.” And how, then, if the Holy Spirit

had not been received by the disciples, did they overcome this entire onslaught of the whole inhabited world, with its wickedness of idolatrous error, its worship of evil demons, its drunkenness, and all its debauchery?
Thus they restrained those people who had formerly been unbridled and given over to desires, and sent them on their way in the fear of God.
And how did they also perform signs and wonders if the Holy Spirit had not been sent to them according to our Savior’s promise? But that it was sent is clear.
For otherwise they would not have had all that power against evil spirits, nor all that boldness before those assemblies of the wise
of the world—ordinary men who spoke by the Holy Spirit. Nor did those words require correction and purification, as he says.

But the Paraclete whom Christ promised to send was not to come in some bodily manifestation, as Christ himself had come, nor to live and conduct himself bodily among human beings in the same way that Christ himself had lived among them.

For this was not necessary, because the complete measure of the order of virtue had been established for it [?] by our Savior, together with another dispensation. Rather, he enters and dwells in the souls of those who believe in him.
And although he is unseen, in his zeal he provides them with testimony to the coming of Christ, together with other powers.
But how could Mani himself, a deceiver who is fleshly and a slave to empty hope, be considered that Holy Spirit who is known but unseen?
And if we say that Christ came in a body, they say that this is a disgrace, and that this did not happen. Yet they believe that the Paraclete became a human being,
as though our Savior had not been able, through his humanity, to dissolve and abolish error and give human beings complete and perfect salvation.

But if they acknowledge that the madman Mani is a human being, one among many, and that he taught by receiving the Paraclete of truth, this first of all has been revealed: he himself is not the Paraclete. For it is not
the case that someone who receives something becomes the very thing he is thought to receive, just as our eye is not light because it receives light. And he lies when he calls himself the Paraclete.
And again, if he received a spirit, which one was it? Was it the one Christ’s disciples received? How, then, is he one of them, when he opposes them on those fundamental matters,

since he rejects all their teaching except for a few small points? For no one opposes himself in all these matters—not even an ordinary human being, much less the Holy Spirit. But it is clear that he received a spirit

that was different and unclean, and openly raged against the teaching of the blessed apostles. It stirred him up to attack their teaching about the one sovereign principle, which is especially clear, by adding another, opposing sovereign principle,

and also their teaching about the creative work of God, who is over all, and again about his providence over everything, and, along with these things, about his governance and his acts of help on our behalf, which were given through the ancient Scriptures for [?] from the God of all.

And again, concerning the begetting of children, Christ’s birth in the body, his entire way of life, his suffering, his resurrection, and everything else, he left nothing intact, so far as he could, of the things those blessed men of earlier times wrote and taught

and spoke by the Holy Spirit. Instead, like pigs, he trampled the pearls of the gospel. Yet he claims, “I was sent by Christ”—the very one who had already ordered and established the world through his true disciples and worked wonders throughout the whole world,
among fishermen, so that before this man’s ancestors’ ancestors were conceived, the whole earth had yielded to God the fruits of reverence for God and had offered God martyrs too numerous to count,

who acted courageously and triumphed for the sake of their truth. It had acquired flourishing churches everywhere, and virginity, endurance, and holiness, so that its afflictions and the gift of the Holy Spirit are clearly evident in them.
Where, then, did this man get the impulse to falsify such things?
And who became his teacher in such madness [?]? Certainly no human being, but only Satan and the evil demons,
his helpers. Because of their envy toward human beings, they taught [?] Jesus, or again they teach [?]. Clearly, God permitted this to test the faithful, in accordance with the earlier saying
of our Savior: “An enemy sowed weeds among the good and pure seed.” He said that these should bear fruit alongside the good seed until the fruit was fully grown.
For these should not be gathered up, lest some of the choice and pure plants also be harmed along with them. But at the harvest a separation takes place, and those fall into the fire,
while the wheat is gathered into storehouses. And again, according to the apostle’s saying: “For there are divisions among you, so that those among you who are approved may be recognized.” And again
he said: “Withdraw from a heretic whose thinking is divided, after one admonition [?]. For you know that he is [?] in contention, sins, and condemns himself.” And so
this applies far more to the man against whom we are speaking. For he invented a mixture of things [?], two opposing principles, in which nothing of the truth at all is mixed.
He is far removed from all true teaching and pieces together the falsehood of his words. And [?] he appears to be a peddler of evil things and a collector of lies.
This very man—for there is nothing so wickedly said by others that he has not taken it for himself as a fine discovery.

For although he said that he was the Paraclete and had come to reveal to humanity things that had never been told or written for anyone, on this account he distorts the apostle’s testimony: “We know a little out of much, and we prophesy a little out of much.
But when perfection comes, what was partial passes away.” And he says, without shame, that he himself is the one who brings perfection.
For he did not introduce even a single account consistently drawn from his own resources. Instead, he gathered the evils scattered among others and prepared one deadly poison from many ingredients.

For Xenophon writes that the sages of the Persians long ago believed in two opposing principles. From there this man too acquired his affinity with barbarian thought. Aristotle, however, used the term “matter.”

He applied this name not to some living principle, as this man did when he adopted and introduced a foreign term that was not his own. Rather, in keeping with the meaning of the name, he called “matter” that which is not alive and has no movement of
its own. This man, however, falsely changed the use of the name to mean evil. He was not merely dishonest in his theft; he was also a wicked schemer, falsifying something that was not his own
to begin with. Plato, moreover, taught the outpouring of souls in particularly explicit language, in error. Again, invoking the sun as a god is especially a custom of the barbarians, and no less
than this, it is also a concern of all the pagan Greeks, without distinction and without exception.
Belief in fate and the horoscope belongs, one might say, to all those whose souls devour them, both in former times and down to the present.
Come then, you false Paraclete, tell us: what new teaching have you introduced into the inhabited world?
And what have you alone discovered, that you should publicize a falsehood not spoken by the ancients? They were considered far superior to you in the errors that you later presented as your own.

You therefore have no right to boast, even of your falsehood. For you are shown to be a dishonest disciple of both Greeks and barbarians. You vainly attach Christ’s name to yourself, and this title drives you into error.
Perhaps, among all those who have strayed from God, a few things resembling the truth may be found in what they taught. Even if these were spoken as though by hitting
a target, they give their speakers no help at all toward reverence for God. For any error concerning God is especially destructive and not
helpful, even if a little truth is found in it. For this knowledge too is [?], because it was not given by God but is a discovery of the human mind.

But this man is an instrument of the slanderer, Satan. He made a collection of falsehoods and mixed absolutely no truth into his counsels. He took pains to make all those evils spoken by others appear new

through erroneous words and inventions of his own. For in this way he imagined himself to be a discoverer of new things, things never spoken before. Indeed, the idolatrous error of many gods can be found in him
to an even greater degree than among the pagans. He wrote falsely in his books: “I worship those gods, those who are exceedingly numerous and cannot be counted.” And foreign names

and barbarian ones he listed, imagining that he differed from the pagans merely by speaking new names. But in the multitude of those he worships, this very man is, without hesitation, a [?] of paganism.

But to return to the subject before us, let us say this: first he excludes from his gospel Christ in the flesh, which is the starting point of his coming to us. In another way, too, he insults his Maker in connection with the body,

and refuses altogether to say that it is God’s work. No less does he also nullify the prophetic word concerning our kinsman, which foretold that Christ would be born from David’s offspring. He raises this question,

an old one among us, already refuted long ago, yet one that he imagines necessarily supports him. For he says, “How is the prophet thought to be speaking the truth when he says that Christ is born from David’s offspring?”

“Since Mary,” he says, “was not of that lineage, and Joseph,” he says, “was not Jesus’ father, if she conceived the Lord in her virginity”—he is plainly fighting against the truth on behalf of the Jews, using the scriptural account.
And there is nothing surprising in this, if those righteous followers of Mani do not understand it.
For even if this were explained and it were shown how the prophecy agrees with the truth, they would nevertheless disbelieve in Christ’s coming in the flesh, since they groundlessly
criticize and disparage everything God has chosen. For if they disputed only the scriptural account concerning his lineage, like the Jews, and did not raise another harsh objection
against the truth, an explanation of this question would cure their unbelief. But now, in their wickedness, they attack this point, and the contentiousness
of the Jews they have added to themselves. But concerning the body, which the mad Mani groundlessly criticizes and mocks, we have spoken in the preceding passages, and we speak again. ⁂
But concerning the scriptural account about David’s lineage, through which kingship is transmitted and restored to Christ in prophecy, let us speak—not to those afflicted with a disease
for which there is no cure, but to those like us. The prophet himself foretold both things: that the virgin would conceive our God-with-us, who is Christ,

and that in the flesh he would come not from another family, but from David, as in the saying, “A shoot from the stump of Jesse.” How, then, are both fulfilled? For if Scripture customarily made lineage known through
mothers, someone would seek [?] Mary’s lineage, and the prophet’s word would be fulfilled. But as for Mary also being considered a descendant of David, this matter is no less unusual, if she

alone among all the women of all time is considered to have been included in the course of the transmitted genealogy. It is clear how different the account concerning her is, even if Mary herself should be from the priestly tribe.

And this may be inferred from Gabriel’s testimony to her kinship with Elizabeth, the high priest’s wife. For this man, apparently, since he was not one of the ordinary people, took a wife from his own tribe according to the law. And let Joseph alone truly be descended from David.
For the succession itself makes this clear, according to the genealogical account of Matthew and Luke, the evangelists who wrote this account. ⁂

And so, because it was fitting for Christ to come and for his body to suffer on our behalf, and for God, who was called Emmanuel, thus to be with us, this was no longer to happen according to the ordinary law of nature,
but beyond it, as its Lord, who is not subject to it at all.

For nature is under its Creator’s authority; the Creator is not under nature. The virgin is therefore brought forward for this service, and Joseph, who is descended from David, is betrothed to her in the role of a husband.
And only as far as this role and the betrothal does the prophecy bring its word into agreement with the truth—not as far as the actual involvement of seed, concerning which it foretold

that he would be born without a man’s seed, through the saying, “Look, the virgin will conceive.” How, then, is the one born without seed descended from David’s seed? For David’s lineage continued as far as
Joseph, who was betrothed to the virgin, and the Creator’s plan was accomplished [?] without seed. Christ’s birth in the flesh was thus symbolically from a husband, for the truth

of the prophecy and of the lineage, but in truth and in actuality it was from the Holy Spirit. Thus the prophecy concerning the virgin was confirmed, and it did not prove false concerning the lineage either, through the symbolic role fulfilled by Joseph.

It was necessary that the one who came into being should be born of a virgin, because it was not fitting that the greater thing—I mean this birth from a virgin—[?], rather than that the lesser thing should be fulfilled with genealogical precision, even in actuality. For this

received, symbolically through the betrothal, a fitting and appropriate spiritual fulfillment. But how else could the birth from a virgin have been accomplished? This is supremely necessary to the divine plan, and could happen only in this way:

that a man should have no part in the conception. For the Creator is not a servant subject to his own creation. But he indicates the lineage symbolically, just as he does many other things—not in order to receive David’s nobility,

but in order to bring his succession to an end with the cessation of the earthly kingdom, in accordance with Jacob’s prophecy. If, then, our Savior’s lineage was not arranged to demonstrate nobility—for he had no need of it.
But so that this might be brought to an end, all this took place through Joseph, who was last in rank and descent, though only in type and mystery, insofar as was fitting
he was an intermediary for the one who was born. For it was David’s glory that his lineage should culminate in Christ, not Christ’s glory that he should be born from David.
And because he himself was destined to bring the priesthood to silence along with the earthly kingdom,

and David’s lineage was also to be cut off, as was Judah’s, so that through him there might be a spiritual kingdom and likewise a priesthood, he apportions his dispensation [?] and joins both tribes together in it: the one

belonging to kingship, namely Judah’s, through Joseph, and the one belonging to priesthood, namely Levi’s, through Mary, so that he might lift kingship upward to himself and transform the priesthood into something spiritual, since in himself he united them both.

For, as we said in the earlier passages, he is the high priest and king of creation, both bodily and spiritual, according to David’s own prophecy, in which he spoke about him in the person of his Father:
“You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.” There the same prophet also declares his kingship, saying:

“The Lord will send the scepter of your strength from Zion”—a scepter whose kingship he did not acquire afterward, but possessed by his very nature. And not only this: he also proclaims his nature at the same time, saying there again,

in the person of his Father, “In holy splendor, from the womb, from of old I begot you, O child.” And with the expression [?] he declares that incorporeal birth, although neither human nor angelic understanding

can follow or approach it, showing that he is his true and beloved Son, who is from him truly and by nature, and was not brought into existence from outside, on the same footing as those who came into being through him from nothing. Furthermore, neither

does he neglect his suffering there, for he says, “He will drink from the stream along the way; therefore his head will be lifted up.” For this reason God also exalted him, not to add to his glory, but to reveal the glory that

was his by nature and had previously been hidden. Thus, in these few words, the blessed prophet David revealed and made clear, insofar as was possible, both his nature—how he is the Son from the Father—
and his kingship, his priesthood, and his saving work, both in his suffering and in his resurrection, and finally his judgment as well, when he said that he would judge the nations.

Although in explaining these things we have gone somewhat beyond what was needed for the subject before us, nevertheless we will accept neither the Jews, who plainly stand at the forefront of the dispute, nor the followers of Mani,
nor any of those heretics who rejected the Old Testament and wickedly dared to blaspheme the Creator of all and the fashioner of the body.

For these people, against whom our argument is particularly directed, are plainly convicted of mistaking one thing for another because of their great ignorance. For they condemn and reproach sin not as people who hate it, but as though using it to prove a point.
And, very senselessly, they blame not the soul that commits it, but the body through which the soul commits it. From this it necessarily follows

that virtuous deeds must also be attributed to this same body, since they too take place through it. Yet it is altogether wrong to blame the tools—or even the craftsman—for both things, good as well as evil,
especially when this craftsman is seen to be a craftsman by nature, and a very skillful one, but to go wrong and fail through carelessness and disregard for what he ought to do.
For if he had received from God a tool that forcibly led him into sin and was entirely unsuitable
for the practice of virtue, the fashioner would be to blame. But if it is readily directed wherever the one to whom it is entrusted wishes, then this tool is not the cause of either outcome,
nor should it be considered so, whether it serves good purposes or evil ones. For by its nature it is excluded from exercising authority, and it works as an aid to the one to whom it is entrusted.
Even if it has certain natural impulses toward sexual desires, this is necessary for reproduction, and it also sometimes provides an occasion for a great victory, when
the mind inclines toward the practice of chastity. As for the other impulses, they are entirely harmless if the mind, which is by nature above them, makes use of them in moderation.
It has authority. And many times in the preceding passages we have said concerning the whole human body that it must be so: it was created by the wisdom of God.
But because they find fault with this body, and speak very strongly against the Son of God, saying, “We absolutely cannot bear to say that he came in it,”
we must not neglect this part of the discussion either. For if he himself did not fashion it, let them say, not that it is evil—for it is not evil—

but that it is foreign to him. But if he is the body's maker, he is not ashamed to clothe himself in his own work. Rather, he honors it all the more by taking it to himself, and through it he imparts his own way of life to everyone.
For that which helps the soul in practicing virtue is not evil. For neither self-control nor righteousness,
nor any other part of virtue would belong to a human being [?] without the body and its inclination toward the opposite, toward which it moves by its nature.
By the soul's drawing it in the opposite direction, it gives the soul opportunities for virtue. Thus the body is the soul's friend,
not only because it dwells with it, but because it also gives the soul victory through its management of the body. For it does not harm the soul when it is moved toward desire,
but helps it by being restrained and held back by it. For restraining this body from falling is nothing other than virtue. This is how it has been placed before the soul,

and the body has no authority by its nature. Thus, if it is governed well, it is shown to be useful and suitable for the soul, filling the role of an instrument. As we said earlier, it helps the mind in everything it wishes.
Since, then, the body has been shown in this way to be good, let us attribute this instrument of great craftsmanship to nothing other than the wisdom of the one who truly
is the craftsman and creator, God. For even if evil existed, it could not have devised this entire structure of the body. Otherwise, evil itself would possess extraordinary wisdom,
whereas evil necessarily means a complete lack of knowledge and understanding. But wisdom and reason belong to the Good One in everything he does.

Yet this man is the advocate of that very evil which has no existence or substance at all. Not only does he testify on its behalf, on his own authority, that it exists, but he also attributes lofty and exalted wisdom
to it, thereby forcefully refuting his own error. Thus both the soul and the body are God's workmanship. But because the soul went astray and became confused by its own choice, the intervention

of the one who made humanity was needed. Thus the prophets themselves foretold that the one who fashioned humanity would come and clothe himself in his own workmanship: its maker would in one respect care for it,
and in another respect honor the whole through that part. For the requirements of his dispensation called for the death of those for whose sake he came. For he came in this way and not otherwise.
For he was different in his nature, and far higher and more exalted. To be with one who was continually being brought so low, he could not reveal himself to him in his own nature.
For, being good, he especially wished to persuade, to be seen, and to seek salvation for human beings, rather than to lead them by force without his coming. Thus Christ,
who is the Son of God from before the ages, clothed himself in a human body because he came to human beings. He took it from a woman, and not from some other source, although he could have done so.

He himself prepared this body for himself, to honor still more what he had fashioned from the beginning, and not to give these people a plausible pretext for saying what they say: that humanity is not his creation. He clothed himself in a body from a virgin,

so that he might become human—not in the manner of a human being, but in the manner of God. For he also brought nature itself into existence under the law of his workmanship. Yet he came even beyond nature,

to those who were in need. He became like them in body, but he did not come in the same way as they did. Let us accept and receive his dispensation, and not dishonor the victory and glory accomplished through the virgin.

But if those impure people cannot bear to think reverently of the holy Virgin, it is possible [?] through an illustration that is not even necessary for the argument, but nevertheless stoops to their ignorance and lack of understanding to refute them. For let us point to the sun,
which falls on every place and dries up moisture without itself becoming wet, and eliminates decay without sharing in decay. If, then, something created is like this, what, then,
shall we say about the Creator? Yet this illustration is superfluous for me. For the Fashioner did not come to something unclean; he came to what he himself had fashioned.
Nor was the Virgin—who, besides the holiness of her virginity, was further sanctified by the Holy Spirit—an unsuitable or unworthy dwelling for the Wisdom at work in the saving plan for humanity.
But the pagan Greeks do not believe this, because it is beyond nature. They say that a virgin cannot conceive.

Our argument now, however, is not directed against them. Rather, since we are considering the Lord of nature and its Creator, it is entirely superfluous to demand that things happen according to nature.

For the Creator is not subject to the order and limits of his own creation. It is always easier for him to change it as he wishes than to make it when it did not exist—although for God nothing is easier or harder than anything else, since everything subsists by his will alone.
But these people, in one respect, criticize nature [?] like enemies of its Creator; and in another, alleging the impurity of the human body, they again blaspheme the Creator and criticize him.
Mani, then, said that our Savior's manifestation took place as a mirage and an appearance,

and not in reality. In this very matter he violently fell in with the heretics who preceded him. For this reason, along with all the other passages in the Gospel that testify to the reality of our Savior's body,

he cut away and mutilated these passages, and made [?] and many substantial divisions in the writings. He also joined together portions of them that were very far apart in their arrangement, this man who was so

bold in his wickedness. Yet on the eighth day our Lord, while still an infant, was not only presented according to the Law: the Shepherd was also circumcised along with the sheep, because he wished to be counted as a lamb among the flock.
And he testified to his ancestry, in fulfillment of the ancient prophecy, so that he might teach us to join the two covenants together in one faith of reverence for God.
But he says that he appeared only in seeming, and that he did not truly appear in a body. Yet John, whom he regarded as trustworthy in many matters, said, “The Word became flesh
and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of Spirit and truth.” He also testified that he not only saw Jesus staying with his disciples
and walking with them, but that he also ate with them, and that he was invited to a wedding feast and did not decline to go.

He even changed water into wine, and through the providential occasion of the shortage of wine he testified that he is the one who does this very thing miraculously every year in the vines of the vineyard.
But if one of his followers should argue that, when the evangelist said, “The Word became flesh,” he said this with reference to participation in matter as they understand it,
and that all similar passages were removed and erased by Mani for this reason, and that our Lord's being seen and walking among human beings does not necessarily indicate a body,
for, he says, he could have appeared to do these things without their actually happening, just as with the angels who ate with Abraham—was even the wine made from water merely something imagined
in the mind, rather than something real, which those invited with him plainly drank in actual fact? Then, on the contrary, the one who seemed to perform the deed was a deceiver,
if he performed the miracle not in reality but through a deceptive visual appearance, as in a dream. But if he truly changed water into wine, what happened was material and bodily.
And the body is certainly not rejected by the one who went to the wedding feast, honored the procreation of children, and miraculously produced wine.

But if he says that John deliberately lied, invented the opposite, and attributed to his teacher something that never happened at all, then it is no longer right, even in a single one of the things he wrote,
that they should be believed on his word. For anyone who has deliberately lied and fabricated even one thing does not deserve to be believed in all the other things either. For if they say
that those evangelists spoke under some delusion arising from the mixture of that evil which Mani teaches, and that it was not at all deliberately that they offered accounts departing from the truth,
then the blame for this error belongs not to their will, but to the opposing nature, which, as they suppose, is its source. But if they did not stumble involuntarily, but

deliberately fabricated these things and related them as though they had happened, although they knew perfectly well that they had not happened at all, they are rightly held guilty as wicked people who are deeply immersed in evil,

and they should not be believed in other matters either. Indeed, blessed John himself, whom they especially suppose to have seen these things, related that our Lord also washed the disciples’ feet, and he himself was one of them.

It is clear that he also experienced the bodily touch of the one who washed him and felt him. Again, he reclined on our Lord’s breast, and through the closeness of his head he felt the solidity of the body of the one

on whose breast he reclined. More importantly, even after his resurrection, when Thomas did not believe that it was he, our Lord himself offered himself to be examined by the touch of hands, and instructed him to put

his hand into the wound in his side and also examine the marks of the nails in his hands. If, then, even after his resurrection our Lord’s body was plainly accessible to human sensation and the touch of hands, what shall we say about before his suffering?
Or is John lying in all these things, together with all his companions, who said that they saw our Lord nailed to the wood? For what illusion or mental image can undergo something

like this? Or how could his body have seemed to be nailed up merely in the imagination? But if John altered all those things, presenting them as having happened when they had not happened in that manner and had not taken place at all,
and fabricated them like an evildoer, how is he an evangelist? And how did his Gospel deceive the whole world?

And how, then, is his tomb glorified with all this grace against demons? For if he wrongs our Savior by saying that he was nailed to the cross, and by all those other things that we have quoted from him, he is not his disciple, nor
does he deserve to be believed, even in small matters. So let them abandon him entirely, and not forcibly drag anything he said into their own folly. Let them take refuge in the madman Mani alone.
Luke also wrote what he had heard from the apostles: when, after his resurrection, they supposed that the one who appeared to them was an apparition they were seeing, our Lord answered them
and said, “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have a body and bones.” Who, then, is this who, when all these things and many others like them are set down in the Gospel,
being an evil demon, would dare to say that the disciples deliberately wrote falsehoods? All these things, then, in which they supposedly erred through the will of matter, not

through their own will—this claim, which they make on the spur of the moment, is a verbal illusion [?]: this is a delusion, and things did not happen as they took place and were seen, and the account of them is false.

But in all those things which they said our Lord did, they introduced nothing from their own imagination. Rather, they framed their account according to what they saw happen to the one who did them. If, then, these things
happened as those whose names we have mentioned wrote, the testimony to our Lord’s body is clear. But if they deliberately lied, this was not an error caused by matter, as they claim.
Rather, the guilt belongs to their own will, and they deserve hatred all the more, not reverence or honor.
Our Savior himself, however, is seen everywhere directing all his teaching toward the good of souls, to instruct them in the fear of God

and in virtue. Yet he also demonstrated no less care in healing the body. How, then, could he have been concerned for the body if he knew that these bodies were things fashioned by evil? For, on the contrary,

he cared for them as his own, as things he himself had fashioned, and freed them from diseases and pains of every kind. And Lazarus, who had completely put off his body, he caused to put this same body on again and rise from the dead

His work was to perform miracles in the body, and through these very acts of help he demonstrated in deeds his power over them. He came to announce eternal life and the kingdom of heaven to human beings.
What would have been remarkable if he had promised life only to souls, whose nature was plainly such that they do not die, unless also
the body, which decays, were to become incorruptible along with the soul? Indeed, this is all the more fitting. For the one who together with [?] should enjoy the victories.

Let us therefore see and consider how many evils Mani introduced, gathered together, and cast into his evil teaching. For he invented a ruling principle without beginning and without origin, opposed to God,
who alone is without beginning, the Being who did not come into existence. And this principle, he says, is always in turmoil and is always stirring up and waging war against God.
How, then, can Christ be thought to have spoken fittingly about peace to his disciples when he said, “I give you my peace, and I leave you my peace”? For if he

has remained with his Father from eternity, according to Mani’s wicked teaching, while evil wages war against him, how did he promise to leave his disciples peace and tranquility that he himself does not possess?
This man dared to set evil in opposition to God, so as to say that it possesses equality with him in being, power, and life. Yet we detest even the error of the pagans,
who wickedly honored evil demons and called them gods. It is not that they do not exist in their own persons from the beginning [?]; rather, they exist, but they are evil.
But this man, besides sharing the sickness of the pagans—for he speaks of many gods—also places what does not exist at all on an equal footing with God, who does exist.

Moreover, he falsely attributes great weakness and deficiency to God, saying that not only was he unable to abolish evil, but he was even forcibly driven by it to establish the world, though he did not wish to, and to make creatures that give satisfaction to evil,
while they themselves suffer harm. Yet why was something required to come into being in the first place if it gained no benefit from its existence?

For if it was deceived and harmed by coming into being, it would have benefited by not coming into being. And how is this characteristic of one who is good: that, in order to free himself and his own from warfare through the world’s coming into existence,
he should create it for the destruction of those who come into being in it? For if he saw no benefit at all for those who come into being, he is supremely a lover of himself and not
a lover of goodness, this one whom he describes. And how much distress he causes his followers, who endure [?] a God who is defeated and cannot fully stand up for his own,
and is driven by force, against his will, not only to do everything but also to suffer! The soul sent from him is confined under guard and in bonds, while the rulers and authorities of matter cruelly
devise schemes against it in the molding of the body and set this before it like an enticing bait, so that what is sent from God’s nature and being is continually caught like a fish.

Moreover, he also blasphemes against the divine governance of everything and abolishes all human reverence for God. For he condemns the necessary reverence that arises from the care of God’s governance
as evil, along with all the other things that occur through divine governance. Along with these, he also insults, ridicules, and mocks the rains, lightning, and thunder.

Oh, the immense and abundant blasphemy, and the madness of the man who rages against God! Oh, the tales without foundation or substance, and the barbarous fabrications! For along with all these things he insults creation,
yet he receives pleasures from it no less than anyone else. Readily disposed and prepared for injustice, and greedy, he receives pleasures more than anyone else.
Readily disposed and prepared for injustice, he is greedy and insatiable in his desire. He delights and takes his ease, and is not ashamed to blaspheme.

He enjoys and insults at the same time; he marvels at the sight and blasphemes with his tongue. At the same time he moves his teeth and insults with his tongue the things he eats. As for his indulgences in reckless behavior outside the law, because, he says,

of matter, he does not condemn them. But he disparages and condemns the procreation of children, and treats sin as a matter of indifference because of pardon [?]. He scorns and insults God’s law. For just as, if he sees a thorn from
wood. In this way that senseless man sees evil conduct among human beings and does not know how great the difference is. Or, although he knows, he conceals it, for the wood cannot be otherwise.

For it came to be this way for a useful purpose. But this person could refrain from doing this, since he has authority over himself. What is easy for him, he wickedly attacks [?]. Yet he introduces necessity and thinks

that he excludes the possibility of repentance, so that no one, even before the judgment, should anticipate it by condemning himself for his own benefit. For he is always dear to bands of robbers and to young men, and among

others his stories are dear as well—to those who find rest under the authority of sin and who, without the restraint of discipline, rush eagerly toward their desires like [?]. These are the people whose

pallor is counterfeit, and whose impudence regards sin and insult to God's creation as trivial. The disfigurement of the appearance of their naturally cheerful complexion is contrived as though it were something fine. And those who refrain from action,
provided only that it can be concealed, dare to do absolutely anything. Their appearance is that of philosophers, but their conduct in secret is that of corrupt Chaldeans and sorcerers.
In what is publicly known, however, it is deceitful. For they want to know things about which they are not permitted to say, “We know.” But they conceal their ignorance of those things
which, more than [?], it would have been better for them to know. And what can anyone say about their conduct in these matters? Perhaps it was without freedom, from that very inventor of error,

that it was handed down to them. He truly counseled them to despise the poor, to whom, because of their abundance, they could have given and shown love. Yet they themselves are exceedingly idle and empty.

They have even taken upon themselves the first fruits of blasphemy against God, who commands them to give everything—these people whose name suggests purity, but whose way of life is impure and full of everything deserving condemnation and of partiality.
But if anyone also sees the deceit of the madman Mani and his contempt for the love taught by the Gospel, he will hate him still more for these things than for those already mentioned.
For he denies the coming of our Savior. Yet, as a mere outward form, he acknowledges this very thing in order to deceive those who believe in Christ. He boldly dares to show that

the saving work of his coming was futile, and says that the labor of his teaching accomplished nothing. “For what,” he says, “can the word do to matter, which is self-existent?” And consequently, of necessity, futile is

every word there is, since, he says, it cannot overcome evil, which is self-existent and did not come into being. Yet, while acknowledging the invincible sovereignty of the adversary, he also introduces a word of instruction and openly fights against himself.
He cuts our Savior's words into little sayings and truncates them all. But he stretches out his own chatter to a boundless length. And besides all these things,
he accuses the Gospel account itself of falsehood, saying that our Lord appeared only as a mirage and did nothing in reality. He says that he seemed to suffer, as though in

the imagination and not in reality. He says that he seemed to suffer, as though in the imagination and not in reality, and that everything was done by some craft of the devil—that is, by a complete deception [?]. Without
sense, he composes lengthy nonsense, borrowing and stitching together many words and confused speeches, stringing them together and inserting one into another. He wrote countless hymns in his books,

and letters without measure, drawing on these things and elaborating on them at great length with superfluous material. As for those other empty words of his, his endless nonsense, his corrupt tradition, and his deceptions directed against those who come to him and are guided by him—

by which his followers habitually entice and ensnare those very people, so that anyone once caught by them in error cannot escape from them at all, or even say that he belongs to himself—they are not even worth writing about.
Let us now bring forward a few passages from the New Testament and explain how he tampers with them and twists them toward his wickedness,

so that through a few examples we may give a taste and show how alien he is to the holy Scriptures. For in his wickedness he first makes use of this saying: “You cannot serve two masters.” And he says
that by naming two masters, he acknowledged those two sovereignties. But he passes over what immediately follows: “You cannot serve God and mammon.” For that other master is a passion.

He named the one belonging to the mind, and did not indicate two first principles. Indeed, if there were two first principles, he would not have spoken falsely, for people would necessarily serve them under compulsion. But since
there is one who is Lord by nature—God—yet we ourselves often willingly set passions above us to rule over us, especially the love of money, which he here identifies by
the name Mammon. By saying, “You cannot,” he turns them toward the possibility of being freed from the passion of loving money. For the apostle himself likewise said,
“Sin shall not rule over you.” For whatever overcomes a person also enslaves him. Even ordinary thinking recognizes the use of such an expression: how the passions of the soul

[?] are set over it like masters. As we commonly say, “So-and-so is enslaved to wine,” and, “So-and-so’s anger rules over him.” This does not mean that the passion itself comes from some beginningless first principle,
but that the person himself enslaves himself to it. Yet he can also free himself from it again. For reason overcomes it, correction suppresses it, shame drives it away, and fear changes it.
But Mani’s disciples and companions force the words, using what amounts to verbal sleight of hand to establish all this impiety. For look at what their founder himself did
to these words, to bring ruin. He took and erased the words of the holy Scriptures that show and declare, beyond contradiction, that there is one beginningless first principle.
But those spoken about other teachings and matters he forcibly strained, dragging them toward something else. For example, John said, “Everything came into being through him,

and without him nothing came into being.” Again, the apostle also said, “There is one God, the Father, from whom everything comes, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom everything comes.” These, he says, are to be taken away and erased.
But he uses the words, “You cannot serve two masters,” as though they were a teaching declaring two first principles. Yet this was not said as a statement about God,
nor was it issued as a teaching about God. Rather, it was given to discipline our habits and conduct, so that we might serve God alone and refrain from the passions of loving money. Everywhere,

however, these words are connected with one another within their own context. Since this is clear, their meaning is only dragged elsewhere by force, from time to time, especially by those who deal unjustly with the truth.
Again, he also brings forward this saying from the Gospel: “A good tree cannot bear bad fruit,
nor can a bad tree bear good fruit. Each tree is known by its fruit.” Here again, either through malicious cunning
or thoughtless confusion, he takes a saying about conduct and habits as a teaching about two mutually opposed natures.

For our Lord himself clearly explains this parable in what follows, saying, “A good person brings good things out of the good treasures in his heart, and an evil person brings evil things out of the evil treasures in his heart. For the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart.”

He plainly called the heart a storehouse because of freedom of will, not a first principle, and he blamed nothing else. For if he had been speaking of something arising from a beginningless first principle,

then [?] the heart as plainly being a receptacle, and these things would not have come from it. But if the storehouse of evil is nowhere else, but only in the heart, then where that storehouse is, there also is the beginning of evil,
which comes into being through the will’s contrivance, and not from some beginningless first principle.
Here too, however, he takes his saying from things belonging to nature to reprove things belonging to the will, using it to illustrate the point. For something that is straightforward
and evident in and of itself stirs the attention and understanding of those being instructed only slightly. But that which supplies testimony from things in nature, in which there is much
that corresponds to what is being said, contains many illustrations and is better able to rouse the hearer. For the distinction between trees is imposed by nature.

For this reason, they cannot be different at another time, but can only be as they are constituted. Human beings, however, have their own will, and for this reason they also admit varied changes of every kind.
Therefore, to make clear how we ought to examine those who approach us, he presents their fruits as evidence exposing their will, just as he says elsewhere: “You will recognize them by their fruits.”
Let us also examine, from another angle, the care and diligence of these [?]. For he said of the bad tree that it cannot produce good fruit.
Conversely, the good tree cannot produce bad fruit. But of the evil person he said that he brings good things out of the treasures in his heart, and he did not say
that he cannot bring out evil things, so that he would not confine and bind the will by nature. Rather, he spoke of something that happens without contrivance, through the will. He is able,
for, along with a change in his wickedness, to change his fruits as well. And John the Baptist also speaks in this way:

“Every tree that does not produce fruit is cut down and falls into the fire.” He applies this to human beings. Let us pass over what is superfluous here [?]. By the threat he does nothing other than change them through fear.

For this judgment would not even be just if he condemned those who fail to produce the fruits of virtue because of a deficiency in their nature. For the tree that does not produce good fruit does not, as an act of

punishment, fall into the fire, but to meet a necessary human need. This is the [?] reason for this nature to exist. But what need does a human being meet, or whom does he serve, by falling into the fire?

Rather, the punishment is necessarily for himself alone, because of the contempt that lies in his own will. Because of this, he is justly and [?] necessarily threatened, to help him change. In the end, however, he is also [?] punished if he treats the fear inspired by the threat as nothing.
Thus, even through these few points in which the truth has been explained, either Mani’s thoughtless folly or his wicked perversity, which opposes the Holy Scriptures, can become clear.
But since he also blames and maligns created things, and furthermore [?] and dares to draw testimony from the Gospel, let us therefore follow him and set out the passages he uses concerning
this. For he also introduces what our Lord said to his disciples: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me first. If you belonged to the world, the world would love its own.
But because you do not belong to the world, and I have chosen you out of the world, for this reason the world hates you.”

“See,” he says, “what he says about the world: how he is a stranger to it and stands opposed to it.” And especially, he says, in the words he spoke elsewhere: “The world hated them because they did not belong to the world,
just as I did not belong to the world.” “How, then,” he says, “can that world be good, when he has utterly rejected it?”
He gathers these passages and others like them as a blind man would, not knowing what he is doing. For in these passages our Lord does not use the word “world” for created things. For not even
one of them hated either him or his disciples. Indeed, these things are otherwise shared equally by the righteous and the wicked.
