Moreover, all of them obeyed our Lord’s command. What world, then, hated either him or his disciples? Was it perhaps the sun, which fled so as not to see his suffering? Or the stars, among which there leaped

that star which, in an extraordinary way, contrary to its usual course, proclaimed his extraordinary birth at its appointed time? Or was it the sea, which at his command immediately became peaceful and, together with the wind, grew still? And the earth—
how did it not show its worship of him, when it brought forth the five loaves with which our Lord fed five thousand men? But it is clear even to Mani himself
that the world which rose against our Savior was not this inhabited world, but the human beings who live in it. For everyone is accustomed to use the names of cities, not for the buildings, but for

their inhabitants. People say, “It pleased the city,” and “The city chose and commanded,” and “The city loved,” or conversely, “The city hated its ruler.” It is human beings that all of us alike customarily mean
and indicate. If, therefore, those who inhabit the world hated our Lord, we should not blame the created world, but the will of those who live in it. For it was about them that our Lord spoke.
Clearly, then, along with what has been said, he introduces and adds: “Remember the words I told you: No servant is greater than his master. If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.”
“And if they kept my words, they will also keep yours.” Clearly, he said this about those people who did not believe in him, and he prepares the minds of those being instructed
to endure persecution. Thus, by “the world” he meant human beings, not the creation, as he made clear.
Elsewhere he said to the Jews: “The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its deeds are evil.” Clearly, he means human beings, and not

other created things. Through these words we can also see the precise meaning of what is being said. For by the name “world” he indicates the intention of those who inhabit it, and says, “It hates me because

I testify about it.” He does not say that it is evil, as though speaking of something unchangeable, but that its deeds are evil. For he condemns the actions themselves, and does not reject the possibility of repentance.

For it is clear and well known that he had compassion on them, since he also came to them, so that, by enduring their hatred at first, he might eventually change them to love him. Clearly, this very thing happened before long. For he did not

rebuke them as though they were unable to repent, or as though they were incurable in themselves—a condition found among the weak—or as though they proceeded from an opposing principle, as that madman claims.
Otherwise, why would he have come to them in the first place? And why would he willingly have endured the insult of their hatred to no purpose?
But in all this he was concerned for the salvation of those who hated him. Thus he says these very same things about his disciples in the form of a prayer to his Father: “I have given
them your word, and the world has hated them because they were not of the world, just as I was not of the world.” And afterward he adds: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but
that you keep them from the evil one.” For it would not have been right for the physicians to be taken away from the sick, since this was why they were chosen in the first place. But if this world,

the world of human beings, were foul and contemptible, he would have asked that they escape from the worthless world. As it is, however, he wishes them to remain in the world, because no opposing principle
exists at all, nor does it possess any share in it. Yet he says that, while they remain, they should be protected by God from the evil one, so that, being healthy themselves, they may heal the sick.
We will say a little later who this evil one is. For now, it has been shown that our Lord clearly loves the world exceedingly, since he also came to it,
and does not wish his disciples to be taken out of it, so that by remaining they may heal those in need. He even sends these very men like sheep among wolves,

not so that they may be torn apart, but so that they may make the wolves themselves peaceable. They were therefore not alien to the world by nature, but only by their will. For in their nature they are like
those who persecute them, but their will differs from theirs; and they endured so that they might change those who persecuted them. For how could those people be alien to the world
who were chosen out of the world itself? For it is clear that the whole batch of dough is like its first portion. Hence it is clear that wherever our Lord rebukes the world, it is human beings
whom he rebukes—those who are evil by their will and not by their nature.
Nor did they come forth from any opposing principle. He therefore came for this purpose: to save those who are healed in their will, without their nature being changed.
And why is it surprising if he spoke about humanity in this way in the Gospel, when at the beginning, in Genesis, he also said: “My spirit shall not dwell in these human beings,
because they are flesh,” and, “The inclination of a human being is earnestly set on evil from his youth”? He used the term “inclination” in place of “will.” For this reason
he rebuked them from the beginning. For he would not have rebuked them at all if they had been driven toward evil actions by some compulsion.

We have said in the preceding passages that human beings were necessarily formed by God in this way: the inclination toward sin is easy for them and very readily available to them, but difficult and arduous [?]
The practice of virtue. Let this now also be added to what has been said: because the rewards of reverence for God and of virtue are great, the toil [?] associated with them is necessarily
imposed on human beings. It does not equal those good things that they hope for and await, but it does provide a fitting basis for enjoying them. For God himself is good,

and he does not wish to give his gifts without distinction or examination, lest his goodness be blamed as altogether inappropriate. Rather, in exchange for very small things, he gives very great things. Furthermore, the very reception of gifts from God,

if it comes to human beings with rational awareness and knowledge, makes its benefit apparent to them. But if it comes without reason and without knowledge, people do not even think that it amounts to anything.

If, then, we receive these things with rational awareness, so that our knowledge of their enjoyment can also explain and interpret it for us, then through reason we are also instructed about that which
makes us worthy, and very fittingly so. For those things whose benefit is revealed and made clear through reason cannot be deserved by anyone apart from reason.

And if it is through reason that we are enabled to become worthy of these things, we are governed by our own will. For when reason enters, all compulsion, chance, accident, and opposition rightly depart. For this fact—that we came into being when we did not exist—
was not brought about through the care of those who came into being. For this is a common gift from the Creator, given equally to all of us, both the righteous and the unrighteous.
But once we had come into being, it was fitting that we should acquire reason and knowledge, and gain for ourselves something worthy of our Maker. This very thing is granted to us through difficulty.
For what is easy to obtain is also easy to despise. One can readily gather many such examples and show that in no
other way was it fitting for the Good One to form a rational human being from the earth, to inhabit the bodily world, except in this manner.
But those from whom the discussion turned aside [?] ask us about the devil, Satan, from whom our Lord asks that his disciples be protected by

his Father. Our discussion also promised a little earlier to give an answer concerning him. They present us with another saying of our Savior concerning this matter, especially the one in which he says, “Now is the judgment of this world;
now the ruler of this world is being cast out.” Through these words they introduce the notion of some opposing sovereignty, as though he had thereby acknowledged a certain ruler
of this world who, they say, is someone else besides God. Yet from the words themselves we grasp the truth of what was said.

But first let us again examine and understand what world he calls the evil one the ruler of. Is it perhaps the other, external things, or exclusively humanity alone? For all created things have their own order,

and they never depart from it. Nor do they suffer any injury from the evil one that would cause them to transgress their Maker’s law. Indeed, they do not have control even over their own movement, but are held by the decree

of their Creator and continually remain in it from the beginning. They proclaim God’s arrangement and order within them. Scripture also says, “At his command the sun and moon rise, and not of themselves.”
But if the evil one is said to be the ruler of the human beings who live in the world, he does not have dominion over them either, as we have clearly shown through many considerations of this kind
in the discussion itself, explaining how this should be understood. Our Lord himself, when speaking with his Father about his disciples, says, “I do not ask that you take them out of the world,
but that you protect them from the evil one.” Thus a person can be delivered from the evil one by coming to God, since the evil one has no coercive authority at all.
The saying about him is also significant: “Now the ruler of this world is being cast out.” For if he is cast out, he is neither self-existent nor possessed of authority by nature.

Rather, through wicked presumption he contrived this authority for himself. As for the manner in which he is cast out, John the Baptist declared beforehand, “Look, the Lamb of God! Look, the one who takes away the sin of the world!”
Through this one statement he made many things clear: what is taken away arose through the choice of those who sinned, not through nature, nor was it committed in an unchangeable manner.

Their conduct shows that human beings themselves are the ones who sin, and also that through sin the evil one deceitfully established his authority over human beings, while God permitted this for the reasons we have mentioned. When sin is thus taken away,

the power of the one who had ruled through error was also dissolved. In this way he was cast out—not in a spatial sense, but through the dissolution of his tyrannical authority, as idolatry was rebuked
and error and the entire worship of evil demons were despised. Judgment was being passed on the sin that prevailed in the world, and the ruler of the world's sin was being cast out.

Thus the transformation of the inhabited world bears witness: all the Romans and barbarians turning toward virtue and the fear of God testify to his being cast out and rejected, and also to the rebuke of the authority over the world

that he had taken for himself. For he would not have been brought down by the teaching of fishermen and limited human beings if he had possessed by nature any authority or what is regarded as substantial existence. Thus the evil one surrendered and was defeated by people who were small even in their [?]

and unpracticed in speech. He had not even attained it [?], nor was he self-existent, nor was authority firmly established in his nature, since he was easily shaken and cast down from his foundation and root. Therefore, just as it was by their own will
that those against whom he schemed were harmed, and they went astray not because of their nature but through the initiative of their own will,
so also the one who deceived them deliberately devised error against human beings because of his wickedness. For the evil one is wicked, but wickedness is a passion

of the mind, and distress or anger whose impulse harms those against whom it is stirred. For this reason nothing is evil by nature. For if someone knows what he is doing, it is by his own will that he is
evil. But if he does not know, he is certainly not evil. Indeed, how can someone act wickedly without knowing what he is doing, if wickedness requires some skill, as well as cunning and deception,
so that he often disguises what is harmful as something helpful, so that it may be accepted unsuspectingly and cause destruction? And where are we to place cunning, deception, and error,

except with someone who acts wickedly? For these things have no place in the mind and thought of someone good. Therefore, if the evil one is certainly also cunning and deceptive, and can conceal himself and hide

through his [?] in the things by which he deceives and brings others low, it is clear that he knows himself and also the person he deceives. He also knows what helps and what harms, both good and evil.
He schemes through wrongdoing, [?] or secretly, for no other reason than either to take revenge as though he had been unjustly [?], or because of his envy
of someone better than himself. For attacking someone out of a desire for money has no parallel in the matter before us, nor is it closely related to it.

Thus it is clear that this evil one, of whom we are speaking, had not previously suffered any harm from human beings. Rather, it was because of his envy that he set the snares of his deception against those
desires, and all the error opposed to God, so that human beings [?] he had previously suffered harm. Rather, it was because of his envy that he set the snares of his deception against those
desires, and all the error opposed to God, so that human beings who live in the flesh might not distinguish themselves before God more than he did, and might not forcefully

rebuke him. Therefore, if he became an enemy because of his envy, knowing what is superior and how it is superior to himself, and knowing the one who is truly blessed and good, whom he envied for this reason, it is in these things that he acts wickedly, not in his nature.

Therefore this evil one is not something evil in his very being. Rather, by his own will he is so deeply immersed in evil that he will not even accept a change in his will. Thus he also deceives all the more, and does not use force to

lead people. For he does not have the power to lead by force, since he has not received permission from God to do this. His practice of deception clearly shows that he himself is not compelled by his nature to be in this condition.
It is therefore clear that he too was created good in his nature by God, and became evil through a change

in his own will. For all rational beings are not bound by the compulsion of nature, but have been honored by God with freedom, so that they may thus offer worship to their Maker by their own will. Therefore he has this: that he became

His existence comes from God, but his being like this comes from himself. As for his being beautiful by nature, as a work of God, let us hear our Savior, who says, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.”
Now the one compared to lightning is always radiant in appearance and beautiful by nature. In Job too, one can find that, when the angels came to stand before God,

Satan also stood among them. He came as one who belonged to their kind by nature, although by his will he was separated from them. Moreover, when God questioned him, he heard the invisible one according to his ability and gave an answer. He is not different in nature

and kind from the angels, nor has he escaped subjection to the one who made him. But because of the patience shown in postponing judgment, he persists in his wrongdoing. Nor is he unaware of the conclusion and final outcome in which his wickedness will be restrained and abolished.
For those demons immediately said to our Lord, “You have come before the time to torment me.” They knew that they would be tormented, and concerning “You have come before
the time to torment me”—they knew that they would be tormented, but they were questioning him about the time, since this was not it. Moreover, they also said
this: “We know who you are: you are the Holy One of God.” By this too they were making it known that it was not through ignorance

of anything, but in wickedness, that they were doing evil [?]. Thus they recognized the Good One, whom they could not have recognized unless they had been beautiful by nature. Nor were they serving a self-existent principle
of some opposing kind, having turned away from obedience to him toward one to whom they were not subject by nature. For one can see that these very beings were not merely
frightened and shaken by our Lord’s command, but immediately fled and were driven out. They abandoned their long-standing dwelling and their places

at his command. Those demons, then, who recognized our Lord, spoke with him, obeyed him, and were driven out by him—how can they be imagined [?] to belong to a self-existent principle? And they were driven out by him.

How can they be imagined [?] to belong to a self-existent principle? And they were driven out by him. How can they be imagined [?] to be devoted to some opposing self-existent principle? For through all these things they were clearly
shown to be under the hand of the one and only self-existent God, and to pay the penalty for the wickedness that comes from their own will [?], which they also openly admitted they were expecting.
Moreover, their chief himself, the devil, Satan, tempts our Lord in the Gospel before knowing with certainty whether he was the one

who was expected to come according to the ancient prophecy. He spoke with him and spent a long time with our Lord, addressing words to him and receiving answers from him, and recalling the words of God.
He brings forward testimonies from the Old Testament, acknowledging that they are divine words—in contrast to the mad Mani. Yet in his error this misguided being also falsely promises our Lord

things over which he has no authority. Thus the very conversation, and his ability to approach the Son of God and speak with him, acknowledge and testify to the loftiness of Satan’s nature, while exposing his will and showing that it is evil.
Furthermore, his very name in Scripture, “the slanderer,” indicates that his nature is far removed from evil, but that his will is deceitful. For he is eager to slander humanity before God,

and through the things he advises he prepares a certain hostility in humanity toward its Maker. He was called “the slanderer” because of his activity, since he introduced a deceitful will and knowingly, deliberately, and willingly acted out of envy.
Thus no opposing evil being at all should ever be regarded as fighting against God as a self-existent being. This being does nothing whatsoever
unless God permits it. Yet he is an unwilling helper: his Maker lets him loose [?] for the governance of human beings, along with many other statements concerning him
of this kind. For rational humanity necessarily needed an opponent for victories in its contests. From that time until now, he has envied humanity because of God.

But God left him alone, knowing in his foreknowledge the outcome of the matter. Humanity, meanwhile, perseveres in its exertion [?] and testing, and its contest became a marvel, for God openly appointed it to the contest.
For a human being in a body can overcome one who is free of a body. If this were not so, the devil would not have received this permission from God.
Human beings would have suffered a great loss, deprived of the one who tests them and trains them for victories. For all those things which it is not fitting for God, by
himself, to set in motion for the training of those who are zealous in their souls, these very things the evil one sets in motion. Against his will, he proves to be a helper to those
who are trained by him, so that God’s providence may be wonderful. For the evil one, against his will, serves God’s will through the victories of human beings.
Likewise, God does not incite the minds of tyrants, who have chosen this for themselves, to persecute those who fear him, because it is not even
fitting for him to do such things for the victory of others. But the evil one, taking advantage of their own inclinations arising from their free choice, inflames and incites those who are able

to persecute. He has crowned many through confession and martyrdom and sent them to God, who appointed him for the contest. God himself permitted this, knowing the benefit of the outcome of these events.
What, then, shall we say about the Jews’ envy, which arose from their own will? If the evil one had not further inflamed it against our Lord, who willingly surrendered himself to the will

of those people, how would the whole world have enjoyed the salvation that came from this? For we must know that the evil one does not establish the beginning of insolence in the mind and thought, for he cannot.

But he inflames and incites the impulse that arises from the will, and against his will he serves God’s providence. He deserves no gratitude at all because of the outcome of those events which through [?]
are arranged to be beneficial through God’s providence. For he acts wickedly, while God, in a wonderful and astonishing way, makes use of his wickedness to direct great events.
Nor, then, because of these things does his rebellion appear acceptable to God, before whom his wickedness is blameworthy. For God did not lack other ways fitting for him,
through which those who entrust themselves to him could be trained in the fear of him and in virtue. But God’s providence concerning the devil, wise in every respect, is wonderful

in this: he allowed this evil one to become such by his own will, although he could have rebuked and silenced him from the beginning. He makes wonderful use of his wickedness to demonstrate his own goodness.

But if someone points to the multitude of human beings who are defeated, and criticizes and disparages providence, let him learn that many are not defeated in combat in the first place, nor do they from
the outset [?] stand against him and then surrender because they cannot endure the devil’s cunning to the end. Rather, of their own will they turn to unjust deeds, even without his advice.
For many whose will is undiscerning need only the stimulus of nature to turn toward desires, exposing their will as blameworthy in every sin, since even entirely without the evil one
they take no pleasure in good things. Nor is it just to charge him with the sins of those who were already caught up in evil ways of life.
But those who show courage in the fear of God are also attacked by the evil one because of his envy. He plots against them in the hope of victory, and trains and tests their will.
God permits this so that, through enduring the impulses in their own nature and through their vigilance against the evil one’s schemes, those who fear God [?]—for great and worthy of God

are the gifts, victories, and crowns reserved for them. For this reason they rightly entered great contests, to become worthy of these things. Nor was the wonder concerning those who are victorious a small one.

Nor is providence unjust toward those who did not give themselves to the contest even from the beginning. For this providence concerning those who begrudged themselves the benefit [?], and concerning the devil, is beyond all human speech.

As for those who suffer harm from this because they did not wish to pursue good things, or who very wickedly chose to be defeated, let us leave this to the Judge. For it is not ours to decide and pass judgment on the things
that please him. But if, because of the many, it had happened that not even a few were victorious, the justice of providence would have been undermined. For if
Because of others who were unwilling even from the beginning to enter the contest, should those who are willing and delight in the struggle also be prevented by them? For to God, at all times

and beforehand, everyone’s intentions are plain. He has no need at all of a trial in order to examine and learn about each person. Yet he permitted the evil one to approach the righteous, to train and test their deeds of endurance, so that not

only would their intentions be plain to his foreknowledge [?], but they would also distinguish themselves and grow through the actual deed, and would show in practice, through their endurance, that his love for them was not merely a favor.

For just as a physician gains distinction and greatness not through the theory of his craft but through its actual practice, so too a righteous person is necessarily shown to be honorable not merely through his intention but also through the testing of his endurance.

And always, this alone is righteousness and virtue: to endure under testing, for training and examination through all our trials, both those that lie within us and those that come upon us from outside.

Thus, then, the evil one himself is put to use for the benefit of human beings. He is also allowed to remain before his punishment for another reason: while he still exists, he experiences punishment through the triumph
and crowning of those who fear God in their struggle against him, and he endures great disgrace. For this battle and struggle of a human being against such an adversary is not an equal one.
For he receives no glory through those who follow his will; they are merely companions who console him in his evil
expectation. But through those who overcome him he is greatly dishonored and put to shame, because, although they are human beings and fight against him in the flesh, they overcome him.

Besides what has been said, if he had been extinguished from the beginning and had received punishment for his rebellion, where would God’s patience have been, and where his great and profound forbearance in rebuking

him? And would it not also have seemed that he could have accomplished something great, since he was quickly removed from the scene? For this is the great thing: while he remains, he is rebuked, and while he does harm, he is shown to be a helper

against his will. He was not quickly removed and cast out of the governance of all things as though he were some formidable power, or bound by some stratagem, as though [?] he could accomplish something by force against God. Rather, as

an evil being, he is mocked and laughed at by those spiritual powers, and in every generation he is defeated and condemned by righteous people through their own will and through the help they receive from God.
For their sake, too, he is allowed to remain for another purpose, being kept for punishment at its appointed time.
The character of his rebellion is not hidden from anyone capable of examining it. For although he is free from every bodily desire because he has no body, there is nothing remarkable about this.

For if, in his own mind, he formed an exalted opinion of himself and became proud, he was overthrown and fell. For an unlawful desire for an expectation contrary to nature commonly deprives a person even of what belongs to nature. For such a conception

is what the divine Scriptures give us to hold concerning him. We can also see and understand from what he has done up to now that his love of power and his rebellion are without measure. For he has concerned himself with being worshiped

instead of God by those whom he leads astray in various ways among every people. He even openly admitted his passion to our Savior himself, saying, “I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.” In the same way, he also pressured the martyrs

and confessors of the church, and through them sought honor for himself as though in God’s place. It seems to me that this Mani himself also suffers from this very thing, since he dares to draw to himself, instead of Christ, those whom he leads astray.
For because he is a disciple of the devil, Satan, this opponent of Christ has been seized by a sickness like his, just as Satan himself opposed God from the beginning.

Thus it was into this very sickness that the devil, Satan, fell by his own will from the beginning. He was deprived of God’s grace and of the unfailing provision of spiritual nourishment that brings delight in the worship and reverence of his Creator.

In him all spiritual beings exist and are nourished in their understanding, so that they may continue in unceasing service and worship at all times, and in the delight that comes from God. But this one fell into wickedness

without measure, so that, despite the ugliness and foulness of his passion, he did not willingly desist from it. For this reason he strives to strip away the good things that are in the minds of human beings.
and especially to the knowledge of God. But because he knows that the soul does not easily depart into wickedness and error opposed to God unless it has first been buried in bodily passions,

he becomes a helper in voluntary evils, and through the lesser evil he prepares the greater, namely, the wickedness of going astray from God. He does not lead anyone by force, but takes the role of an adviser toward

such things. In this way he has also been called the ruler of the world, just as the gods of the nations are not gods. For the use of names is often determined by what is put into the minds of those who go astray and also of those
who lead others astray. For he is the ruler of the world and of the sin practiced among human beings in the sense that he has contrived to be regarded as such. For he does not even

have any permanent authority over anything at all unless God permits it. Yet God necessarily allows him freedom of action, and through a varied strategy of every kind he prepares an arena and a battle for the person who fears God

and Christ, so that he may imitate God in everything. He fights against Christ by means of Christ’s name, as he supposes. God necessarily permits [?] this very thing so that those who are chosen by their own will may thus be revealed.

At the end he also imitates the coming of our Savior, in which he appeared as a human being, as the Old Testament and also the New declared beforehand [?]. For he saw that Christ’s coming in the flesh brought about his condemnation without force.

For it would not have been a great thing if it had happened by force. Rather, through the strategy of wisdom it dissolved his rebellion and brought the whole inhabited world over to the knowledge of the truth. Finally, he too, in his jealous rivalry over this victory, seeks, in order to lead people astray,

open and acknowledged worship for himself from everyone. But he does not succeed in leading many astray. Christ himself comes again and sends him to that place prepared long ago for him and for those who share his mind,

the place of punishment, doing this merely through the manifestation of his divinity. The words of the apostles plainly teach us this very thing. But now, for his own consolation, he prepares companions for himself, those
whom he finds readily disposed to this by their own will, just as he himself was from the beginning. Then he appears as their accuser, as at that time
when our Savior lived among us and said, “The ruler [?] of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” He was revealing that he does this very thing against each of the righteous,
accusing them and reproaching them for the sins each has committed, so that he may drag those who are caught into a share in his own destruction.

But God does not give him authority to compel the will by force. Rather, he prepares contests for human beings so that, through the freedom of their own will, they may be watchful and vigorous against him.
Moreover, even in the case of those who have little ability to fight against him, he does not give him complete freedom to impose on them anything heavier or harder than they can bear,
as it is said, “God is able not to allow you to be tempted beyond what you have the strength to bear.” He also holds back contests that would come before their proper time, until
the soul is fully armed with faith. Evidence of this is our Lord’s statement to Simon Peter: “Look, Satan has asked for you, to sift you like wheat.

But I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail.” It is therefore clear that it belongs to God, who established the contest, to determine both when and how much each person should be exercised [?] and tested in the contest [?].

Satan has no authority at all to carry out such a scheme. For he wishes to bring temptation upon each person beyond that person’s strength, and to impose it at an improper time, when their minds are not prepared.
But the just Judge restrains both his harsh attacks and his untimely arrival. Consequently, even those who fall and are drawn into weakness
have not fallen because he fought against them beyond their strength, but so that they may thus necessarily be convicted of having had no love in their souls for virtue grounded in the fear of God.

There is, however, the case of someone who has excelled in many things and then considers himself great and becomes proud. For this reason he is openly caught, having been handed over to defeat in the contest, so that

he may experience his weakness and inadequacy in practice, and may also learn, concerning those things in which he previously excelled, to attribute their cause to God in humility of mind. Thus a single blow will become for him
Delivering from a great sickness. For this is a greater evil: that someone should become proud even over great victories, rather than sin because of the weakness of his will, being human.
Our Lord therefore established this excellent pattern of testing as an example, and was tempted by Satan before Satan clearly recognized who he was. He allowed him time for as long as he wished.
When this pattern that he had established was complete, he said to him, “Get behind me, Satan!” Like a master, he authoritatively rebuked the wicked servant who was subject to his lord. Who,
then, in the face of all this subjection and servitude, authority and wonderful ordering, would dare suppose that Satan is an opposing principality without beginning, standing against God?
But the followers of that madman Mani say in their perplexity, “Who taught him this rebellion? Or who came and planted in his mind all this
evil?” Now this question is reasonable for those who have not already become entangled in Mani’s error. But among those against whom our argument is directed,
it is expressed more out of blindness and error than knowledge. Nevertheless, since this question has been raised, it is perhaps necessary to give an answer.

For all rational beings, including the intelligible beings, and humanity along with them, which was created among them, naturally possess a love of honor. For it is through the desire for victory and glory before God that we are spurred to training and toil.

This is the good that those who train themselves in the fear of God and in virtue hope for and await: that we may be counted worthy before God of the prizes, crowns, and heavenly and glorious victories that surpass our knowledge. Paul clearly expressed this very thing:

“The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to be revealed in us.” Without the hope of noble glory, no good deeds at all are undertaken. By their nature, then, they possess this
good thing—all rational beings do—the love of victory and glory before God, which urges them toward diligence and perseverance in serving and worshiping God. Whoever, then, is humble by his own will

uses the great possession inherent in his nature for virtue. He does not in any way transgress even the law of nature because of the desire implanted in him, nor does he acquire glory for himself through shameful schemes. Rather, through love

for God, constant service and worship of him, and humility of mind, he strives for noble glory. But someone who hastens toward this glory of which we have spoken, without discipline or experience of goodness, through a lack
of good will abandons the path of hope toward God, which leads through humility, and devises other paths, and [?], and corrupts the good, pure seed through bad cultivation.

Thus many also tumble and fall into vainglory in confusion, exchanging true glory for this false, human glory. While wishing to be glorified, they are instead deprived of glory, because they have not rightly used
what is inherent in their nature. Our Lord himself defined the character of this striving by his word, saying, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

Thus the devil himself, who was not a devil from the beginning, used his natural desire without sound judgment and fell into deprivation of glory through the wickedness by which he exalted himself. And he did not
learn this rebellion from someone else, nor was he incapable of devising this scheme for himself. For he possessed that seed which is good by nature, but he used it without [?] sound judgment.
For he has authority over it, and the mind of every rational being is free in cultivating the seed inherent in its nature. But using natural things without sound judgment everywhere produces
sins. If, then, the devil’s pride, which arose by his own will, had amounted to a small evil, his case would likewise have been less serious. But if, through a desire for glory in opposition to God,
who made him, he turned aside and rebelled and wished to be worshiped, let us consider and see how great is the audacity of his rebellion.
Furthermore, all rational beings naturally possess knowledge of everything pertaining to virtue and evil, lowliness of mind and pride, humility

and arrogance, and all those things that are spoken of as opposites of one another, so that knowledge of them and authority over them are implanted in their will. The choice of virtue was given by the good Creator.

For them, freedom, belonging to the image [?] of their Maker, adorns all the rational beings who have come into existence. For anyone deprived of authority over himself is deprived of victory and is driven by compulsion like an irrational creature,

and does not worship and serve as a rational being. But it was not characteristic of the Good One that rational beings should be fashioned by him in this way, since they would not even be considered rational beings.

Thus, then, the devil stumbled through his pride and rebelled. His nature did not change, for it was not within his power to change God's handiwork. Rather, he turned his mind toward evil, since he himself had authority over it.

For his nature is beautiful, because it is God's handiwork. His will, however, underwent a change of his own making. For from the beginning he was fashioned beautiful in his own being; his nature, however, is neither good nor evil.

For goodness is established through the honoring of knowledge only in created rational beings, while its opposite, evil, is contrived through the mind's devising, by the authority that exists in a free nature because of the ungrudging goodness

of the Maker. These opposites, then, are subsequently added to their individual being and their nature, which is beautiful and is not itself designated by either of them. Thus, what is beautiful is so in its own being, in its form

and appearance; but what is good becomes so through choosing those things that truly help. It is also possible to demonstrate this from Scripture itself, which says, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very beautiful.” Clearly it is of their own being that it

speaks. For goodness is added through the mind's choice to those who possess a mind. For he says, “A good person brings good things out of the good treasures in his heart.” By “heart” he indicated the leadership and direction

of the mind, and by “good things” he showed what consists not in a substantive being but in an action or a word. For a substantive being does not come out of the heart. Rather, through mind and heart, a person brings forth and displays the fruit that he chooses and loves.

For people too can be seen who are very similar in their bodily constitution but differ very greatly from one another in the disposition of their wills. When they are silent and doing nothing, someone who meets them cannot distinguish them

because of the similarity of their constitution, although there is a difference in their wills. Experience is needed to examine the character that subsequently develops through the habits of each of them. Thus, then, sight itself sees one thing:

the beautiful form of everything—I mean God's handiwork. But the fruit of the will alone possesses this distinction. Consequently, if we inquire about those who are good in their very being, God alone is found to be so.

For our Savior also said this: “No one is good except the one God alone,” whose goodness admits no change whatsoever. Yet the one who said this about his Father is also good like him, because he is from him.

The prophet also said of the Holy Spirit, “May your good Spirit guide me on level ground.” But everything that comes afterward is called good through effort and the mind's willing choice, not by nature.

These things, then, we have said to the best of our ability concerning the subject that compelled us to turn our discussion toward the devil, in agreement with the holy Scriptures, from which we receive our provision of the knowledge of truth concerning this:

to see how he is neither evil by nature nor a beginningless ruling power that fights against God. Nor is he preserved from eternity until the end for the purpose of causing harm, but necessarily for the benefit

of those who through him are trained and tested in reverence for God and in virtue. Nevertheless, unless someone from among [?] has spoken carefully, or afterward speaks and demonstrates these very things to refute
the one who hates God in every respect—namely, that the devil is not a ruling power opposed to God, fighting against him by his very nature—[?]. For the person who loves the truth is not contentious.

Let us also bring forward all those statements of the apostle that this wicked man forcibly drags into his own way of thinking, and through our discussion let us free them from his evil interpretation. For first, in response to his insolence toward the holy Scriptures, [?], and concerning

his alien teaching, consisting of those tales that surround him, he acknowledges and says, “Paul himself said that he knew a little out of much and prophesied a little out of much; and when perfection came, that which was little was abolished.”

“Therefore,” he says, “since perfection has come into my hands—into my own hands—even what was partial is being set right and purified.” But it seems to me that his followers deliberately blind their minds, if they do not
understand how the blessed Paul assigns perfect knowledge to the world to come. For if perfect knowledge has now been granted to those who are still in the body, what more would these people have

when they receive the blessedness they await? For human beings have no blessedness beyond perfect knowledge, insofar as they are capable of it. Yet those who have been deprived even of that partial knowledge because of the evil teaching of the error and wickedness
of the mad Mani think that they have received perfection. But Paul the apostle said, “Now we see as in a mirror,” clearly because we are in the body, “but then face to face,”
because we will encounter the truth of God without bodily density. Thus we are not mistaken now, nor will we then know it inadequately, within the limits of our capacity.

Yet this partial knowledge has not only not been abolished; it has also adequately grasped the whole of perfection! But the man who claims perfection for himself is, in truth, a complete liar, despised by the whole church of God and by everyone who has any understanding.
If, therefore, that partial knowledge has not been abolished, it is clear that perfection has not come, as the apostle said. Thus, in this way too, they are exposed as distorting the statement.

And when they advise people not to come anywhere near the storms of persecution, but instead to offer sacrifices and do everything the pagans command them, they improperly use the apostle’s statement:

“I became all things to everyone, so that I might save everyone.” It is as though someone were to profess medical skill and seek to heal the sick, but were himself seized by an incurable disease and, before all the others,
were to die. For the whole concern of our Savior’s teaching is this: that we ought to go even as far as death for reverence for the truth of God. If, therefore, those who teach are always ready
to change over to the ways of their persecutors, when will they convert those who are mistaken about reverence for God? But it is clear that such is the intention of wickedness: this very thing, too,
always uses even helpful things to cause harm and injury, contrary to what Paul said: “For those who love God, he makes everything work together for good.”
Therefore, by this statement too, he indicates something different. For when dealing with Jews, he drew on Jewish teaching, and for those under the law he supplied proofs about Christ from the law.
But when dealing with pagans, who are without the law, he drew from those poets of the Greeks.

He incorporated their words, as when he said, “We are his offspring,” to abolish the error of paganism; and again, when he said, “One of their own said,” he was speaking of one of them. And the message of reverence for God, which was his concern,
he extended to everyone. He said, “I became all things to everyone, so that I might gain everyone.” For if he had fled from the storm of persecution and himself changed sides,

no one would have paid attention to his words; rather, his actions would have carried greater weight. But how, then, was he himself beheaded by Nero at the end of his life, and became an ornament and a seal [?]
of the city of the Romans? For they are unwilling to face a storm for the sake of falsehood. But those who have been found worthy of the grace of truth through the Holy Spirit
surrender even their bodies to the persecutor, so that in this way they may preserve for themselves their original confession of Jesus.
And when they say, “We are the chosen,” they cite the Gospel’s statement: “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

And again, in this they appear to be remarkable zealots for their master’s [?]. For before the true choosing, which our Lord foretold that he would carry out at his second coming, these people, outside the hope of the truth, have shown themselves consistently chosen for wickedness.
Along with these things, they also say, “What do you say about this, that the apostle himself plainly cries out, ‘I see another law in my bodily members, fighting against the law of my mind

and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my bodily members’?” “See,” they say, “how he acknowledges the opposition and conflict within us, arising from the mixture of good and evil.” They put forward these [?], and against them

They launch arrows. For the apostle himself first praises the Law and says beforehand, “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person.” If, then, he calls [?] the Law the law of God, where

can Mani’s blasphemy against the Law be placed? And again, if there are opposing laws, belonging both to God and to Matter, why does the Good One pointlessly set up an evenly matched struggle against evil? For an evenly matched struggle
involves a war that never ends. Not even after much toil and exhaustion can the opposing parties come to peace. And what law of sin could Matter, which knows nothing, have established?

But apparently they speak in their madness, or grope like blind people without knowing. For how can they attain insight into and understanding of the divine Scriptures when they are full of the folly of madness [?]?

What the blessed apostle sets forth through the words placed before us is as follows. His discourse was addressed to Jews who were contending beyond all measure on behalf of the Law in order to abolish faith. He wished, in a remarkable way, to reprove them,
so that they might ascend and rise to something superior to the commandments of the Law—I mean, to faith. But so that this may be clearly understood: the Law was given to the Jews because faith
in God was not in them. For faith, rather, lays down a law; a law is not laid down for it. By itself it discovers what pleases God and does not learn it from outside. Now

faith in God is knowledge of God through visible created things and natural reasoning, together with love and devotion toward him, with the natural knowledge of virtue and evil that is pleasing to God.

Therefore, those who, because they are buried in the [?] of desires through their voluntary sins, give faith no place within themselves, need to learn from outside what those who possess faith know from themselves and within themselves.
Yet when they hear such commandments concerning the knowledge of God and virtue, if they do not, through

what they hear, come to love the one who commanded them things suited to their benefit, and draw and seize for themselves some faith and love toward him, and learn that they are acting wrongly and sinning

through the instruction they receive when they hear the commandment of the Law, they will not reject these things, nor will they greatly desire to leave behind the pleasure of sins. For a word heard from outside,
without an awareness accompanied by feeling and love on the part of those being instructed, is always liable to be ineffective. Perhaps what was spoken by the prophet may help with this:

“If you do not believe, neither will you understand.” Since, therefore, the Jews were in this condition, the Law was given to them as to people who did not believe. For the law is not laid down for the righteous.
And again, because faith and love toward God were not in them, they persisted in ignorance and wrongdoing.
For faith produces righteousness and love of God. When this is absent, the commandments concerning virtue are weak.
“What help and benefit, then,” someone may perhaps say, “did the Law provide?” Did it not turn away from evil those who were trained by it? It provided this first good service: it prepared
those who were in an evil condition. For it exposed the sin that had been hidden. Once this was exposed and became manifest, there was hope of change.
For even an illness in the body does not go away completely as long as it remains hidden. But when it is revealed, it receives the care appropriate to it.

So too the habit of sins, which over a long period had previously escaped the awareness of knowledge because it was buried in desires—for, because of the mind’s corruption, it could not even perceive the evil things
it was doing, nor did it even know that they were evil. It had been so gripped by habit that it even altered the natural conception of things. But the Law

that was laid down awakened knowledge and understanding, and also awakened the faculties of perception inherent in its nature, so that it might now proceed toward discerning things according to their own nature, approach them and see, and then also know
what virtue is and what evil is. Thus it became a great help and an initial benefit to those who lacked awareness.

He had anticipated them in the giving of the law, for it was about this that he said, “But the law came in so that sin might increase.” This was not so that sin would become greater through addition or causation, but because it was hidden,

so that it might be revealed. “But where sin increased, there grace abounded.” For the location of the sore was discovered, so that, once exposed, it could be healed. In this way this too was revealed, though it had not been known.
Nor would it have been grace, even if it had previously forgiven sins many times, unless this very thing had first been condemned by the law. Necessarily, then, grace was preceded by
the law itself, so that it might explain beforehand the gift belonging to grace itself.

This, then, is the whole benefit that comes from the law, and such is its character. But because the Jews were always without faith at the giving of the law [?], and were continually instructed, yet never approached

the acceptance of the truth, see now what blessed Paul does in this passage of Scripture before us. In his discourse he takes on the character of a man who lives under the law without faith, who knows

now, through those external commandments, that injustice and transgression of the law are evil, but because of the prior hold of habit is not moved to depart from sin. He says, “For I know that the law is spiritual,
but I am fleshly.” Who, then, is this “I”? It is not Paul, who wrote this, but the person in whose character he wrote, who is under the law and is still sold to sin. By being sold,
he means habit and its prior hold. For this being sold does not belong to nature; rather, it is something that comes in from outside. “For I do not do what I want.”
What, then, is this? It is what the law commands. “Instead, I do what I hate.”
This is what the law rejects. So I hate it because I have learned through the law that it is evil, but I do it because I am overcome, because I have learned through the law that it is evil,
but I do it because I am overcome by habit. “But if I do what I do not want, I declare that the law is good.” For if [?] I do not want to, because through
the law I have learned that it is evil, but I do it because I am overcome by habit. “But if I do what I do not want, I declare that the law is good.” For if
[?] he says, “I do not want to sin,” then, as it were, behind sin’s back, I openly side with the law as something excellent and helpful. “But now it is no longer I who do it,
but sin that lives in me.” For it has been there a long time and claims the place as its own.
Through the old habit established in me, it overcomes the external teaching of the law that stands against it. For healing from outside is not the same as undoing and changing from within,
unless another, good impulse springs up and grows within through faith, and we drive the long-established habit of sin out of its dwelling.

Again, he adds afterward, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person.” This means: I agree with it, I choose those very things, and its commandments are acceptable to me in my mind itself.
For this is the inner person who has now been instructed about virtue and evil, enough to know them, but not so as to choose. But because, without faith,
I know the help of the law, yet I am overcome by the habit of sin. “For I see another law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind.” Thus, in my mind itself I am healthy,

but in my long-established habits I am sick. He says “in my members” because of the bodily character of desire and sin. He says that it “wages war” and “takes me captive.” For once I recognize that the commandments of the law are good, I am again led into slavery and stolen away to the law of sin.

For the habit that has taken hold and become established over a long time is stronger than any law that existed. He says “in my members” because it is through them that sin is carried out. For it does not merely

entice from outside, nor does it lead by force. But because it has held on for a long time, it is, he says, no different from compulsion. Appropriately, then, he adds afterward, “I am a wretched person!”
Who is this “I”? It is not the one who said, “I have run the great contest, finished my race, and kept my faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is kept for me,
which my Lord will give me on that day.” Who, then, is it? Rather, it is the person who performs the slavery of the law without faith, in order to deny.
For the Jews to come out into the faith of the gospel and not always remain like children under a lawgiver. “I am miserable,” the man says. For upon the miserable man, harshly, at times,
they lay the yokes of the law, and he longs to carry them out. At other times, the old man within us, with his bodily sins, is dragged before him [?]. “And I have no way out. For I know what is good,

but I do not carry it out completely. Who, then, will rescue me from this body of death—of death? Unless,” he says, “a powerful goodness dawns within me, the body itself, through bodily passions, brings before me death

of condemnation, establishing it in my nature.” He calls it a “body of death,” not because of this common death, but because of the death that comes from condemnation and is fitting if the things of sin persist. He,

however, says, “Who will rescue me from this body?” not so that he might live without a body on this earth, which is impossible. For he is not protesting against the formation of our nature, but seeking to put off

the habit of sin practiced through the body, and to be rescued—not from the body, for how could he be rescued from that with which he lives?—but from what has taken hold through it. This is something else, outside the body's formation, which entered

through it and previously [?]. Because he knows that it can be healed and that he can be freed from it, since it took hold not by nature but through an evil choice, he says, “Who will rescue me?” But as for how he himself

can be rescued, he says, “If a great goodness drives out the evil that came before [?], who, then, will rescue me, except the grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ?” This is so that he may give thanks for the grace

of the new covenant, as though addressing the Jews who had not yet believed in Christ. How, then, and in what manner did he give thanks for grace? Clearly, it was by recognizing the grace that comes through Christ:

“For he became my teacher of faith in place of the commandment of the law, and made and prepared me to be a lawgiver to myself. I have come to be above the commandments, and I do not need to listen like
the Jews; instead, I give laws to others, like Moses. Nor do I hear from outside and then incur condemnation through disobedience. Rather, from within I conceive and give birth to a good intention.

And I become righteous like Abraham. For these are mine: faith and the love of God, which was added to me along with a good intention in agreement with it. I have acquired excellent possessions that are easy to obtain.”

He then adds, “There is therefore no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,” who do not walk according to the flesh. For through faith and the love of God they conquered and drove out what had been troubling

them through the passions of the body. For he says, “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed us.” And what is the law of the Spirit? It is not the one conveyed inward through hearing; rather, through faith it exists and dwells in the heart itself,
as in the statement made previously about those who believe in Christ: “I will put my law in their hearts.”
But he says, “It has freed us from the law of sin,” not from the law established by God, the law in which the one who admires it rejoices. He does not call this
“the law of sin,” but rather the one of which he says, “But I see another law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive
to the law of sin that is in my members.” For, like a law, as I said before, that habit had taken hold in the members of the body through bodily sins. He said that Christ, through
faith, had freed him from it. He had been miserable and unable to live in full conformity with God's law because he lacked faith and love toward him. He then adds an explanation concerning
all these things and says, “For what the law could not do, because it was weak through the body.” And in what respect was the law weak through the body? Because it did not change the body's desires,
since it did not bring faith, because those being instructed were unable to receive anything more. “Therefore, what the law could not do, because it was weak through the body,”
God himself did: “He sent his Son in the likeness of a sinful body.” For because he took a body but kept that body without sin, he therefore says “in the likeness,” and not simply “in a sinful body.”

And he says that in this way he condemned sin. From then on, his very fellowship with us put the bodily passions to death through faith. And he says that henceforth we ought to advance and rise from the law to faith.

And from Moses to Jesus, the truth; and from Judah to Christ; and from the written text to the Spirit, so that we do not remain under the commandments of the law, without love for God and faith, and find ourselves driven by force, as though under restraint.
For he says that when we love God, we will have no need of laws. How, then, are we to love him? If we believe the gospel and learn how God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh
to us, we will love him, cherish him all the more, love him, and die for him. For love of him we will not spare even our own natural body, much less any desire that is temporary.
In this way, then, the blessed apostle spoke with care against the Jews.
But Mani uses those mysteries to construct his manifest error. We, however, if we are to do so, are prepared to explain them one by one.
Of those passages from the divine Scriptures that Mani's followers draw upon in error, another written work would be required of us to pursue them. Therefore, from those that are most pressing,

we will explain one or two statements on which they rely without justification. Thus we will consider that, by analogy with these, we have also sufficiently exposed their wicked treatment of the others.
For as for that other passage of the apostle, which they shamelessly exploit, who would not be astonished at it on learning about it? For Paul himself, most earnestly and with his whole soul,

developed his argument about the resurrection of the dead, and with many testimonies and demonstrations confirmed faith in the resurrection [?] of everyone. And the whole life of virtue and reverence for God,
he says, is altogether empty if this teaching about the coming to life of the dead is not true.
Because of some small ambiguity they found in the statements about this, they set aside the whole lengthy discourse and retained only two statements that contain an ambiguity

and require explanation. These they kept for themselves, saying, 'The apostle himself expressly declared: “But this I say, my brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption
inherit what is incorruptible.” Therefore,' they say, 'there is no resurrection of the dead.' They neither consider the meaning of the preceding passages, in which much was said, nor do they

go on to what was said afterward. Instead, like people who are unjust in disputes over matters [?], they choose to keep in mind what they themselves prefer—their own wickedness, rather than righteousness.
For the apostle had already said, 'Whether, then, it was I or they, this is what we preached, and this is what you believed. But if Christ is proclaimed as having risen from the dead,
how can some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?' And again: 'If it is only in this life that we have hoped in Christ, we are more pitiable than all people.

But now, look: Christ has risen from the dead and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For just as death came through a human being, so also the coming to life of the dead comes through a human being.

For just as in Adam we all die, so in Christ we will all live. But each person in his own place: Christ the firstfruits, and afterward those who belong to Christ at his coming, and then the end.' And along with these statements, he afterward

speaks with demonstrations, as though answering the question of those who do not believe: 'Someone will say, “How are the dead raised, and with what body will they come?”' And, as though replying to this foolish person, he says,
'You are a fool! The seed you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And what you sow is not what emerges with its stalk, but a bare grain of wheat or of some other seed.
And God gives it a body as he wishes.' Through these demonstrations, which take place every day, he awakens the minds of those who doubt to an awareness of God's power, for whom everything is easy.
Then, because it is reasonable to raise this objection—that those who rise will once again be held by those same bodily experiences, by desires and pains, by comforts and afflictions,

if they receive the very same body—he then, aptly and wonderfully, cures this objection and replaces it with the truth through what follows in his discourse. For this is what he says: 'This I say, my brothers:
flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit what is incorruptible.' How, then, does he say that the body rises, if flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God

They can [?]. Once the body has risen, the body is no longer subject to suffering, as he says, nor is it a dense physical body that is again governed through blood and subject to suffering. For this reason he next brings forward a clear explanation of this difficulty.
For he says, “This is a mystery: we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.” Thus there is a change for those who are alive at the resurrection.

What is given to us through the change is a superior physical body, no longer flesh and blood weighed down by the weakness of suffering. For not everything that is a physical body is necessarily also flesh. The sun, the moon, and the whole heavenly order—

all these are physical bodies, and they are not flesh at all. He says that our body, when it rises, takes on something of this likeness, so that the souls of the saints may dwell in their bodies. And from then on it no longer

needs bodily nourishment, nor does it fall prey again to desires, distress, and pain. Rather, it is more fully in harmony with the soul in all its worship and divine service, and it no longer opposes it in any way.
For the struggles cease, since the soul has passed into rest at God's command.
And because through these statements he has clarified his whole argument, he also explains the manner of the resurrection, saying, “In the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise
imperishable, and we shall be changed. For this perishable thing is destined to put on imperishability, and this mortal thing to put on immortality.”

If, then, what is perishable puts on imperishability, the statement that corruption does not inherit what is imperishable is true. For if someone were to say that the flesh rises and lives again together with the passions inherent in it,
and that it experiences and performs those very same things together with the soul, this would be a statement containing no good hope.

But if this is a change, it receives a superior and blessed condition. He makes this very point clear by way of demonstration, saying, “This perishable thing is destined to put on imperishability.” And the soul's instrument, with which it labored, is justly restored to it.
This is not, however, for loss again, or for toil and weariness, but so that the souls of those who live may enjoy blessedness, receiving their bodies, which dwell with them.
These are no longer full of heaviness, earthliness, and fleshly desire, as they were at the beginning, at the time when it was fitting for them to distinguish themselves in the struggles for virtue.
Thus the apostle clarifies the teaching about the resurrection through many statements and introduces an account of the blessedness associated with it.
But they go astray in the opposite direction, and through statements made about the resurrection they deny the resurrection.
Either they attribute weakness to God, as is their custom—for this is what they do throughout their entire discourse, everywhere granting superiority to that evil which has no existence—
or they charge him with injustice, if the body that labored together with the soul in its conduct here is not to be restored to it and share its enjoyment of gifts and victories.
But because in other places in his letters the apostle also makes many statements that provide, as it were, an occasion for considering these matters, when he speaks about the devil,
saying that God leaves him unattended because of his wonderful providence, as in the statements already mentioned and other remarkable matters, whoever examines the force of these words in his mind

understands and perceives that they do not at all indicate some other self-existent sovereignty without a beginning. On the contrary, they indicate that he is subject to God, and that God continues to inflict upon him the punishment

he deserves, and that whatever this being is thought to do and is able to do depends on our own will. Such is the statement, “You too, who were dead in your offenses and sins, in which you formerly conducted yourselves,

according to the course of this world and according to the ruler of the authority of the air and [?], which is now at work in the children of disobedience. Among them we too all formerly lived in the desires

of our flesh, doing the will of our body and our thoughts.” For is it not clear that, by calling them dead through sins arising from stumbling, he rules out the compulsion of every opposing sovereignty?
For the stumbling that brings a fall belongs to someone who was standing, and it is recognized as involving contempt. A stumbling fall does not belong to someone who has never stood. And he adds,
“in your sins,” and they are blamed for them because the sins were their own. For they would not have been blamed in the first place if they had committed these acts under some compulsion.

What compulsion, then, comes from a self-existent primordial principle? He goes on to say, “In which you formerly walked,” indicating that their turning was voluntary, although Mani had not even appeared, as if
in a dream, in the world at that time. For it must be one of two things: either knowledge was reserved for this man, in accordance with the madness of his falsehood, and this testimony
of the apostle is entirely invalid concerning those who at that time felt remorse and repented, escaping from error; or healing came in vain to those who turned
to God through the apostle’s teaching. His statement is as conclusive as possible: clearly, they could even have been the ancestors of this man’s ancestors. And the apostle rightly says,
“In which you formerly walked, according to the course of this world.” For it is in this world that the things belonging to error have their time.
They cease along with the ages, which cease along with the world. And he says, “According to the ruler of the authority of the air.”
For he is the ruler of those who have inclined toward sins of their own will, and he is their helper. But he says “the authority of the air” because neither above
nor below does he have any dominion or kingdom. For he is not permanently lord of creation, nor of our will. He is lord only if we wish it.
“Among whom we too all formerly lived.” Notice how he also includes himself in repentance along with the others, so that sin is not firmly fixed in any place at all.
Everywhere he finds fault with the will, not with a primordial principle. Rather, he presents the devil as a helper who inflamed the voluntary inclination toward sins.

For what prevented him from saying openly and declaring clearly that he is not the ruler of the authority of the air, but the ruler of all the worlds, according to this man’s fable, confused though it is? Rather, he also clearly

indicates that the evil one becomes evil by his own will, and is not evil through the compulsion of his nature. He also indicates concerning us that we take the first step voluntarily, on our own initiative, in wishing to sin [?]. Then, afterward, he too becomes our helper.
He says, “That which is now at work in those who are disobedient.” All disobedience is a voluntary turning away from what is rightly said. For someone who does not have
the ability to oppose what is said—how can an accusation of disobedience be brought against him? He goes on to say, “Among whom we too all formerly lived in the desires
of our flesh, doing the will of our bodies and our thoughts, and we were children of wrath.” Notice, then, how he finds fault with those who do the will of the body,
and not with the body itself, since the direction of its natural impulses is in their hands. “We were doing the will of our body and our thoughts.” Through “body” he indicated those who act,

and through “thoughts” he showed that they act by their own free choice, apart from all compulsion. He says, “We were children of wrath,” not of self-existent matter, but of wrath, because we were doing things

that [?] wrath. In saying that we were children of wrath, he indicates, according to ordinary common usage, that our will itself was subject to such [?]. Thus he clearly finds fault with all these things as arising from
the will, just as, much later, he writes to these same people: “Therefore, let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children

who are disobedient.” Again, he calls them children of disobedience, not of a beginningless primordial principle. “Therefore, do not become their partners. For you were darkness, but now you are light

in our Lord.” For if he were naming something on the basis of its essential being, rather than its voluntary actions—whether the evil one or the ruler of the authority of the air and of the spirit—how could the very same people be darkness at one time,
and become light at another? For if they were once that darkness which this man falsely describes to no purpose—for it does not exist—and yet they became light
in our Lord, has darkness, then, changed into light? But it is clear that all the Scriptures give rational beings names drawn from comparisons, just as our Lord also said to Peter,

“Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood have not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.” Yet when, a little later, he said something showing a lack of faith, he said to that very same man, “Get behind me, Satan.”
And because of the resemblance of his words, he gave this name to the one whom he had blessed a little earlier.
105. We too are accustomed, when someone asks us what a human being is, to give a single description of the whole human being, defining, as far as possible, what his nature is.
But if we are asked what a particular person is like, we describe him from his likeness, which we think we know through experience, just as also those to whom
the apostle wrote that they were once darkness—not in their own being, for darkness has no independent being at all, but in their will, because of their ignorance of the truth of God,

which arose from their contempt. They then became light—not that they were changed into the nature of light, but that they were educated and raised to the knowledge of the truth. Likewise, the blessed Simon Peter was called Satan,
although he was not Satan, because of an unbelieving statement. So too, in calling a human being evil or a devil, he does not accuse him with reference to his own being, but from the likeness
of his will he gives him this name. Thus there is no evil being whose nature is opposed to God, but opposing wills that are forcibly contrived and introduced.
They also rush to the statement that he made: their struggle was not against flesh and blood, but against rulers, against authorities, and against the world-rulers of this darkness,
and against the evil spirits beneath heaven. Through these words the blessed apostle himself prepares those who are anointed for the contests of the fear of

God to be very diligent. For this reason he first said, “From now on, be strengthened in our Lord and in the power of his [?], and put on the armor of God, so that you can stand against the schemes of the evil one.”

After these words he says that their struggle was not against flesh and blood. If, then, the evil one comes with schemes, chooses a time suitable for his deceit, and contrives an appearance of our piety,

so that what he does may thus be easily concealed, how is it not with an evil intention and thought that he makes his approach? And if he knows that he is deceiving and drawing others toward evil, and this depends—
as we also said earlier—clearly on his envy, since through what is superior he comes to know that it is superior, and because of his great wickedness he cannot possess this,

then it is clear from this that he himself is by no means blameless. For if he were evil in his being and nature, he would not even know what he was, nor would he know that the one opposed to him was better than he.

Therefore, because he was speaking about the skill and schemes of his [?], directed toward deceit and harm, so that no one should suppose that by vigilance [?] alone he could stand against him, he says, “Put on
the armor of God”—clearly meaning faith, fear, and worship through the Holy Spirit. For it is not by using bodily armor that a person escapes his deceits. He also lists against

whom the struggle is, so that no one might suppose that in the wilderness he has no adversary, become overconfident, and be caught and defeated. He lists rulers, authorities, and the world-rulers of this darkness,
because the devil too arranged his own order, after the likeness of those above, through those who rebelled with him. For it is clear how he joined with many and became the head of the rebellion.
For who was he, alone and on his own, to suppose that he could accomplish anything? For just as God was patient throughout all past time, when all humanity had, as it were, rebelled,
so then too he patiently bears with the devil and those with him, both for his sake and for the sake of the providential arrangement that has been mentioned.
Human beings thus received repentance and forgiveness because they are in the body and fell through error. But those others turned away from repentance and moved toward the rebellion
that came first, and demonstrated God's patience toward them. For they deprived themselves of God; it was not God who withdrew from them. He called them world-rulers,
not because they rule heaven, earth, water, or fire, nor because they control anything else, but only this darkness. And what is this darkness?

By way of illustration, he indicates the ignorance that prevailed among human beings. Since they held sway over this ignorance, which overflowed upon human beings throughout this world, they were called world-rulers. And as by a command

They were revealed so that fear and watchfulness would be established among human beings and they would take refuge in God. He says “under heaven,” or, as some read, “in heaven,” to show that they are not foreign to God's creation.

For although they are within the bounds of creation, they turn aside and rebel against God. He bears with them very patiently, necessarily so, just as some people bear with those who transgress the law.
They are under one authority, like all the others. Nor should the followers of Mani rely on that statement of the apostle, in which he speaks of those
